docs.title: Curated Answers (design)
docs.text:
Status: partly built

The config and its checks (PR 1), indexing and candidates (PR 2), matching and running verified queries (PR 3), the playground badge, the demo file and nl2sql curated test (PR 4), preferred tables (PR 5) and feedback proposals (PR 6) are built; see Curated answers and Datasources for how to use them. Each pull request in Implementation plan updates this page and the reference docs it touches.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Before the model plans a query, check whether the business has already provided a trusted answer to the question. If it has, run that answer and say so. If it has not, run today's pipeline unchanged.

Curated answers come in three kinds:

Kind What the data team writes Where This milestone Verified queries A SQL query with typed parameters, and the questions it answers the curated section (curated.yaml) Built Preferred tables Views or tables the planner should reach for first each datasource's preferred_tables: Built Business metrics A named expression (revenue = SUM(...)) the planner refers to by name the curated section, metrics: Designed only, deferred

A thumbs-up on a generated answer becomes a proposal for a verified query in the review queue, which a person reviews and accepts. Nothing writes curated.yaml but a person's accept (Wave B, D42: see The review queue).

docs.title: Who does what
docs.text:
• The data team writes the configuration. They know SQL, they keep config in git, and they review changes like code. They run nl2sql curated validate and nl2sql curated test in CI.
  • The person asking never sees the configuration. They ask a question and get an answer; when a verified query produced it, the answer is labelled Verified with the query's id.
  • The engine loads and validates the file at startup, indexes the questions with nl2sql index, and matches each question against them at run time.

docs.title: curated.yaml
docs.text:
Since 0.5 the verified queries are the curated section of nl2sql.yaml, usually its own file (curated: { file: curated.yaml }); see Curated Answers. The models and the checks that need the datasources are in nl2sql/config/curated.py.

The section is optional. When it is absent the feature is off and the pipeline is exactly the generated one. One section covers every datasource, keyed by datasource id.

datasources:
  chinook:
    verified_queries:
      - id: top_customers_by_revenue
        description: "Customers ranked by invoiced revenue in a calendar year"
        questions:
          - "Who are our top {n} customers by revenue in {year}?"
          - "Best {n} customers in {year}"
        params:
          n:    { type: int, default: 10, min: 1, max: 100 }
          year: { type: int, min: 2000, max: 2100, example: 2012 }
        sql: |
          SELECT c.CustomerId,
                 c.FirstName || ' ' || c.LastName AS customer,
                 c.Country,
                 ROUND(SUM(il.UnitPrice * il.Quantity), 2) AS revenue
          FROM Customer c
          JOIN Invoice i      ON i.CustomerId = c.CustomerId
          JOIN InvoiceLine il ON il.InvoiceId = i.InvoiceId
          WHERE CAST(strftime('%Y', i.InvoiceDate) AS INTEGER) = :year
          GROUP BY c.CustomerId, customer, c.Country
          ORDER BY revenue DESC, c.CustomerId
          LIMIT :n
    metrics:            # designed only; deferred
      - name: revenue
        description: "Invoiced revenue, before refunds"
        expression: "SUM(InvoiceLine.UnitPrice * InvoiceLine.Quantity)"
        table: InvoiceLine

The models, all extra="forbid" so a misspelt key is an error rather than a silently ignored one:

  • CuratedFileConfig: version: int = 1, datasources: Dict[str, CuratedDatasource].
  • CuratedDatasource: verified_queries: List[VerifiedQuery], metrics: List[MetricDefinition] (parsed and validated so the format is fixed now, but not used until metrics are built).
  • VerifiedQuery: id (a slug, unique within its datasource), description, questions (at least one), params: Dict[str, ParamSpec], sql.
  • ParamSpec: type (int, float, string, date), optional default, min/max (numbers and dates), choices (strings), and example.

example is a refinement of the agreed design: it is the value used to fill a placeholder before embedding and to run nl2sql curated test when a parameter has no default (year above). Without it a required parameter is embedded as its own name ("... in year").

docs.title: Verified queries are SQL
docs.text:
A verified query is written as SQL in the dialect of its datasource, not in the engine's internal plan format. The data team already has this SQL; asking them to translate it into PlanModel JSON would make the feature unusable.

This does not weaken the model emits a typed plan, never SQL: no model wrote this SQL. A person wrote it, reviewed it and committed it. The model's only part is to pick a query by id and supply parameter values, and those values are always bound parameters (:name, SQLAlchemy's named style, which every adapter's driver translates), never interpolated into the text. A value cannot change the shape of the query.

Nor does it break no dialect-specific SQL outside nl2sql/adapters/. That rule is about engine code, and curated.yaml is data the operator owns, like datasources.yaml. The engine never inspects the SQL by dialect name: it parses it with sqlglot using whatever adapter.get_dialect() returns.

docs.title: Preferred tables
docs.text:
Preferred tables are not in curated.yaml. They are one optional list on a datasource in datasources.yaml, because they describe the datasource and not an answer:

datasources:
  - id: chinook
    connection: { ... }
    preferred_tables: [v_customer_revenue, v_monthly_sales]

DatasourceConfig (nl2sql/datasources/models.py) gains preferred_tables: List[str] = []. The package never creates a view: the data team creates them in their own database, and nl2sql index picks them up as it picks up any table (every built-in adapter snapshots views; see Views in snapshots). A name is the bare table name or schema.table, case ignored. One that is not in the indexed schema is a warning in nl2sql doctor and the index status, not an error.

At question time a preferred table is ranked first:

  • When the schema is small enough to be passed whole (SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FULL_SNAPSHOT_MAX_TABLES, 15 by default, which covers every demo database), the schema retriever lists preferred tables first and marks them preferred ("preferred":true) in the planner's schema block, and planner instruction 14 says to plan against a preferred table when it answers the question.
  • Otherwise Retriever.retrieve_schema_context() results are re-ordered so any preferred table it found comes first, and a preferred table it missed is added when its similarity is within 0.05 (PREFERRED_MARGIN) of the least similar table picked.

Nothing about access changes: a preferred table the caller's scope denies is hidden from the planner exactly like any other.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The file is checked at three moments, each catching what it can.

At startup, Runtime.from_config checks the config's curated section after the datasources are built. A broken section fails startup with a ConfigError, as a broken datasource does. These checks need no database and no index:

  • the YAML parses and matches the models;
  • every datasource key is a configured datasource;
  • query ids are unique within a datasource;
  • every {placeholder} in a question is a declared param, and every declared param appears in at least one question;
  • the SQL parses with sqlglot in the datasource's dialect, is exactly one statement, and is read-only (see Guards);
  • the :name placeholders in the SQL (exp.Placeholder nodes) are exactly the declared params;
  • defaults, examples, min/max and choices agree with the declared type.

A section that includes a file that does not exist (curated: { file: ... }) is a config error, so startup fails rather than turning the feature off: a typo should not silently turn verified answers off in production. Leaving the section out turns the feature off.

nl2sql curated validate runs the startup checks plus the ones that need the index: every table the SQL reads (exp.Table nodes, minus CTE names) exists in the schema the datasource's live index build was made from (the snapshot its build pointer names). It prints a report table and exits non-zero on any error, modelled on nl2sql policy validate (cli/commands/policy.py). Like that command it calls a facade class, CuratedAPI (nl2sql/api/curated_api.py, exported from nl2sql), so the CLI holds no logic an SDK or REST caller would also need.

nl2sql curated test runs each verified query once against its database, with every param at its default or example value, through the same guarded execution path the pipeline uses, reading at most a few rows. A column renamed in the database then fails CI instead of failing a user. It runs as the operator, with no role, as nl2sql index does.

docs.title: Indexing
docs.text:
nl2sql index embeds each phrasing of each verified query as an entry of a new chunk type, curated.verified_query, in the existing vector store. The model is VerifiedQueryChunk(BaseChunk) in nl2sql/indexing/models.py, beside TableChunk and the others.

  • Text. The phrasing with every placeholder filled by its example or default ({n} → 10, {year} → 2012), because a raw {n} embeds poorly. The description is embedded as one more entry of the same query.
  • Metadata. {id, type: "curated.verified_query", datasource_id, query_id, schema_version}, and the build_id every entry gets. The agreed design called the key datasource; it is datasource_id, the key every other chunk, the active-build filter and index health already use.
  • Ids. Deterministic, as BaseChunk requires: curated.verified_query:<datasource_id>:<query_id>:<n>.

The entries must be written in the same build as the datasource's schema entries. A build replaces every entry of its datasource, so curated entries written on their own would be deleted by the next schema re-index, or would delete it. IndexingOrchestrator.index_datasource() therefore appends the curated chunks (built by a small CuratedChunkBuilder) to the schema chunks before it writes the build.

Changing curated.yaml does not need a schema re-index (a change from the agreed design; see Re-index cost). nl2sql index --refresh writes a new build per datasource through the same write, switch and clean-up as any other, except that every entry is rendered again from the live build's stored snapshot and the entries that did not change keep their stored vectors (IndexingOrchestrator.refresh(), 0.8; it was --curated-only and refresh_curated() before): no schema read, no model call, and only the changed entries (here the verified queries) are embedded.

Staleness. The build's pointer also records curated_hash, next to its build_id, schema_version and built_at: a SHA-256 of that datasource's section of curated.yaml, as canonical JSON. IndexHealth (nl2sql/indexing/health.py) compares it with the file as it is now and reports "curated.yaml changed for 'chinook' since it was indexed; run nl2sql index --refresh --datasource chinook". nl2sql doctor and the facade's engine.index.health() show it. Only the verified queries are hashed: metrics are not indexed yet, so editing one asks for nothing. It is a warning, not a failure: the stale entries still point at queries that exist, and the matcher re-reads every query from the loaded file, never from the index. A query id that is in the index but no longer in the file is skipped. IndexHealth gains a warnings list for this; problems stays the list that makes ok false.

docs.title: Where the step goes
docs.text:
A new node, curated_matcher (nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/curated_matcher/), becomes the graph's entry point, ahead of datasource_resolver:

flowchart TD
    Q(["Question"]) --> M{"Curated answers configured<br/>for a datasource this role may read?"}
    M -- no --> R["datasource_resolver"]
    M -- yes --> S["Vector search over curated.verified_query<br/>allowed datasources only, top K"]
    S --> F{"Best similarity at or above<br/>CURATED_MATCH_FLOOR?"}
    F -- no --> R
    F -- yes --> L["One structured-output call:<br/>pick a candidate and fill its params,<br/>or none_of_these"]
    L -- "none_of_these, or the call failed" --> R
    L -- a candidate --> P{"Params valid?<br/>type, min/max, choices, required"}
    P -- no --> R
    P -- yes --> A{"Every table the SQL reads<br/>allowed for this role?"}
    A -- no --> R
    A -- yes --> X["Run the saved SQL with bound params<br/>through the adapter, row-capped"]
    X -- failed --> R
    X -- rows --> G["layer_router"]
    G --> AG["aggregator: save the result, write the manifest"]
    AG --> AS["answer_synthesizer: reply from the 20-row preview"]
    AS --> V(["Answer, source = verified"])
    R --> D["decomposer, SQL agent, aggregator, answer_synthesizer:<br/>today's pipeline, unchanged"]
    D --> GEN(["Answer, source = generated"])

Running it before the resolver, rather than between the resolver and the decomposer, means a verified answer also skips the resolver's answerability call: a verified answer costs two model calls (the match and the reply) instead of four or more. The matcher does the one thing from the resolver it needs itself: it limits the search to datasources the role may read, Scope.reaches_datasource() for each datasource, before searching, so Datasource access is policy-gated holds on this path too and the model only ever sees candidates from readable datasources. When the caller pinned a datasource (GraphState.datasource_id), only that one is searched.

When it does not answer, the matcher returns nothing but its own trace record and the run continues at datasource_resolver as if it were not there. When the run is plan-only (execute=False) the matcher is skipped.

A refinement made in PR 3: the node is added to the graph only when curated answers are on (a curated section with at least one verified query) and the run executes. Otherwise datasource_resolver stays the entry point, so with no curated file the graph, the trace and the answer are exactly what they were before, rather than gaining a node that does nothing. The first diamond above is therefore decided once when the graph is built ("configured") and again at run time ("this role may read", not_configured).

On a match, the node fills the state the way a one-sub-query generated run leaves it, so nothing downstream needs a second code path: a DecomposerResponse with one SubQuery (its intent is the question), the ExecutionDAG from build_execution_dag(), the artifact_refs entry, and a SubgraphOutput with plan_source="verified", the SQL, row_cap, truncated and its checks as ValidationChecks. It then routes to layer_router, which finds the scan already done and sends the run to aggregator. The aggregator saves the result and writes the run's manifest (the 0.3.0 result saving and paging), and answer_synthesizer writes the reply from the preview, as today.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
1. Candidates. Retriever.retrieve_verified_query_candidates(query, datasource_ids, k) searches entries of type curated.verified_query in the live builds of the allowed datasources. It is a plain similarity search, not MMR: several phrasings of one query are exactly what should match, so the pool is fetched at k × phrasings, de-duplicated by (datasource_id, query_id) keeping each query's best cosine similarity, and cut to CURATED_MATCH_TOP_K (5). The search is recorded with the same record mmr_search() writes, so the trace and the playground's retrieval view can show it. If no allowed datasource has a verified query, there is no search and no embedding call.
  2. Floor. If the best similarity is below CURATED_MATCH_FLOOR (0.6), the run falls back with no model call.

  3. Choice. One structured-output call, through the existing structured(llm, schema) in nl2sql/llm/wires/, which every provider and keyless replay already support. The prompt presents the candidates like tools: a qualified id (chinook.top_customers_by_revenue, since ids are unique only within a datasource), the description, and each param with its type, bounds, choices and default; plus the option none_of_these. The model is told to pick a candidate only when it answers the whole question as asked, and otherwise to pick none_of_these. The schema is fixed, so its name on the wire is fixed:

    class ParamValue(BaseModel):
    name: str
    value: str          # typed and checked by code, step 4

class VerifiedQueryChoice(BaseModel):
    """Pick the verified query that answers the question, or none_of_these."""
    query_id: str       # a candidate id, or "none_of_these"
    params: List[ParamValue] = Field(default_factory=list)
    reason: str = ""

    Params are a list of name/value strings rather than a per-query schema so that one schema serves every candidate set (a dynamic schema would change the tool on the wire from run to run, which replay keys on) and so no provider's strict-schema rules about open objects apply. The prompt puts the question after a User Query: line, a marker extract_question() in nl2sql/llm/replay.py already recognises, so a recording can key this call on the question like the decomposer's. The node's model is configured like any other step's: LLM_AGENTS in nl2sql/llm/providers.py gains "curated_matcher": "curatedmatcher", and PIPELINE_STEPS in nl2sql/pipeline/steps.py gains the step.

    The model never sees every verified query, only the top K for this question, and never sees the SQL. 4. Params. Code, not the model, decides whether the values are usable: an unknown name, a value that does not parse as the declared type, a number or date outside min/max, a string outside choices, or a required param (no default) left empty all fall back. A param the model left out takes its default. 5. Access. Every table the SQL reads (sqlglot exp.Table nodes, CTE names excluded) must pass Scope.allows() with its schema (the datasource's default schema when the SQL names none), the scope the logical validator and executor already ask. If one does not, the run falls back, and the normal pipeline then enforces the policy as it always does. The user is not told a verified query exists that they may not use. 6. Run. The saved SQL runs with the bound params through SqlExecutorService and the adapter, the result is saved to the artifact store, and the run continues at layer_router as described above. If execution fails, the run falls back with a warning; the failure is in the trace for the data team, and nl2sql curated test is how they catch it before a user does.

Every fallback has a reason code in the matcher's trace record: not_configured, no_candidates, below_floor, none_of_these, model_failed, unknown_query, param_invalid, param_missing, policy_denied, capability_missing, execution_failed. A fallback is never an error of the run.

docs.title: Worked examples
docs.text:
All on the demo's Chinook database, with the query in the example above.

(a) A match. "Who were our top 5 customers in 2012?" as analyst. The best candidate is top_customers_by_revenue (the phrasing "Best 10 customers in 2012" is close), above the floor. The model picks it with n=5, year=2012. Both are ints within bounds; Customer, Invoice and InvoiceLine are allowed for analyst. The SQL runs with {"year": 2012, "n": 5} bound and returns Richard Cunningham (25.84), João Fernandes (24.77), Fernanda Ramos (24.75), Joakim Johansson (24.75) and Mark Taylor (22.77). The answer carries source = {type: "verified", id: "top_customers_by_revenue", params: {n: 5, year: 2012}}.

(b) A near miss. "Top 5 customers by number of tracks bought in 2012." The same query is the best candidate and clears the floor, but it ranks by revenue, not by tracks. The model sees the description and picks another candidate that does rank by tracks if one exists, or none_of_these. With none_of_these the run continues at the resolver and the answer is generated, source = {type: "generated"}.

(c) A missing or out-of-range value. "Who are our top customers by revenue?" matches, but year has no default and the question gives none: the model leaves it empty and the run falls back (param_missing). Asking the user "which year?" belongs to the later Conversation milestone. "Top 500 customers in 2012" matches with n=500, beyond max: 100, and falls back (param_invalid); the generated pipeline then answers it under its own row limit.

(d) No access. The same question as (a), asked as viewer, whose policy allows no Customer, Invoice or InvoiceLine. The candidate is found and chosen, the access check refuses Invoice, the run falls back (policy_denied), and the logical validator refuses the generated plan with the usual SECURITY_VIOLATION. The refusal is the same one viewer gets today.

docs.title: v1 limitation: one question, one query
docs.text: Matching runs once, on the whole question. A question with two parts ("top customers in 2012 and how many tickets did they open") is either not matched or matched to none_of_these, because the prompt asks for a query that answers the whole question, so it falls back to the generated pipeline. Matching each decomposed sub-query against verified queries is a later step.

docs.title: The same guards as generated SQL
docs.text:
Verified SQL runs through the guards generated SQL runs through, plus one generated SQL does not need:

  • Read-only. Generated SQL is read-only by construction (PlanModel.query_type is Literal["READ"]). Human SQL is checked instead: exactly one statement (sqlglot.parse returns one), its root is a query (exp.Query: a SELECT, a set operation, or a WITH around one), and no node anywhere in the tree is a write or DDL (Insert, Update, Delete, Merge, Create, Drop, Alter, Command). This is checked at load and again before running. The datasource's own read-only connection (SQLite always opens read-only) and database grants stay the backstop, as they are for generated SQL.
  • Policies. Every table read must be allowed for the asker (step 5 above). A view is checked by its own name, as policies name it; what the view reads underneath is the database's grant to decide.
  • Row limit. The row ceiling is the one the generator uses: min(limits.row_limit or RESULT_ROW_LIMIT, RESULT_ROW_LIMIT), from the datasource's limits. Rather than rewrite a person's SQL to add a LIMIT (which would mean rendering their placeholders back through sqlglot in every dialect), the executor stops reading the stream at the ceiling. ExecutorRequest gains max_rows; the executor's _Stream stops after that many rows and the result is flagged truncated exactly as a capped generated result is. A query whose own LIMIT :n is lower is never cut. This is a refinement of the agreed design, which named the guard but not the mechanism.
  • Result saving and paging. The result is written with artifact_store.write_batches() and the manifest by the aggregator, so paging (engine.results.page) and CSV export (engine.results.csv) work for a verified answer as for any other.
  • Time. The run is inside run_with_graph()'s GLOBAL_TIMEOUT_SEC like every node, and the datasource's limits.timeout_ms applies.

docs.title: Bound parameters through the adapter
docs.text:
The SDK already has a place for them: AdapterRequest.parameters (nl2sql_sdk/contracts.py, "Optional parameter bindings"). But no adapter reads it. SqlAlchemyAdapter.execute_sql() and execute_batches() call conn.execute(text(sql)) and drop it, and SqlExecutorService never sets it. Sending parameterised SQL to an adapter that ignores the parameters would fail at best, so it must not be sent at all. The change, inside the package boundaries:

  • SDK (pydantic and the standard library only, unchanged in that respect): a new capability, DatasourceCapability.SUPPORTS_BOUND_PARAMETERS, and a docstring on AdapterRequest.parameters saying values are bound by name to :name placeholders and never interpolated.
  • SQLAlchemy base adapter: execute() and execute_batches() pass request.parameters to conn.execute(text(sql), parameters) when there are any, and capabilities() declares the new capability. Every built-in adapter (SQLite, Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, DuckDB) inherits both. With no parameters the call is byte-for-byte today's, so generated SQL is unaffected.
  • Engine: ExecutorRequest gains parameters and max_rows; SqlExecutorService.execute() copies parameters into the AdapterRequest. The matcher checks ds_registry.supports(ds_id, DatasourceCapability.SUPPORTS_BOUND_PARAMETERS) before choosing a query with params, and falls back (capability_missing) when an adapter cannot bind; it fails closed, as SUPPORTS_SQL does. A third-party adapter opts in by binding and declaring the capability. nl2sql curated validate warns about a datasource whose adapter cannot bind.

sqlglot parses :name as exp.Placeholder in the SQLite, Postgres, MySQL, DuckDB and T-SQL dialects, which is what validation reads the placeholders from.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text:
Every answer says where it came from:

  • QueryResult (nl2sql/api/query_api.py) gains source: AnswerSource, {type: "verified", id, datasource_id, params} or {type: "generated"}. The REST API's response model, QueryResponse, subclasses QueryResult, so POST /query and the final event of POST /query/stream carry it with no change to nl2sql-api beyond its docs.
  • SubQueryResult.plan_source and SubgraphOutput.plan_source gain the value "verified", next to "llm" and "cache".
  • The trace records the matcher as a node: the candidates with their similarities, the floor, the model's choice and reason, the params after checking, and the fallback reason code if it fell back.
  • The playground shows a badge on the answer, "Verified · top_customers_by_revenue", with the params on hover. A generated answer shows no badge. Built in PR 4 beside the question, in the shape of the Recorded run label rather than next to the plan-cache line, which only Debug shows: whether an answer was verified matters to every reader. The Plan station, which has no plan to show, names the query and its values instead.

docs.title: Feedback proposals
docs.text:
Replaced in 0.8

nl2sql curated proposals export and its file writer are gone. A thumbs-up now files a verified_query proposal in the review queue, and an admin's accept writes curated.yaml (Wave B, Q1: The review queue). The section below is the 0.4 design, kept as history.

A thumbs-up on a generated answer is already stored, one row per run, in the feedback table of the state store (nl2sql/storage/sqlite.py), with the question, role, status and SQL. That row is the proposal; nothing new is stored and nothing writes curated.yaml.

nl2sql curated proposals export --out curated.proposals.yaml turns thumbs-up runs into draft verified queries in curated.yaml's shape, under the datasource the run used: an id derived from the question (a slug, _2 on a clash), a description placeholder, the question as the one phrasing, no params, and the run's SQL with its literal values, under a header telling the reviewer to replace literals with {params}/:params, drop the row-cap LIMIT the generator added, and move the entry into curated.yaml. Without --out it prints to stdout. It is modelled on nl2sql feedback export --good (feedback/drafts.py), and like it skips runs with no SQL or more than one statement, refuses to write over the config's own files (nl2sql.yaml and every file it includes), and lives in nl2sql.feedback.proposals (opt-in, imported lazily by the command). It also skips runs whose answer was already verified, runs that did not succeed, runs on more than one datasource and rows rated before the datasource was recorded, and proposes each question once per datasource, from its newest thumbs-up. Built in PR 6.

The id comes from the question rather than the trace id (the first draft of this design said proposal_<trace id prefix>) because a reviewer keeps it: how_many_customers_are_in_brazil reads as what the query is, a trace prefix does not. The description is a placeholder rather than the question, so an unreviewed entry is obvious.

Two refinements of the agreed design. First, there is no separate "approved" state: the person reviewing the exported drafts and committing them is the approval, as for gold drafts. Second, the feedback row does not record the datasource or the answer's source today, so the feedback table gains two nullable columns, datasource_ids and source, written by feedback/record.py's run_record().

curated.yaml stays the single source of truth, in git. Neither the REST API nor the playground ever writes it.

docs.title: Demo
docs.text:
nl2sql init --demo (which nl2sql demo runs the first time) writes curated.yaml with six Chinook verified queries (top_customers_by_revenue, revenue_by_year, monthly_revenue, sales_by_country, best_selling_genres, top_artists_by_tracks_sold), included by its nl2sql.yaml; NL2SQL.demo() builds the same section in code. The queries are data in datasets/chinook.py (CHINOOK_VERIFIED_QUERIES), and nl2sql index indexes their questions with the schema, so the hosted Space's image has them too. No guided question was added: two of the existing ones ("What is the total revenue per year?", "Which genre sells the most tracks?") are phrasings of verified queries, and a new guided question would have no recording.

The keyless demo replays recorded model answers, keyed on the structured-output name and the question. The matcher's call is a new name (VerifiedQueryChoice), recorded for every guided question since the recordings in cli/demo/recordings/chinook.json were made again for 0.4.0 (python scripts/record_demo_answers.py, which needs the owner's key). A guided question that matches a verified query replays verified, badge and all; the others replay the model's none_of_these and then their generated answer. A verified run never reaches the decomposer, so ReplayStore.covered() counts a question whose recorded choice picked a query as covered too.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning the curated section absent Present: curated answers are on. Absent: off. (0.4's CURATED_CONFIG and CURATED_ENABLED.) settings.curated.match_floor 0.6 Cosine similarity the best candidate must reach before the model is asked (0.4's CURATED_MATCH_FLOOR). settings.curated.match_top_k 5 Candidates shown to the model (0.4's CURATED_MATCH_TOP_K).

The floor is a similarity in the configured embedding model's space, and models spread their scores differently. PR 2 calibrated it on the local ONNX model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) with five Chinook verified queries (the example above, revenue by year, best-selling genre, tracks per artist, revenue by country) and the best candidate's similarity for 24 questions:

Questions Best similarity 12 that a verified query answers, reworded 11 between 0.713 and 0.963; "biggest spenders last year" 0.479, and to the wrong query 6 near misses ("top customers by number of tracks", "albums per artist", "revenue by month") 0.582 to 0.813 6 unrelated ("list all playlists", "media types", the weather) 0.123 to 0.438; "Which tracks have no composer?" 0.681

0.6 keeps every match the embeddings can make with a margin above 0.1, and drops five of six unrelated questions with no model call. Near misses mostly clear it, as they should: telling a near miss from a match is the model's choice (none_of_these), not the floor's. A question with no phrasing close to it, like "biggest spenders", is not rescued by any floor; another phrasing in curated.yaml is the fix. Calibration with OpenAI's embeddings is still open: it needs the owner's key.

docs.title: Invariants this touches
docs.text:
No invariant is weakened. PR 3 made these changes in invariants.md, each with its enforcement point:

  • New: Verified SQL is human-authored, read-only and parameter-bound. The model picks a verified query by id and supplies values; it never writes or edits its SQL, and values are bound, never interpolated. Enforced in the curated config model, the read-only check and the matcher.
  • SQL Generation Enforces a Row Limit Cap extends to verified SQL, through the executor's max_rows.
  • Datasource Access Is Policy-Gated gains the matcher as an enforcement point.
  • determinism.md's "the AST is checked ... before any SQL exists, on every path" becomes "on every generated path"; a verified path has no AST, and its checks are the matcher's.

invariants.md was not edited in the design PR, because its sections name enforcement points and none existed then; PR 3 added them.

docs.title: Business metrics (deferred)
docs.text:
The format is fixed in this milestone (metrics: in curated.yaml, parsed and validated), but nothing uses it yet. The sketch:

  • Each metric is indexed as the existing, so far unused, schema.metric chunk (MetricChunk in nl2sql/indexing/models.py), so schema retrieval returns the metrics a sub-query is about.
  • The planner refers to a metric by name: a new Expr kind metric with a metric_name, which, like func_name, is model text, so the logical validator must check it against the datasource's metrics before anything else reads it.
  • The validator also requires the metric's table in the plan and allowed for the role; the generator parses expression with sqlglot in the adapter's dialect and splices the expression tree in place of the reference.

This is the hardest part of the feature, which is why it waits. A metric is an aggregate, so it cannot be nested in another aggregate or used in a WHERE; its table must be joined at the right grain or the sum fans out across a one-to-many join; and the decomposer already has a MetricSpec (SubQuery.metrics) with a different meaning, so the names need sorting out first. Every rule the generator would need, the validator has to enforce first, so the planner gets a retry rather than a dead end.

docs.title: Also out of scope
docs.text:
• An MCP server exposing ask, plus one tool per verified query. The typed params are already a tool's input schema, so this is close to free once verified queries exist.
  • Per-sub-query matching, so one part of a multi-part question can be verified and the rest generated.
  • Asking a follow-up question for a missing value, instead of falling back; that is the Conversation milestone.

docs.title: Implementation plan
docs.text:
Six pull requests for verified queries and preferred tables, each written test first and each updating its docs in the same PR (this page, configuration/, the node catalog, the CLI and REST references).

1. Config, loader and nl2sql curated validate. nl2sql/configs/curated.py, ConfigManager.load_curated(), the CURATED_CONFIG and CURATED_ENABLED settings, the startup load in Runtime, the read-only and placeholder checks, CuratedAPI.validate() and cli/commands/curated.py. New page docs/configuration/curated.md; the settings table in configuration/system.md. Tests: tests/unit/test_curated_config.py (models, unique ids, placeholder and param agreement, defaults against types), tests/unit/test_curated_sql_checks.py (one statement, read-only, writes and DDL refused, CTEs, placeholders read in every built-in dialect), tests/unit/test_cli_curated_validate.py (report and exit codes, a table missing from the indexed schema), and a startup test that a broken file fails Runtime.

2. Indexing, staleness and candidates. VerifiedQueryChunk, CuratedChunkBuilder, the orchestrator writing curated chunks in the datasource's build, curated_hash:<id> in the collection metadata, IndexHealth.warnings, the doctor line, VectorStore.retrieve_verified_query_candidates() and CURATED_MATCH_TOP_K; calibrating CURATED_MATCH_FLOOR (the setting lands here, its use in PR 3); nl2sql index --curated-only. Tests: tests/unit/test_curated_chunks.py (placeholder filling, ids, metadata), tests/unit/test_vector_store_curated.py (same build as schema, a schema re-index keeps them, active-build and datasource filters, de-dup by query, the curated-only refresh), tests/unit/test_index_health_curated.py (hash changed is a warning and ok stays true), tests/unit/test_index_curated_refresh.py (a curated-only refresh reads no schema, makes no model call and keeps the schema entries).

3. The matcher and execution. The curated_matcher node and its prompt, VerifiedQueryChoice, param checks, the access check, SUPPORTS_BOUND_PARAMETERS in the SDK, parameters in the SQLAlchemy base adapter, ExecutorRequest.parameters and max_rows, the graph's new entry point and route, CURATED_MATCH_FLOOR, source on QueryResult, plan_source="verified", LLM_AGENTS and PIPELINE_STEPS, the trace record, and the invariant edits above. Tests: tests/unit/test_curated_params.py, tests/unit/test_curated_matcher.py (each fallback reason), tests/sqlalchemy_base/test_bound_parameters.py (values bound, never interpolated: a value of 1; DROP TABLE x is a value), tests/unit/test_sql_executor_max_rows.py, an entry in tests/architecture/test_boundaries.py if the SDK change needs one, tests/unit/test_pipeline_steps.py (already fails until the step is listed), and tests/e2e/test_curated_fake_llm.py, worked examples (a) to (d) end to end against Chinook with FakeLLMServer rules keyed on VerifiedQueryChoice, plus a run with no curated file whose graph and answer match today's.

4. Playground badge, demo file and nl2sql curated test. The badge in web/playground/src/, curated.demo.yaml written by the demo, CURATED_CONFIG in the env template, CuratedAPI.test() and the command. Tests: a vitest case beside results.test.js for the badge, tests/e2e/test_playground_curated_fake_llm.py, tests/unit/test_cli_curated_test.py (a renamed column fails), and the demo setup test for the new file. The owner then re-records the demo answers. Built. nl2sql curated test binds each param's default, else its example, runs the query read-only through the adapter (the static checks first, only the first batch of rows fetched) and exits 1 on any failure; CuratedAPI.test() returns the report.

5. Preferred tables. DatasourceConfig.preferred_tables, the ordering in the schema retriever for both the full-snapshot and the retrieval paths, planner instruction 14, views in the SQLAlchemy base adapter's snapshot, and the index health warning for a preferred table that is not indexed. Tests: tests/unit/test_schema_retriever_preferred.py (ordering, the preferred marker, a denied preferred table still hidden), tests/unit/test_datasource_preferred_tables.py (config, registry, warning) and tests/adapters/unit/test_snapshot_views.py (SQLite and DuckDB).

6. Feedback proposals. The two feedback columns, nl2sql.feedback.proposals, and nl2sql curated proposals export. Tests: tests/unit/test_curated_proposals.py (shape, skips, refusal to write over curated.yaml), and a store migration test for the new columns. Built.

Gold data. No existing gold entry changes. Tier 1 runs hand-written plans through the code nodes, and a verified answer has no plan, so tier 1 runs with curated answers off (it sets no CURATED_CONFIG, and PR 3 makes that explicit in evaluation/tier1.py) and needs no new entries. The verified path's own end-to-end check is the fake-LLM test in PR 3. Measuring how often real questions hit a verified query belongs to a later tier 2 run, with new entries added beside the existing ones, never in place of them.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• The floor. Is one global CURATED_MATCH_FLOOR enough, or does each embedding model need its own default? Measured on the local model in PR 2 (0.6, see Settings); OpenAI's embeddings are not measured yet.
  • Views in snapshots. Resolved in PR 5: no built-in adapter did. All five (SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, DuckDB) snapshot through the SQLAlchemy base, which read only get_table_names(). It now reads get_view_names() too, and a driver that cannot list views logs a warning and keeps its tables. PostgreSQL materialized views are still not read.
  • Re-index cost. Resolved in PR 2: a curated.yaml change must not cost a schema re-read or a model call. nl2sql index --refresh (--curated-only before 0.8) renders the entries again from the stored snapshot, keeps the stored vectors of those that did not change, embeds the verified queries and switches to the new build. A flag rather than detecting "only curated.yaml changed" on a plain nl2sql index, because knowing whether the schema changed means reading it.
  • The synthesizer's context. Resolved in PR 3: on a verified answer the answer synthesizer is given the query's qualified id and description, in a Verified Query section added to its prompt, so it can say "invoiced revenue, before refunds" rather than guess what the numbers mean. A generated answer's prompt is unchanged.

docs.title: What "deterministic" means here
docs.text:
The word is used narrowly and it does not mean "the same question gives the same answer". Model output is not reproducible. What is stable is the shape of a run:

  • Stable sub-query and DAG ids. Both are SHA-256 content hashes over canonical JSON, not counters or UUIDs (decomposer/node.py, decomposer/dag.py). The same decomposition always yields the same ids. Identical sub-queries hash alike, so a repeat takes an ordinal suffix (sq_<hash>_2) rather than sharing the first one's id.
  • Sorted layer order. The topological sort sorts each ready set and each dependent set, so the execution layers of a given DAG are fixed (execution/dag.py).
  • Fixed graph topology. The node sequence is compiled, not chosen by the model; only the retry loop varies, and only in how many times it runs.
  • Validation before generation. The AST is checked against the retrieved schema and the RBAC policy before any SQL exists, on every generated path. A verified query has no AST: its SQL is a person's, checked read-only at load and again before it runs, and the curated matcher checks its values and the role's access to every table it reads (Curated answers).

Everything else is best effort:

  • temperature defaults to 0.0 and seed=42 is pinned when the client is built (llm/registry.py). An agent configured with temperature: null sends no temperature at all, which models such as gpt-5.5 and gpt-5-mini require (they reject 0 with HTTP 400); those agents run at the model's default temperature, so their variance is higher. See LLM configuration → Temperature. The seed is sent to every provider because all three speak the OpenAI protocol, but only OpenAI interprets it, and even there it is documented as best effort; OpenRouter and Ollama ignore it. Temperature 0 is not a reproducibility guarantee either — it reduces variance, it does not remove it.
  • Vector retrieval ranking, wall-clock schema versions, artifact timestamps and retry jitter are all non-deterministic; the sections below say exactly where.

If you need a byte-identical run, record the model's responses and replay them (nl2sql/llm/replay.py); that is what the key-free demo mode is built on.

docs.title: The plan cache: determinism from the architecture
docs.text:
The model cannot be made deterministic (gpt-5.5 rejects temperature: 0, and seed is best effort), so repeat determinism comes from the pipeline instead. The AST planner is the LLM call that decides the SQL; the validator, generator and executor after it are deterministic code. A plan that passed validation and executed is therefore pinned and reused (pipeline/plan_cache.py):

  • Where it sits. At the AST planner, per sub-query. The decomposer turns the question into sub-queries, and the planner plans each one from its intent, datasource_id and the schema snapshot at schema_version. Caching there reuses exactly the output that decides the SQL, and a multi-datasource question reuses each of its sub-queries' plans independently.
  • The key. (normalised sub-query intent, run date, planner provider and model, knowledge digest, datasource_id, schema_version). Normalisation is case-folding, collapsing whitespace and stripping trailing .?!,;:, and nothing else; matching is exact, never by similarity. A sub-query without a schema_version is never cached.
  • The planner's model. The ast_planner agent's effective provider and model, as the run sees it (a caller's own choice of model for the step included). Another model may plan the same question differently, so after engine.llm.replace a plan written by the old model is never served. Its entries stay, and swapping back hits them again (LLM configuration → Replacing the LLM at runtime).
  • The glossary. The datasource's knowledge digest (Wave B, D57): a changed definition of "revenue" plans again, and swapping the glossary back hits the old entries. A plan whose planner answer carried other readings is never stored (D47).
  • The run date. The planner is told today's date (settings.pipeline.today, else the UTC date) and writes "this year" or "the last 30 days" as literal dates, so a plan made yesterday would answer for yesterday's window. Every entry is keyed on the run date, date-relative or not, because nothing in the intent or the plan says reliably which answers depend on today. A plan is therefore reused for the rest of the day it was made, or for as long as settings.pipeline.today pins the date.
  • Invalidation. Automatic through the schema version: a re-index with a changed schema registers a new version, which misses. A new day misses too. Plans for a version the store evicts are deleted with it. There is no TTL and no LRU.
  • Always re-validated. A hit replaces only the planner's LLM call (and so the refiner, which only runs after a rejected plan). The logical validator, generator and executor run on the cached plan every time, so a plan cached for admin is still refused for viewer, and a policy change applies to the next request. Only a first attempt reads the cache; a retry after a rejected plan always asks the model.
  • What is stored. Only plans that passed validation and executed without error, written by the sub-query wrapper (pipeline/graph_utils.py). A refused plan, a failed plan and a plan-only (--no-exec) run are never stored.
  • Where it is stored. The state store (storage.state): the plan_cache table of <storage.path>/state.db with the built-in sqlite store. Deleting a schema snapshot deletes the plans cached on it.
  • Controls. PLAN_CACHE_ENABLED=false turns reads and writes off (System configuration); nl2sql cache clear empties it. nl2sql demo --record turns it off so every planner answer is recorded, and nl2sql trace replay uses it only when the recorded run did.
  • Visible. QueryResult.sub_queries[].plan_source is "cache" or "llm", QueryResult.usage.plan_cache_hits counts hits (a hit adds no planner tokens), the trace's ast_planner execution shows ast_planner_response.plan_source: "cache" with no LLM calls, and the nl2sql.plan_cache.lookups counter records hits and misses (Debugging).

What the cache does not pin: the decomposer still calls the model, so a repeat hits only when the decomposer produces the same sub-query intent (after normalisation). A differently worded intent is a miss and is planned afresh. Given a hit, the SQL is identical, and so are the rows, because the generator gives every result a total row order.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Determinism matters because the pipeline composes multi-step planning, execution, and aggregation; stable identifiers and ordering are required for reproducible DAGs, consistent merges, and auditability.
  • The system implements determinism in specific places (hashing, sorting, and schema fingerprinting) but also contains explicit nondeterminism (LLM outputs, vector retrieval ranking, timestamps, random retry jitter, and external calls).
  • Scope: planning (IDs + DAG), retrieval (vector ordering), execution ordering (DAG layers), artifacts (content hashing), and state merges.

docs.title: Inputs and Identifier Stability
docs.text:
• Deterministic: Sub-query and post-combine op IDs are derived from sorted JSON payloads with SHA-256 (pipeline/nodes/decomposer/node.py).
  • Non-deterministic: GraphState.trace_id defaults to uuid.uuid4(); subgraph IDs incorporate this value (pipeline/state.py, pipeline/graph_utils.py), so identical inputs produce different IDs unless a trace ID is supplied.
  • Non-deterministic: User query interpretation depends on LLMs in the decomposer, planner, and refiner nodes. These nodes set nothing themselves; temperature (default 0.0, omitted when configured as null) and seed=42 are applied once, where the client is built in llm/registry.py, and neither makes the output reproducible (pipeline/nodes/decomposer/node.py, pipeline/nodes/ast_planner/node.py, pipeline/nodes/refiner/node.py).

docs.title: Planner and DAG Construction
docs.text:
• Deterministic: The decomposer sorts nodes and edges by IDs and roles before constructing the DAG, so the same decomposition always gives the same layers (pipeline/nodes/decomposer/dag.py).
  • Deterministic: DAG layers are computed with a topological sort that sorts ready nodes and dependents, yielding stable layer ordering given the same node/edge sets (execution/dag.py).
  • Non-deterministic: The AST planner is LLM-driven; the PlanModel content is not stabilized inside the node (pipeline/nodes/ast_planner/node.py).
  • Deterministic (conditional): Once a sub-query's plan has validated and executed, the plan cache pins it: the same normalised intent, datasource and schema version, on the same run date, with the same planner model and the same glossary (its knowledge digest), reuse that plan without a planner call, and it is validated again on every use (see The plan cache).
  • Deterministic: Generated SQL always has a total row order. The generator always appends LIMIT, so it also orders by every selected column: after the plan's own ORDER BY terms, the remaining selected columns follow as ascending tie-breakers, in select order. Aliased items are ordered by alias, never by position, and constants are skipped. Given the same plan and data, a truncated result is always the same rows in the same order (pipeline/nodes/generator/node.py).

docs.title: Retrieval Ordering and Chunk Selection
docs.text:
• Non-deterministic: Vector retrieval uses max marginal relevance search; ranking and ties depend on vector store behavior and similarity scores, with no secondary deterministic tie-breaker in code (indexing/retrieval.py).
  • Deterministic: With one datasource registered, or an explicit datasource_id, the resolver runs no vector search. Its answerability prompt lists datasources sorted by id with sorted keys and sorted tables, so it is byte-identical across questions up to the trailing question.
  • Deterministic: With more than one datasource, the candidates come from an exact ranking of every datasource entry (cosine similarity, ties by entry id), not Chroma's approximate search, so the same index and question give the same candidates. Once chosen, and narrowed to those the answerability verdict names, they are sorted by id, and the decomposer's datasource block (description and sorted, capped table names per datasource) is byte-identical whatever order the search returned them in (pipeline/nodes/datasource_resolver/node.py).
  • Non-deterministic: Schema retrieval builds the table/column set from vector retrieval metadata and uses dictionary/set iteration without sorting; final relevant_tables ordering follows input ordering (pipeline/nodes/schema_retriever/node.py).
  • Partially deterministic: Table chunk column names are sorted for the table chunk payload, but chunk emission order depends on the schema contract’s insertion order (no sorting over tables.items() or columns.items() for column chunks) (indexing/chunk_builder.py).

docs.title: Schema Authority and Versioning
docs.text:
• Deterministic: Schema fingerprints are computed from sorted tables, columns, and foreign keys with JSON serialization; same schema contract yields the same fingerprint (schema/fingerprint.py).
  • Deterministic: Snapshots are immutable. Storing a snapshot whose contract and metadata match a stored one returns that version and writes nothing; any other snapshot is a new version (storage/sqlite.py).
  • Non-deterministic: Schema versions are time-based (YYYYMMDDhhmmss_<hash8>). Which version is live is decided by the index's build pointer, not by time (storage/sqlite.py, indexing/orchestrator.py).
  • Deterministic (conditional): If schema_version is provided by a sub-query, schema retrieval resolves that exact snapshot; otherwise it uses the latest available version, which is time-ordered (pipeline/nodes/schema_retriever/node.py).

docs.title: Validation Gates
docs.text:
• Deterministic: Logical validation normalizes names, validates aliases, and uses sorted comparisons for expected schema/alias matching (pipeline/nodes/validator/node.py).
  • Deterministic: Policy enforcement uses explicit namespaced checks and deterministic set membership (pipeline/nodes/validator/node.py).

docs.title: DAG Execution Order and Node Sequencing
docs.text:
• Deterministic: Aggregation executes layer-by-layer in DAG order, with ordered inputs computed by role rank and node ID, and terminal nodes sorted by ID (aggregation/aggregator.py).
  • Deterministic: Router selects the next scan layer based on the DAG layers and existing artifact refs (pipeline/graph_utils.py, pipeline/routes.py).

docs.title: Subgraph Composition and Routing
docs.text:
• Deterministic: Subgraph selection has a single outcome -- sql_agent when the datasource declares supports_sql, otherwise no subgraph (pipeline/graph_utils.py).
  • Deterministic (conditional): Scan payloads and subgraph outputs are built from explicit state fields; content is deterministic given the input state (pipeline/graph_utils.py).

docs.title: Retry Mechanisms and Backoff
docs.text:
• Non-deterministic: Retry backoff includes random jitter; sleep time is a function of random.uniform and wall-clock timing (pipeline/subgraphs/sql_agent.py).
  • Deterministic (conditional): Retry routing decisions depend on current retry count and error retryability flags; deterministic if state is unchanged (pipeline/subgraphs/sql_agent.py).

docs.title: Artifact Storage and Hashing
docs.text:
• Deterministic: Artifact content hashes are computed from a sorted JSON payload (columns, row_count, path), giving stable hashes for the same payload (execution/artifacts/store.py).
  • Non-deterministic: Artifact refs include created_at=datetime.utcnow(); this is time-based and changes for each creation (execution/artifacts/store.py).
  • Deterministic (conditional): Upload paths are deterministic given tenant_id and request_id, but the request ID origin is external to this module (execution/artifacts/store.py).

docs.title: State Mutation and Merge Semantics
docs.text:
• Deterministic: Decomposer returns sorted sub-queries, combine groups, and post-combine ops by ID to stabilize downstream ordering (pipeline/nodes/decomposer/node.py).
  • Potentially non-deterministic: GraphState merges dict fields with a last-write-wins reducer and concatenates lists; in parallel branches, merge order is not constrained in this code (pipeline/state.py).

docs.title: Hashing/Fingerprinting
docs.text: • Deterministic: Stable hashing is consistently performed with sorted JSON and fixed separators for sub-query IDs, schema fingerprints, and artifact content hashes (pipeline/nodes/decomposer/node.py, schema/fingerprint.py, execution/artifacts/store.py).

docs.title: Time-Based Logic and Runtime Controls
docs.text:
• Non-deterministic: Schema versions and artifact creation timestamps are derived from wall-clock time (storage/sqlite.py, execution/artifacts/store.py).
  • Deterministic (conditional): Pipeline timeout handling is based on monotonic time; timeouts and cancellations depend on wall-clock progression and runtime scheduling (pipeline/runtime.py).

docs.title: External Calls
docs.text:
• Non-deterministic: LLM-driven nodes (decomposer, planner, refiner) invoke external LLMs. The client is pinned to seed=42 and the configured temperature (0.0 unless an agent sets temperature: null) in llm/registry.py, which narrows the variance without eliminating it (pipeline/nodes/decomposer/node.py, pipeline/nodes/ast_planner/node.py, pipeline/nodes/refiner/node.py).
  • Non-deterministic: Vector store retrieval depends on external embeddings and search behavior (indexing/retrieval.py).
  • Non-deterministic: SQL execution delegates to external executors and underlying databases, which can return different results across time or state (pipeline/nodes/executor/node.py).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Failure in this system is represented as structured PipelineError objects accumulated in graph state, explicit exceptions that short-circuit a node/subgraph, or runtime timeouts/cancellations handled by the orchestrator. Most node failures are captured and returned in state rather than raising, so the graph can continue unless routing logic or wrappers explicitly stop or crash. Recovery is limited to a local retry loop inside the SQL agent subgraph, and to parse-and-retry inside each structured LLM call (an answer that does not parse is asked for again, up to the agent's parse_retries, then MODEL_OUTPUT_INVALID; see Parse-and-retry); there is no graph-level replay or global retry.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
• Missing or invalid configuration raises during context construction (e.g., missing vector store path or collection name), preventing pipeline startup.
  • Explicit datasource overrides fail if the datasource is unknown or not allowed, returning SECURITY_VIOLATION or INVALID_STATE.
  • Missing LLMs for specific nodes (e.g., refiner) return MISSING_LLM errors.
  • A model provider refusing or failing a call (rejected key, rate limit, quota, timeout, outage, unknown model) returns a fatal PROVIDER_* error from whichever LLM node made the call, in place of that node's own failure code below. See provider failures.

docs.title: Retrieval
docs.text:
• Vector store calls are wrapped by VECTOR_BREAKER; breaker open or retrieval errors propagate into resolver or schema retriever.
  • Resolver returns SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED if no candidate datasources are found, or if more than one datasource is registered and there is no vector store. With one datasource registered it runs no vector search.
  • Resolver returns QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE when its answerability check finds no allowed datasource can answer the question; the run ends before the decomposer. A failed answerability call returns SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED with the model's error, or a PROVIDER_* error when the provider refused it.
  • Schema retriever falls back to full schema snapshot if vector retrieval yields no tables; if schema store returns None, it silently returns an empty table list.

docs.title: Planning
docs.text:
• Decomposer LLM failures return ORCHESTRATOR_CRASH (critical) and empty responses; a provider's refusal returns a PROVIDER_* error instead.
  • AST planner LLM failures return PLANNING_FAILURE and a None plan.
  • A decomposition that cannot be turned into an execution DAG returns PLANNER_FAILED and no execution_dag; the layer router ends the run.
  • A join or compare combine group left with fewer than two inputs (a sub-query dropped as restricted, unresolved or unsupported) returns PLANNER_FAILED the same way, before any scan runs, rather than answering from the side that remains.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• Logical validation returns structured errors for missing tables, columns, invalid plan structure, or security violations.
  • Logical validation is the only validation gate; there is no physical/dry-run validation node in the graph.

docs.title: Execution
docs.text:
• SQL generation failures return SQL_GEN_FAILED.
  • Executor returns errors for missing SQL, missing datasource, missing executor, or executor crashes.
  • A query the database rejected as wrong (the adapter's ResultError.retryable) returns EXECUTION_FAILED, which is retried through the refiner; a refusal (permission, timeout, connection, read-only) returns DB_EXECUTION_ERROR, which is fatal. The message is the adapter's safe_message: one short line, no SQL, no stack trace (see the SDK).
  • Execution is in-process on the pipeline thread pool. A driver-level crash is not contained and terminates the process; only Python-level exceptions become PipelineError values (see ../execution/isolation.md).

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
• Schema store uses SQLite or in-memory storage; failures manifest as exceptions on read/write (not caught in callers).
  • Artifact store is invoked by the SQL executor; aggregation loads artifacts via PolarsDuckdbEngine.load_scan() using ArtifactRef URIs. A single store serves the local, S3, and ADLS backends; only local is verified against real storage (see ../storage/artifact-store.md).
  • Result store and execution store are in-memory only and not used for recovery.

docs.title: How nodes fail
docs.text:
• Most nodes use try/except and return a PipelineError (with severity + error code) in their response.
  • Some routing logic raises PipelineExecutionError directly (e.g., no compatible subgraph found) — an NL2SQLError carrying the PipelineError payload on .error, since a router may only return routing decisions and cannot report the failure as a state value the way a node does.
  • Nodes often return partial state plus errors (e.g., resolver returns a response plus errors).

docs.title: Propagation
docs.text:
• GraphState.errors and SubgraphExecutionState.errors accumulate errors via list reducers.
  • Downstream nodes generally do not halt unless routing logic explicitly stops (SQL agent checks) or a wrapper crashes.

docs.title: Local handling
docs.text:
• SQL agent uses retry routing based on PipelineError.is_retryable.
  • Other nodes do not retry; they return errors and allow the graph to proceed unless missing required inputs causes downstream failures.

docs.title: Containment
docs.text: • Each subgraph runs with its own SubgraphExecutionState. Errors inside the subgraph are merged back into the main graph state.

docs.title: Abort vs continue
docs.text:
• SQL agent subgraph routes to END when:
  • The planner fails to produce a plan and errors are non-retryable.
  • Logical validation returns non-retryable errors.
  • The executor returns anything but a retryable EXECUTION_FAILED (including success).
  • Retry count reaches sql_agent_max_retries with a blocking (ERROR/CRITICAL) finding.
  • Cancellation is detected.
  • If errors are retryable and retry budget remains, the subgraph loops through retry_handler -> refiner -> planner.
  • Validation findings that are only WARNING (COLUMN_NOT_FOUND with LOGICAL_VALIDATOR_STRICT_COLUMNS=false; it is on by default) also loop while retry budget remains, but never end the sub-query: once the budget is spent the plan proceeds to generation.

docs.title: Sub-query status
docs.text:
• wrap_subgraph derives SubgraphOutput.status from the final attempt, not from the accumulated errors: success when the sub-query ended with SQL and, when executing, a result artifact; otherwise error.
  • SubgraphExecutionState.errors is an additive reducer, so it keeps every attempt's errors (the planner reads them as retry feedback). SubgraphOutput.errors keeps them too.
  • A successful sub-query sends those errors to the run's warnings as RunWarnings with its sub_query_id (a recovered ERROR marked detail.recovered) rather than its errors. A failed one sends them to errors, adding a MISSING_SQL error if none of them was blocking.

docs.title: Partial recovery
docs.text:
• Recovery is limited to re-planning and refining within the SQL agent. There is no partial recovery at the aggregator or graph layer.
  • A sub-query that ends early (no plan, a refused plan, no SQL) is reported as status: error by the wrapper; it does not crash the run.

docs.title: Request termination
docs.text:
• run_with_graph terminates early on cancellation (CANCELLED) or global timeout (PIPELINE_TIMEOUT).
  • Once the run's token is cancelled, a callback refuses to start the next node or send the next model call, so a cancelled run stops at the next step instead of running to the end; the step in flight finishes.
  • PipelineExecutionError (raised where a router cannot return a PipelineError as a value) is unwrapped and its structured payload returned unchanged, keeping its own error_code, severity, node and is_retryable.
  • Other unhandled exceptions in graph execution return UNKNOWN_ERROR with stack trace.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: • Signal handlers are restored after execution. There is no explicit cleanup of artifacts or partial state.

docs.title: User-facing errors
docs.text: • Errors are returned in the final state, and QueryResult.errors carries them; a run that finished with an ERROR or CRITICAL error has status: "error". nl2sql run exits 1 on it.

docs.title: Retry scope
docs.text:
• Only the SQL agent subgraph retries: planner failures, validation errors, queries the database rejected as wrong (EXECUTION_FAILED), and, once each, an empty result filtered on a value that does not exist when a close one does (VALUE_NOT_FOUND) and a COUNT over rows a join repeated (JOIN_FAN_OUT) go back through the refiner.
  • Other nodes (resolver, decomposer, generator, aggregator, answer synthesizer) do not retry.
  • A retry tells the planner and refiner about the latest attempt only, as {node, error_code, message}.

docs.title: Backoff
docs.text:
• Exponential backoff with jitter in retry_handler using:
  • SQL_AGENT_RETRY_BASE_DELAY_SEC
  • SQL_AGENT_RETRY_MAX_DELAY_SEC
  • SQL_AGENT_RETRY_JITTER_SEC

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.text:
• Subquery IDs are stable hashes, so retries regenerate the same subquery IDs.
  • Executor writes artifacts keyed by subquery IDs; overwrite semantics depend on the artifact store implementation (not present in this repo).

docs.title: Partial writes
docs.text:
• Executor returns an ArtifactRef only on successful adapter execution.
  • Aggregator expects an artifact for each scan node; missing artifacts raise and are surfaced as AGGREGATOR_FAILED.

docs.title: Overwrites
docs.text:
• RESULT_ARTIFACT_PATH_TEMPLATE renders the artifact path for every backend from the metadata the executor supplies (tenant_id, request_id, sub_query_id, dag_node_id, subgraph_name, schema_version); an unfillable placeholder raises rather than writing a bad path (see ../storage/artifact-store.md).
  • With the default template, paths are <backend root>/<tenant_id>/<request_id>/<sub_query_id>.parquet: the sub-queries of one run never share a file, and repeat execution of the same sub-query with the same trace ID targets the same object. A custom template with no sub-query placeholder gets -<sub_query_id> added to its file name, so it cannot collide either.
  • A failed aggregation ends the run with its AGGREGATOR_FAILED error; the answer synthesizer is not called on an empty result.
  • A join/compare input that reached its datasource's row cap ends the run with RESULT_TRUNCATED before combining, since its missing rows could make the answer wrong; a capped union input runs and adds a RESULT_TRUNCATED warning (see nodes/engine_aggregator_node.md#row-cap-before-a-combine).

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: • No cleanup or rollback is implemented for artifacts or partial aggregation results.

docs.title: What can be retried
docs.text: • SQL agent planner/validation loop for retryable errors (non-fatal error codes and non-critical severity).

docs.title: What must restart
docs.text:
• Any graph-level failure (timeout, cancellation, unknown exception) requires a new run.
  • Resolver failures, decomposer failures, generator failures, executor failures, and aggregator failures have no local recovery and require a new run.

docs.title: What is unrecoverable
docs.text: • FATAL_ERRORS or CRITICAL severity errors (security violations, missing datasource ID, missing LLM, invalid state, and every PROVIDER_* error, since a retry would make the same call to the same provider) terminate the subgraph or graph without retry.

docs.title: Replay Support
docs.text: Replay is not supported. There is no persisted graph state or execution log to re-run nodes; state is kept in memory and discarded after completion. Artifact references are stored in state only and are not used for graph replay.

docs.title: Known Gaps
docs.text:
• No dry-run or cost-estimate gate runs before execution. The SUPPORTS_DRY_RUN / SUPPORTS_COST_ESTIMATE capability flags are gone with it: nothing queried them.
  • VECTOR_BREAKER is the only circuit breaker; LLM calls and SQL execution have no breaker and no fast-fail path.
  • There is no process isolation around SQL execution, so a driver crash is unrecoverable at the engine level.
  • Subgraph wrapper assumes executor output is present; earlier failures can cause wrapper-level errors.
  • Pipeline completion does not imply success: read QueryResult.status and errors, not whether the run returned.
  • No graph-level retries or replay; only subgraph local retries.
