docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Generates a structured SQL AST plan using an LLM with structured output: the planner's answer is a PlannerAnswer, the default plan (PlanModel) and, for an ambiguous question, up to two alternative readings.
  • Exists to translate natural language intent into a deterministic, machine‑verifiable plan.
  • Sits after SchemaRetrieverNode in the SQL agent subgraph.
  • Class: ASTPlannerNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/ast_planner/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Serve a pinned plan from the plan cache on a first attempt, without an LLM call.
  • Return a plan the run pins (state.pinned_plan: a supplied, approved or chosen plan) without an LLM call, through after_plan() with plan_source set to its source.
  • Serialize relevant_tables into the planning prompt.
  • Pass user intent, expected schema, and error feedback to the LLM.
  • Run the plan.after hooks on the plan (the planner's or the cached one) in after_plan(), the one place every plan the validator gets passes through.
  • Run plan.after on each alternative reading too (checked_alternatives()): one a hook denies is dropped, one it changes is kept as changed.
  • Return ASTPlannerResponse with the PlanModel the hooks let through, ambiguous_phrase, the alternatives the hooks let through and every alternative the planner offered (alternatives_offered), the planner's own plan (planner_plan, which the plan cache stores) and its plan_source ("llm", "cache", or "supplied", "approved" or "chosen" for a pinned plan). Only an "llm" plan is ever cached.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - SchemaRetrieverNode - RefinerNode (retry loop)

Downstream: - LogicalValidatorNode on success - retry_handler on retryable failure

Trigger conditions: - Executed after schema retrieval and during retry loops.

flowchart LR
    SchemaRetriever[SchemaRetrieverNode] --> Planner[ASTPlannerNode] --> Validator[LogicalValidatorNode]
    Refiner[RefinerNode] --> Planner
    Planner --> RetryHandler[retry_handler]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From SubgraphExecutionState:

  • sub_query.intent (required)
  • sub_query.expected_schema (optional)
  • sub_query.metrics, filters, group_by, order_by, limit: rendered by semantic_context_of() as compact JSON into [SEMANTIC_CONTEXT] (empty when the sub-query has none). The system message tells the model to apply all of it, filters on a metric as having, order_by as the plan's order_by and limit as the plan's limit, and that a most/least/top-N question needs an order_by on the ranked value and a limit; one example shows it.
  • relevant_tables (required for schema grounding)
  • knowledge_used (optional): the terms and rules the schema retriever picked, rendered as [BUSINESS_CONTEXT] by business_context_of() (nl2sql/knowledge/render.py); {} when there are none
  • errors (optional feedback for retries)

Validation performed:

  • No explicit validation; relies on LLM structured output schema.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to SubgraphExecutionState:

  • ast_planner_response (ASTPlannerResponse)
  • reasoning with plan summary
  • errors on planning failure

Side effects:

  • LLM invocation via llm_registry (none on a plan cache hit).
  • Reads the plan cache in the schema store. It never writes it: the sub-query wrapper stores a plan only after it validated and executed.

docs.title: Plan cache
docs.text:
The planner is the call that decides the SQL, so a plan that already passed validation and executed is reused (pipeline/plan_cache.py).

  • Key: (normalised sub_query.intent, sub_query.datasource_id, sub_query.schema_version). When the sub-query has an order_by or limit, they are appended to the intent part (... | order_by=album_count desc | limit=1), so a top-1 and a top-5 of the same intent are different entries. The run date is always appended (... | today=2026-10-12): the planner is told today's date and writes relative dates as literals, so a plan from another day misses. So are the planner's model and the datasource's knowledge digest (... | knowledge=<sha256>, Wave B D57): a changed definition plans again, and swapping the glossary back hits the old entries. Normalisation case-folds, collapses whitespace and strips trailing .?!,;:; the match is exact. No schema_version, no caching.
  • Read: only on a first attempt (retry_count == 0 and no errors). A hit returns ASTPlannerResponse(plan=<cached>, plan_source="cache") and makes no LLM call; a retry after a rejected plan always asks the model.
  • Never trusted: the logical validator, generator and executor run on a cached plan exactly as on a fresh one, so RBAC and policy changes apply.
  • Written by wrap_subgraph (pipeline/graph_utils.py) only when the sub-query produced SQL and executed without a blocking error. Refused, failed and plan-only runs are not stored. Nor is a plan whose planner answer carried alternatives or an ambiguous_phrase (D47), keyed on alternatives_offered, so a reading plan.after or the caller's scope dropped still keeps the plan out of the cache. alternatives_offered carries over to a retry: a question an earlier attempt read two ways is never cached, however clear the retry's answer. What is stored is planner_plan, the plan before any plan.after hook changed it. When a hook changed it, that plan was not itself validated in the run that stored it; a hit is safe anyway, because it passes plan.after and the validator again every time.
  • Controls: settings.pipeline.plan_cache (default true) and nl2sql cache clear.

See Determinism → The plan cache.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. On a first attempt, look up the plan cache; on a hit, pass the cached plan through plan.after (step 5) with plan_source="cache" and stop.
  2. Render relevant_tables with render_schema_for_prompt (see below).
  3. Build the feedback string from the latest attempt's errors only, one JSON object per line with node, error_code and message (nl2sql.pipeline.retry_feedback): an earlier attempt's errors, stack traces and details are never sent.
  4. Build expected_schema payload from sub‑query.
  5. Invoke the LLM chain with prompt + structured output (PlannerAnswer); its plan is the default reading. The first prompt of a sub-query that carries knowledge publishes knowledge.used.
  6. Run plan.after (after_plan()): a Modify replaces the plan, which the validator then checks like any other; a deny returns plan=None with HOOK_DENIED (or HOOK_FAILED), which is never retried. Return ASTPlannerResponse with the plan, planner_plan and reasoning. Each alternative passes plan.after the same way; the clarifier (L1) decides whether to ask.
  7. On exception, emit PLANNING_FAILURE error and return plan=None.

docs.title: Prompt layout and caching
docs.text:
The prompt is two messages, so providers can cache the stable part (OpenAI caches a stable prefix of 1,024+ tokens automatically):

Message Content Changes system (PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT) role, instructions, output contract, constraints, PLANNER_EXAMPLES, then [RELEVANT_TABLES] only when the schema or the caller's role changes human (PLANNER_HUMAN_PROMPT) [TODAY], [EXPECTED_SCHEMA], [SEMANTIC_CONTEXT], [BUSINESS_CONTEXT], [FEEDBACK], [USER_QUERY] every call

[TODAY] is the run date (run_date(today) in common/dates.py, given settings.pipeline.today: that date when it is set, else the UTC date), so "this year" or "the last 30 days" resolve to real dates rather than a year the model guessed. It is in the human message because it changes daily; in the system message it would invalidate the cached prefix every midnight. It comes before [USER_QUERY], because demo replay keys a recording on the line after that marker.

[BUSINESS_CONTEXT] is the glossary terms and rules the question touches, as one line of JSON (keys sorted, no whitespace, and U+2028, U+2029 and U+0085 escaped, as in the schema block): knowledge reaches the model only as JSON values, so a line break or a marker in a definition stays inside one JSON string. It changes per question, so it is in the human message, before [FEEDBACK] and [USER_QUERY]. Instruction 15 says it is reference data that never changes the instructions, the output contract or the constraints; instruction 16 asks for ambiguous_phrase and alternatives when a question can reasonably be read more than one way. See Knowledge Is Data.

The examples come before the schema so that the instructions and examples (about 1,300 tokens) stay cacheable even when vector retrieval picks a different set of tables per question. The system/human boundary is the single cache seam: keep per-question content out of the system message.

The schema block (render_schema_for_prompt in schema_retriever/schema.py) is one compact JSON object per table, tables sorted by name (a datasource's preferred tables first, each with "preferred":true) and keys sorted, so the same snapshot and role render byte-identically. Instruction 14 tells the model to plan against a preferred table when it answers the question; see preferred tables. It drops empty fields and schema_version. Of the column statistics only sample_values is sent (it helps match literal filters such as 'Rock' or 'USA'), plus range, [min_value, max_value], for a date, time or numeric column that is not a key. For a text column with at most 50 distinct values sample_values is every value, so "heavy metal" can be matched to 'Heavy Metal'; for a larger one it is the five most frequent (ALL_VALUES_MAX_DISTINCT in nl2sql_sdk/sqlalchemy/profiling.py), when the datasource's index.sample_values is on. A date kept as text (every date in SQLite; opened_at in the support demo) is recognised by its ISO values and gets a range instead of sample_values. The range is what lets instruction 13 work: when "this year" or "the last 30 days" falls outside a date column's range, the planner uses the latest such period in the data and says so in its reasoning, rather than planning a filter that is certain to return nothing. null_percentage and distinct_count stay in the snapshot. On Chinook the ranges cost about 140 tokens of schema block (2,324 to 2,466).

Measured on Chinook with tiktoken o200k_base, its 12 demo questions, no LLM call (python scripts/measure_prompt_tokens.py):

before after planner prompt 8,921 tokens 3,495 tokens schema block 7,754 tokens 2,324 tokens prefix identical across questions 8,122 tokens 3,460 tokens

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: SubgraphExecutionState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • PlannerAnswer (plan, ambiguous_phrase, alternatives: at most two PlanAlternatives, each a label and a plan)
  • PlanModel
  • ASTPlannerResponse

DISTINCT in the plan language: PlanModel.distinct: true is SELECT DISTINCT, and a func expr with distinct: true is a distinct aggregate such as COUNT(DISTINCT x). The system message's instructions and one of its examples say so; a function named DISTINCT is rejected by the logical validator.

Dates in the plan language are two portable functions, described once in the system message and the same for every database: DATE_PART(unit, date), an integer, and DATE_TRUNC(unit, date), the period's first day as YYYY-MM-DD, with the unit a string literal year, quarter, month or day. The prompt names no database; each adapter renders the functions (see the generator). Subqueries and window functions are not in the language. offset pages through the plan's order_by (rows 11 to 20 are limit: 10, offset: 10); a plan with an offset and no order_by is rejected by the validator.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Asks instead of guessing: when the planner read a phrase of the question in more than one way, and two or three readings pass the checks, it ends the sub-query with the options rather than running the most likely one.
  • Sits on the logical validator's "valid" edge, before the generator, so every path from the planner to the generator still passes the validator.
  • Makes no model call.
  • Class: ClarifierNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/clarifier/node.py
  • Design: Wave B, section 7 (D47).

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Run each of the planner's alternative readings through the validator's own checks (LogicalValidatorNode.check: the static checks and the caller's scope) and drop those that fail. A reading that names a table the caller cannot read is never offered, and never listed as an assumption.
  • Render each remaining reading to SQL with the generator and drop one whose SQL another option already has (the default reading comes first). At most three options: the default and two alternatives.
  • End the sub-query with NEEDS_CLARIFICATION when it may ask, and publish clarification.requested.
  • Otherwise let the default plan go on, keeping the readings that passed on ast_planner_response.alternatives, which the explanation lists as assumptions.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - LogicalValidatorNode, when the plan passed

Downstream: - GeneratorNode, unless it asked - END, when it asked

flowchart LR
    Validator[LogicalValidatorNode] -->|valid| Clarifier[ClarifierNode]
    Clarifier -->|ok| Generator[GeneratorNode]
    Clarifier -->|asked| End[END]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From SubgraphExecutionState:

  • ast_planner_response.plan, ambiguous_phrase and alternatives. Each alternative already went through plan.after in the planner node, as the plan did: one a hook denied is not there, one a hook changed is there as changed.
  • sub_query, relevant_tables and user_context, for the validator's checks.
  • clarify: set by wrap_subgraph when the run's clarify is on and the sub-query is the run's only one.

From the runtime: settings.clarify.enabled, and the run's pinned knowledge for the datasource's knowledge digest.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• No alternatives: nothing (it passes straight through).
  • Otherwise ast_planner_response with alternatives cut to the readings that passed and were not merged. alternatives_offered (every reading the planner gave, set by the planner node) is left as it is, so an answer with readings is never cached (D47), even when none was left for this caller.
  • When it asks, also one PipelineError: NEEDS_CLARIFICATION, severity INFO, never retried. Its details carry what the result needs to build the ClarificationRequest: phrase, datasource_id, schema_version, knowledge_digest, sub_query and options (id, label, plan; the default reading, a, has no label from the planner). The result adds the question, the asker and each option's explanation (result_from_state in api/query_api.py).

docs.title: When it asks
docs.text:
All of these hold:

  1. The planner named the phrase (ambiguous_phrase) and at least one alternative passed the checks and was not merged. A phrase the glossary settles is not asked (D48): the flag and the alternatives are dropped and the default plan goes on. A phrase is settled when a term's name equals it, or exactly one term lists it as a synonym (case-insensitive); "sales" listed by two terms stays open. The plan is still never cached, since the planner's answer carried readings (alternatives_offered).
  2. state.clarify is on: the run's clarify (run_query(clarify=...), default true; evals pass false) and the run has exactly one sub-query.
  3. settings.clarify.enabled is on (the default).
  4. No attempt of the sub-query has executed yet. After a sanity retry (VALUE_NOT_FOUND, JOIN_FAN_OUT) the re-plan's default reading runs, so the flagged attempt's rows are never the answer, and the readings that passed are assumptions. wrap_subgraph never counts a sub-query that asked as succeeded, nor returns its artifact.

The prompts are the same either way: clarify only decides whether the clarifier ends the run.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
def __call__(self, state: SubgraphExecutionState) -> Dict[str, Any]

check_clarifier in build_sql_agent_graph routes end when the state holds a NEEDS_CLARIFICATION error, else ok. The layer router ends the run on it (nothing is executed, aggregated or synthesized), and wrap_subgraph reports the sub-query with status needs_clarification and no MISSING_SQL error.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• clarification.requested (sub_query_id, phrase, options), an operator event, never on the caller's stream.
  • No policy.decision and no denial warning for an alternative that names a denied table (check(..., audit=False)): that reading is dropped and reaches no caller. The plan the caller gets is audited as always.
  • node.started and node.finished as every step.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Answers a question with a verified query from curated.yaml when one fits, before the model plans anything.
  • Searches only the verified queries of datasources the caller's role may read, asks the model once to pick one and give its parameter values, and checks the values and the role's table access in code.
  • Runs the saved SQL with the values as bound parameters, under the row ceiling, and hands the result to the aggregator and the answer synthesizer as a one-sub-query run.
  • Falls back to the generated pipeline for anything else, with a reason code; a fallback is never an error of the run.
  • Class: CuratedMatcherNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/curated_matcher/node.py
  • Design: Curated answers

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Limit the search to datasources that have verified queries and that the caller's Scope reaches (reaches_datasource()) (the pinned datasource_id only, when one is given).
  • Retrieve candidates with Retriever.retrieve_verified_query_candidates() (top settings.curated.match_top_k), skipping a query that is in the index but no longer in the file.
  • Ask no model when the best similarity is below settings.curated.match_floor.
  • Make one structured-output call, VerifiedQueryChoice.
  • Check the chosen values (params.resolve_params): type, min/max, choices, required.
  • Check every table the SQL reads against the caller's Scope (allows()), and that the SQL is still one read-only query.
  • Check the adapter declares SUPPORTS_BOUND_PARAMETERS before running a query with parameters.
  • Run the SQL through SqlExecutorService with ExecutorRequest.parameters and max_rows.
  • On a hit, fill the state the way a one-sub-query generated run leaves it.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
The node is in the graph only when curated answers are on: CURATED_ENABLED is true, the curated file is loaded and holds at least one verified query, and the run executes (a plan-only run has no matcher). Otherwise the graph starts at DatasourceResolverNode, exactly as without curated answers.

Upstream: - Entry point (no upstream nodes).

Downstream: - layer_router on a hit: the scan is already done, so it sends the run to EngineAggregatorNode, then AnswerSynthesizerNode. - DatasourceResolverNode on any fallback.

flowchart LR
    Matcher[CuratedMatcherNode] -->|verified| Router[layer_router]
    Router --> Aggregator[EngineAggregatorNode]
    Aggregator --> Synth[AnswerSynthesizerNode]
    Matcher -->|fallback| Resolver[DatasourceResolverNode]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From GraphState:

  • user_query (str, required): searched, and shown to the model.
  • datasource_id (Optional[str]): when set, only this datasource is searched.
  • user_context (UserContext, required): the role's datasources and tables.

Context dependencies (Runtime):

  • curated: the loaded CuratedFileConfig. The matcher reads every query from it, never from the index.
  • vector_store: retrieve_verified_query_candidates().
  • policy_engine: scope(user_context, datasource_id).
  • ds_registry: dialect, adapter row limit, supports().
  • vector_store: the run's pinned Retriever: the candidates, and the schema version of the datasource's live build, stamped on the sub-query.
  • llm_registry: the choice's model, agent name curatedmatcher (falls back to default).

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
On a hit, mutations to GraphState:

  • verified_match (VerifiedMatch: datasource_id, query_id, description, params)
  • decomposer_response: one SubQuery (id verified_<query_id>, intent the question) in one standalone combine group
  • execution_dag: build_execution_dag() of that response
  • artifact_refs: the saved result
  • subgraph_outputs: one SubgraphOutput with plan_source="verified", the SQL, row_cap, truncated, and the checks read_only, params and policy
  • reasoning

On a fallback: nothing the rest of the graph reads. execution_failed also adds a warnings entry.

Always, outside the state (the trace keeps the node's whole return):

  • curated_match: matched, reason (a fallback code or None), detail, floor, candidates (datasource_id, query_id, similarity), choice (the model's query_id, params, reason), params (after checking).
  • retrieval: the search's record, shaped like the resolver's, when a search ran.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Searchable datasources: registered, allowed for the role (* allows all), the pinned one alone if pinned, and holding verified queries. None: not_configured, no search and no embedding call.
  2. Candidates. None (or none still in the file): no_candidates.
  3. Best similarity below settings.curated.match_floor: below_floor, no model call.
  4. One VerifiedQueryChoice call. It raised (no recording in a replay, a provider error): model_failed. none_of_these: none_of_these. An id that is not a candidate: unknown_query.
  5. Values: an unknown name, a name twice, a value that does not parse or is out of bounds: param_invalid; a param with no default left out or empty: param_missing. A param left out takes its default.
  6. Tables: any table the SQL reads not allowed for the role: policy_denied. The normal pipeline then enforces the policy as always; the user is not told a verified query exists.
  7. Capability: a query with params on an adapter without SUPPORTS_BOUND_PARAMETERS: capability_missing.
  8. Run with the values bound and max_rows set to min(limits.row_limit or row_limit, row_limit) (limits is the datasource's, row_limit is settings.results.row_limit). Failed or no result: execution_failed, with a warning.
  9. Fill the state and route to layer_router.

docs.title: The choice prompt
docs.text:
System message (curated_matcher/prompts.py), then the question after a User Query: line, which nl2sql.llm.replay.extract_question recognises:

You decide whether one of the verified queries below answers the user's question. A data team wrote and checked each one; you cannot change what a query does, only pick one and give its parameter values.

Rules:
1. Pick a query only when it answers the whole question as asked: the same measure, the same ranking or grouping, the same filters. A query about something close but different (ranked by another measure, grouped another way, a different entity) does not answer it.
2. When no query answers the whole question, set query_id to "none_of_these". When unsure, choose "none_of_these": the question is then answered another way, which is better than a wrong answer.
3. Use the id exactly as listed (datasource.query).
4. Give a value for each parameter the question states, as text: an int as digits, a date as YYYY-MM-DD, a string exactly as one of its choices when it has them. Leave out a parameter the question does not state; never guess a value the question does not give.
5. Give the reason in one short sentence.

Verified queries (JSON):
{candidates}

{candidates} lists, in ranked order, each candidate's qualified id (chinook.top_customers_by_revenue), its description, and its params with type, bounds, choices, default and required. Never the SQL.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
def __call__(self, state: GraphState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • VerifiedQueryChoice, ParamValue, VerifiedMatch (curated_matcher/schemas.py)
  • VerifiedQueryCandidate (indexing/models.py)
  • ExecutorRequest.parameters, ExecutorRequest.max_rows
  • SubgraphOutput with plan_source="verified"

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• No model writes or edits the SQL; the model picks an id and supplies values, which code checks and the driver binds.
  • The candidates block is serialized with sorted keys in ranked order.
  • The search and the choice are as deterministic as the embedding model and the configured temperature and seed.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: The node never adds an error to the run. Every failure, including an unexpected exception, is a fallback with a reason code: not_configured, no_candidates, below_floor, none_of_these, model_failed, unknown_query, param_invalid, param_missing, policy_denied, capability_missing, execution_failed.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• No retry: a fallback runs the generated pipeline instead.
  • Idempotent for the same input state and the same model answer.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• A verified answer costs two model calls (this choice and the answer) instead of four or more.
  • Below the floor, or with no candidates, a fallback costs one embedding call and no model call.
  • The result is read in batches and the stream stops at max_rows.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: curated_matcher
  • The trace records the node with its curated_match record and the search; the choice call is recorded like every LLM call, under node curated_matcher.
  • QueryResult.source says verified with the query id and values, or generated.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Picks the datasources a question goes to: an explicit override, the only registered datasource, or routing (five signals fused with reciprocal rank fusion) when more than one is registered.
  • Enforces RBAC and the schema version mismatch policy before planning.
  • Refuses a question no datasource can answer, with one small structured LLM call, before the decomposer runs.
  • Sits at the entry of the control graph and gates the pipeline.
  • Class: DatasourceResolverNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/datasource_resolver/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Choose candidate datasources:
    • an explicit datasource_id is used as given;
    • with exactly one datasource registered, that one is used and no vector search runs;
    • otherwise Retriever.route() ranks the datasources the caller's scope reaches (see Routing).
  • Validate datasource IDs against the registered adapter list.
  • Enforce RBAC datasource access.
  • Judge answerability over the allowed candidates, refuse with QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE when none can answer, and forward only the candidates the verdict names, at most settings.routing.max_datasources of them.
  • Give each forwarded datasource its description and a capped table list, for the decomposer to route on.
  • Populate DatasourceResolverResponse in GraphState.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - Entry point (no upstream nodes), or CuratedMatcherNode when curated answers are configured and it fell back.

Downstream: - DecomposerNode if resolution succeeds. - Terminates early (END) if no datasource is allowed, or the question is not answerable.

Trigger conditions: - The control graph's entry node, unless curated answers are configured; then it runs whenever the curated matcher did not answer.

flowchart LR
    Resolver[DatasourceResolverNode] -->|answerable and allowed| Decomposer[DecomposerNode]
    Resolver -->|denied or not answerable| EndNode[END]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From GraphState:

  • user_query (str, required): the question; used for routing (more than one datasource) and for the answerability check.
  • datasource_id (Optional[str]): explicit override for datasource selection.
  • user_context (UserContext, required): RBAC enforcement.

Context dependencies (Runtime):

  • vector_store: the run's pinned Retriever. Its route ranks the candidates when more than one datasource is registered and no override is given, and gives each datasource's live schema version and snapshot (the snapshot's description and table list feed the answerability check and the decomposer's routing context).
  • ds_registry: adapter registry for registered IDs.
  • rbac: filters allowed datasources.
  • llm_registry: the answerability check's model, agent name datasourceresolver (falls back to default).
  • settings.routing (candidates, max_datasources, floor_ratio) and settings.retrieval.decomposer_tables.

Validation performed:

  • Datasource override must exist in the registry.
  • RBAC must allow at least one candidate.
  • At least one allowed candidate must be judged able to answer.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to GraphState:

  • datasource_resolver_response (DatasourceResolverResponse)
  • errors (list of PipelineError) on failure
  • reasoning (how the candidates were chosen, and the answerability reason) and warnings

Side effects:

  • One LLM call (the answerability check) once the role check passes.
  • Routing's five index searches (one embedding of the question) when more than one datasource is registered and no override is given.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Candidates:
    • state.datasource_id set: it must be registered (INVALID_STATE otherwise); it is the only candidate.
    • Exactly one datasource registered: it is the only candidate; no vector search.
    • Otherwise: the vector store must exist (SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED otherwise). The scope filter comes first: the registered datasources the caller's role may not read are left out, and none left is a CRITICAL SECURITY_VIOLATION with no search and no model call. Retriever.route then ranks the rest (the description, example, verified-query, table and column signals, fused with reciprocal rank fusion), keeping the top settings.routing.candidates (3) and dropping any whose best similarity is under settings.routing.floor_ratio (0.5) times the most similar one's. Only the tables the role may read vote: a table or column entry of a hidden table, or a verified query that reads one, is dropped before ranking and never reaches the trace. The description signal ranks every datasource entry exactly, so no reachable datasource is missed by the approximate search. No candidate is SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED (with a re-index hint when the index is empty).
  2. Role check: candidates the role may not read are dropped. None left is a CRITICAL SECURITY_VIOLATION, and no model call is made.
  3. Schema version mismatch policy (fail returns INVALID_STATE; warn adds a warning).
  4. Answerability check over the allowed candidates only (see below). An empty verdict returns QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE.
  5. Narrow to the verdict. After routing, only the allowed candidates the verdict names go forward, at most settings.routing.max_datasources (3) of them, the best by fused score first; a candidate the verdict rejects never reaches the decomposer, and a verdict naming only unknown ids is QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE. With an override or a single datasource there is one candidate, and a non-empty verdict accepts it.
  6. Attach routing context to each forwarded datasource, from the snapshot its live build was made from: description, tables (sorted bare table names, at most settings.retrieval.decomposer_tables, 30) and more_tables (how many were left out).
  7. Return DatasourceResolverResponse with the forwarded datasources (sorted by id), their IDs as allowed_datasource_ids, and unsupported IDs.
  8. On exceptions, log and return SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED with the exception text; a provider's refusal of the model call is a PROVIDER_* error instead (see provider failures).

A single registered datasource is the shortcut, not the usual case: with more than one - the demo registers three - routing runs, and nothing else in the flow changes.

docs.title: Order of checks
docs.text:
The role check runs before the answerability check, so:

  • a caller with no allowed datasource gets the RBAC refusal and the model is never asked;
  • the model sees only datasources the role may read;
  • a question that is answerable but touches tables the role may not read passes this node and is refused by LogicalValidatorNode's table policy, as before.

docs.title: Answerability check
docs.text:
A structured call (AnswerabilityResponse: answerable_datasource_ids, reason) with this prompt (datasource_resolver/prompts.py). The system message:

You check whether a question can be answered from the datasources below, before any SQL is planned. For each datasource you see its description and the tables it holds, not its data.

Rules:
1. List the id of every datasource that could hold data relevant to the question, even partly. A question that needs several datasources lists all of them.
2. Be conservative. When you are unsure, treat the question as answerable and list the datasources that might answer it. Refusing a question that could have been answered is worse than running one that finds nothing.
3. Return an empty list only when the question is clearly about something none of these datasources hold, such as the weather, general knowledge, or small talk.
4. Use only ids from the list below.
5. Give the reason in one short sentence.

Datasources (JSON):
{datasources}

The human message:

User Query:
{user_query}
  • {datasources} is a JSON list, one entry per allowed candidate, sorted by id, with sorted keys: description (the datasource description from the live build's snapshot, which indexing takes from the datasources config) and tables (sorted bare table names).
  • The instructions and datasources come first (the system message) and the question last (the human message), so the prompt is byte-identical across questions up to the question and a provider's prompt cache can serve the prefix. OpenAI caches only prompts of 1,024 tokens or more, so with one small datasource nothing is cached; the prefix grows, and becomes cacheable, with more datasources.
  • The verdict refuses and narrows: an empty list refuses the question, and after routing only the allowed candidates it names reach the decomposer. It cannot add a datasource the role may not read.
  • For Chinook on its own the rendered prompt is about 260 tokens (o200k_base), plus the AnswerabilityResponse function schema; the demo now registers three datasources, so its prompt is correspondingly longer.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: GraphState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • DatasourceResolverResponse
  • ResolvedDatasource
  • AnswerabilityResponse
  • PipelineError

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Candidate choice is deterministic for an override or a single datasource.
  • Routing's ranking may vary with more than one datasource (approximate searches; ties in fused score go to the smaller id).
  • The answerability prompt is serialized deterministically; the verdict is a model call at the configured temperature and seed.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • INVALID_STATE (unknown datasource override; schema version mismatch under fail)
  • SECURITY_VIOLATION (RBAC denial)
  • QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE (ERROR: no allowed datasource can answer the question; QueryResult.status is error)
  • SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED (no candidates, no vector store with several datasources, or exceptions)

Exceptions are caught at the node boundary and logged with logger.error.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• No internal retry logic.
  • Idempotent for the same input state, except vector retrieval ranking and the model's verdict may vary.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• One small LLM call per question once the role check passes; it saves the decomposer, planner and synthesizer calls on every unanswerable question.
  • Routing (one question embedding, five index searches, no model) only with more than one datasource.
  • RBAC checks are in-memory operations; schema lookups are store reads.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: datasource_resolver
  • The answerability call is recorded like every LLM call: usage under node datasource_resolver in QueryResult.usage, and in the run trace keyed by node, sub-query, attempt and call.
  • Vector retrieval uses VECTOR_BREAKER at the vector store layer.
  • Returns a retrieval record in its update for the run trace: the query embedded, one search record per routing signal (route.description, route.examples, route.curated, route.tables, route.columns: the pool with similarities, each datasource's best entry picked) and a routing record (each signal's datasource ranking, the fused scores and ranks, the datasources kept and those dropped with why); or skipped: true and why (an explicit datasource_id, a single registered datasource, no vector store). The answerability check is not part of it: it is an LLM call and is traced as one. See Debugging a run.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• LLM agent datasourceresolver in the LLM config (optional; see LLM configuration)
  • settings.routing.candidates, max_datasources and floor_ratio, and settings.retrieval.decomposer_tables (see Settings)

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Replace this node in build_graph() to change resolution behavior.
  • Extend retrieval by modifying the node or the vector store retrieval strategy.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Tenant scoping is not implemented in vector retrieval.
  • The answerability check sees table names, not columns or data, so it refuses only questions clearly outside every datasource.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Decomposes the user query into datasource‑scoped sub‑queries and combination operations.
  • Produces deterministic IDs for sub‑queries and post‑combine ops.
  • Sits after DatasourceResolverNode and before the layer router.
  • Class: DecomposerNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/decomposer/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Invoke the LLM to produce DecomposerResponse.
  • Filter sub‑queries by resolved/allowed/unsupported datasources.
  • Stabilize IDs using a hash of sub‑query content.
  • Normalize and sort combine groups and post‑combine operations.
  • Refuse a decomposition with more than settings.routing.max_sub_queries sub-queries (QUESTION_TOO_BROAD).
  • Mark each join key's column on its own copy of the sub-queries, and copy each side's declared dtype onto the key pair.
  • Build the ExecutionDAG the layer router walks and the aggregator runs (decomposer/dag.py). The DAG is a pure function of the response above, so it is code here rather than a node of its own.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - DatasourceResolverNode

Downstream: - layer_router

Trigger conditions: - Executed only when resolver_route returns continue.

flowchart LR
    Resolver[DatasourceResolverNode] --> Decomposer[DecomposerNode] --> Router[layer_router]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From GraphState:

  • user_query (str, required)
  • datasource_resolver_response (DatasourceResolverResponse, required)

Validation performed:

  • Raises if no resolved datasources are available.
  • Filters out sub‑queries that reference missing, restricted, or unsupported datasources.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to GraphState:

  • decomposer_response (DecomposerResponse)
  • reasoning (completion status)
  • errors on failure

Side effects:

  • None beyond LLM invocation.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Validate resolver response; raise if no resolved datasources.
  2. Build resolved_payload and schema_version_map. The payload has one entry per resolved datasource, sorted by id: datasource_id, description, tables (sorted bare table names, at most 30, set by the resolver) and more_tables (how many tables were left out, present only when some were). The resolver fills these for every path, so an explicit datasource_id or a single registered datasource gets the same context as a vector search. The index metadata (chunk id, type, schema version) is not sent.
  3. Invoke LLM chain with user_query and resolved datasources. The prompt is two messages: the system message holds the fixed instructions and output format (cacheable), the human message holds the resolved datasources (as JSON with sorted keys) and then the question. Rule 1 tells the model to pick each sub-query's datasource from these descriptions and tables. A sub-query carries its own filters (a threshold on a metric included), order_by and limit: "the artist with the most albums" is order_by album_count desc, limit 1. post_combine_ops are only for operations across two or more combined sub-queries, and the prompt's example has none. The answer is a call to the DecomposerResponse tool whose arguments are the decomposition itself; both the prompt and the tool's description (the model's docstring) say not to wrap them under another key, which Claude did on the anthropic wire while the tool had no description.
  4. The system message states the limit, settings.routing.max_sub_queries (rule 10, "Use at most 6 sub_queries"). A decomposition with more ends the run here with QUESTION_TOO_BROAD: "This question needs more than 6 separate queries. Ask about fewer things at once." No DAG is built and the model is not asked again: a model that ignored the limit once usually does again, and the question is what has to change (Wave A, D29).
  5. A join/compare group needs exactly one left-hand input (left, base or primary) and one right-hand input (right, compare or secondary); two of one side, or a third input, is a ValueError for parse-and-retry. With two left-hand roles, which side was which used to turn on the sub-query ids, which the node rewrites, and the run crashed.
  6. DecomposerResponse requires each join/compare key to name a column in the expected_schema of its side's sub-query (a side or sub-query prefix such as right.customer resolves to the bare name), with a dtype, and the two dtypes to be coercible: a number or a boolean never joins a date. A violation is a ValueError, which parse-and-retry sends back to the model with the reason.
  7. fold_single_input_ops() then moves every filter, sort and limit op on a combine group with one sub-query (used by no other group) into that sub-query: filters are appended, order_by terms appended, and the smallest limit kept. With one input there is nothing to combine, and left as post-combine ops they reached only the aggregated answer, never the sub-query's SQL or rows (the first gpt-5.4 tier 2 run returned every row for ten superlative and top-N questions this way). A group with an aggregate or project op is left to the aggregator.
  8. For each LLM sub‑query:
  9. Validate datasource existence and RBAC allowance.
  10. Assign deterministic ID via _stable_id(), over the intent, metrics, filters, group_by, order_by, limit and expected schema.
  11. Two sub-queries the model wrote identically hash to the same ID, but each is still a sub-query of its own (a combine group may name both), so a repeat takes the next ordinal: sq_<hash>, sq_<hash>_2, and so on. Both run, and the DAG gets one scan node per sub-query. Before this, the shared ID gave the DAG one node id for two nodes, and the run ended with PLANNER_FAILED ("contains a cycle").
  12. Attach schema version.
  13. Remap combine groups to stable sub‑query IDs. An input whose sub-query was dropped in step 4 is removed from its group, and a group left with no inputs is removed. A join or compare group left with fewer than two inputs is refused: the run ends here with PLANNER_FAILED, before any scan runs, and no DAG is built. The message names the group and why each input was dropped (restricted_datasource, no_datasource, unsupported_datasource) but not the datasource. The model is not asked again: a restricted or unresolved datasource is not something a new decomposition changes. Before this, the group was kept with its one input and the engine returned that side alone as the "join", so "customers with an open ticket who spent the most" was answered as "customers who spent the most", with no error. A union that lost an input still runs on the inputs that remain; the dropped intent is reported in unmapped_subqueries.
  14. mark_join_keys() sets ExpectedColumn.join_key on the engine's own copy of each sub-query (true on each join-key column, false on every other) and copies each side's declared dtype onto the pair (JoinKeyPair.left_dtype, right_dtype). The three fields are SkipJsonSchema: they are not in the model's tool schema, and whatever the model sent for them is replaced. join_key is left out of the stable id (step 4) and of the expected_schema the planner is shown. The logical validator reads the flag and the aggregator the dtypes (Wave A, D30).
  15. Assign deterministic IDs to post‑combine ops.
  16. Sort sub‑queries, combine groups, and post‑combine ops.
  17. Check every post-combine op against the columns its combine group will produce (post_combine_problems()). A sub-query's result columns are its expected_schema names (the logical validator holds each plan to them), and the combined columns follow by the engine's own rules in nl2sql/aggregation/columns.py: a join/compare drops the right-hand join keys and suffixes any other right-hand name the left also has with _right. A group whose sub-query declares no expected_schema is not checked. If an op reads a column that will not exist, the model is asked once more, with the reason appended to the human message ("PREVIOUS ANSWER REJECTED: ..."). A second rejected answer ends the run here with PLANNER_FAILED and the same reason, before any scan runs; nothing after the decomposer can ask for a new decomposition, so this used to fail in the aggregator after every scan.
  18. Return DecomposerResponse.
  19. On exception, emit ORCHESTRATOR_CRASH error.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: GraphState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • DecomposerResponse
  • SubQuery
  • UnmappedSubQuery
  • PostCombineOp

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Stable IDs are generated via SHA‑256 hash of sub‑query content; identical sub‑queries are told apart by an ordinal suffix (_2, _3, ...).
  • Ordering of outputs is explicitly sorted.
  • LLM output is non‑deterministic unless configured deterministically.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • PLANNER_FAILED when a decomposition is rejected twice (step 9), with the reason;
  • QUESTION_TOO_BROAD when the decomposition has more than settings.routing.max_sub_queries sub-queries; never retried;
  • PLANNER_FAILED when a join/compare combine group has fewer than two inputs (step 5), for example because RBAC dropped one side;
  • ORCHESTRATOR_CRASH on exceptions; a provider's refusal of the call is a PROVIDER_* error instead (see provider failures).

Logs failures via logger.error.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• One internal retry: a decomposition whose post-combine op reads a column its combine group will not produce is asked for again, once, with the reason (step 8). When recording, the retry's answer replaces the first under the same question, so replay serves the corrected decomposition.
  • Idempotent for fixed LLM output; otherwise LLM variability can change output.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• One LLM call per pipeline execution.
  • Hashing and sorting are in‑memory and low cost.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: decomposer
  • Adds a reasoning entry on completion or failure.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: • LLM configuration for agent name decomposer via llm.yaml.

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Modify DECOMPOSER_PROMPT for different decomposition strategies.
  • Replace or wrap node in build_graph() for custom behavior.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• No fallback when LLM fails.
  • Output quality depends on LLM configuration and prompt.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Executes the ExecutionDAG over persisted artifacts using the aggregation engine.
  • Exists to combine scan results deterministically into final result sets.
  • Sits after layer_router and before AnswerSynthesizerNode.
  • Class: EngineAggregatorNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/aggregator/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Load scan artifacts from artifact_refs, lazily, as polars scans.
  • Execute combine and post‑operation nodes in DAG order, as one lazy plan.
  • Save each terminal result as its own artifact, and produce AggregatorResponse with those artifacts and a preview of each.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - layer_router (after all scan artifacts are available)

Downstream: - AnswerSynthesizerNode, when aggregation succeeded - End of run, when it failed (aggregator_route in pipeline/routes.py)

Trigger conditions: - Router dispatches to aggregator when no pending scan nodes remain.

flowchart LR
    Router[layer_router] --> Aggregator[EngineAggregatorNode] --> Synth[AnswerSynthesizerNode]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From GraphState:

  • execution_dag (required)
  • artifact_refs (required)

Validation performed:

  • None in node; aggregation service raises on missing artifacts.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to GraphState:

  • aggregator_response (AggregatorResponse)
  • reasoning and errors

Side effects:

  • Reads artifacts from the artifact store.
  • Writes one artifact per terminal result, in the run's folder: <tenant_id>/<request_id>/result_<node_id>.parquet with the default template (see Artifact Store).
  • Writes the run's result manifest beside them, <tenant_id>/<request_id>/manifest.json (see Artifact Store).

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Read execution_dag and artifact_refs.
  2. Check every combine input against its row cap (see Row cap before a combine below). A capped input to a join/compare ends the run here with RESULT_TRUNCATED; a capped input to a union adds a RESULT_TRUNCATED warning and aggregation goes on.
  3. Invoke AggregationService.execute(dag, artifact_refs).
  4. A join/compare combine casts both sides of each key to one type before the join, in polars, non-strictly (Wave A, D30). The types are the ones the decomposer declared (JoinKeyPair.left_dtype, right_dtype): each side is cast first to its own, then both to the type they meet as (nl2sql/aggregation/join_keys.py: text is parsed as the other side's type, two numbers meet as a whole number, a date and a datetime as a datetime, a number and a boolean as a boolean by 0 and 1). A number goes straight to the number type, and two keys declared float whose frames hold integers join as integers: a float cannot tell ids above 2^53 apart. A cast never changes a value, it nulls it: 7.9 or a decimal 7.50 cast to a whole number is null, not 7 or 8. Text is stripped of surrounding spaces, on both sides of a text key too. Timestamps of any unit and zone become naive UTC microseconds; text becomes a date or timestamp only by the ISO formats (2024-01-02, 2024-01-02 13:00[:00[.fff]], the same with T, a trailing Z or a +02:00 offset), never by inference, and a TIME key declared a date or timestamp is null. Text parsed as a number loses its padding, so "007" and "7" both match 7: a key of zero-padded codes should be joined as text, or it may fan out. A value that does not convert becomes null and matches nothing; AggregationService.execute counts them per side (PolarsDuckdbEngine.unconverted_join_keys) and the node adds a JOIN_KEY_UNCONVERTED warning for each, carried to QueryResult.warnings: "3 of 412 support.customer_ref values are not numbers and joined nothing." No dialect is involved: this is compute on result frames.
  5. A join/compare combine resolves each join key against its frame's columns. A key written with a side or sub-query prefix (right.customer, sq_2.customer) resolves to the bare column when only that exists; an unknown key is left for polars to report. A join/compare with fewer than two inputs raises (AGGREGATOR_FAILED) instead of returning the one frame it has; the decomposer refuses such a group before anything runs, so this is the last line of defence.
  6. A post-combine op (PolarsDuckdbEngine.post_op) applies every field it carries, in SQL's order: the reshaping its operation names (aggregate groups with polars' group_by, project selects expected_schema), then its filters (after an aggregate they filter the aggregated rows, as HAVING does), its order_by, and its limit. A filter op with order_by and limit, as the decomposer's prompt used to show, keeps all three.
  7. Before polars is asked for any column, a post-combine op's attributes (group_by, metrics, project's expected_schema, filters, order_by) are checked against the combined frame. An attribute the frame does not have is refused with the columns it does have, and a side-qualified one (right.customer) with the reason — see No anti-join below. The decomposer runs the same check on the decomposition before anything executes (nl2sql/aggregation/columns.py, shared with this engine) and asks the model again once, so here it is the last line of defence.
  8. AggregationService.execute returns each terminal node as a polars LazyFrame: the scans are ArtifactStore.scan_parquet, and the combines and post-combine ops only add to the plan, so no sub-query result is loaded whole before it is written.
  9. Save each terminal result with ArtifactStore.write_lazy, which streams the plan into a parquet artifact, and build AggregatorResponse:
  10. computed_artifacts[node_id]: the saved result's ArtifactRef, with the whole result's row_count and columns (sub_query_id unset).
  11. results: one ResultSummary per saved result (node_id, columns, row_count, and truncated: a sub-query upstream of the node in the DAG was cut at its row cap), also written as the run's manifest.json. QueryResult.result_manifest carries it, and the facade's paging and CSV export read the result by it.
  12. terminal_results[node_id]: the first settings.results.preview_rows rows, read back from that artifact. This is what the answer model is shown; it is not the whole result.
  13. Return success reasoning.
  14. On exception, emit AGGREGATOR_FAILED, on the state's errors and on AggregatorResponse.errors. The graph's aggregator_route then ends the run: the answer synthesizer is not called on the empty result, so the aggregator's error is the run's outcome and no model call is spent explaining {}.

docs.title: Row cap before a combine
docs.text:
The generator caps every sub-query at its datasource's row_limit, bounded by the settings.results.row_limit ceiling (100,000, also the cap when none is set), unless the plan asks for fewer rows itself, and records that cap as row_cap on its response and on the sub-query's SubgraphOutput. The cap is applied in each sub-query's SQL, before the combine: a join input with 2240 rows under a row_limit of 1000 reaches the aggregator as 1000, and every match the other 1240 held is silently lost. The wrapper marks such a sub-query's SubgraphOutput.truncated, which QueryResult and the answer carry (see AnswerSynthesizerNode).

So before combining, the aggregator looks at each combine input whose result has row_cap rows or more:

  • join / compare: refused. The run ends with RESULT_TRUNCATED (through aggregator_route, so no answer is synthesized), naming the sub-query and the cap. Missing rows mean missing matches, so the combined answer could be wrong, and a wrong answer is worse than none.
  • union: a warning. The rows a union returns are still right, only possibly incomplete, so it runs and a RESULT_TRUNCATED warning with the sub-query's id is carried to QueryResult.warnings.

A result of exactly row_cap rows may be complete; telling the two apart would mean fetching one row more, so it is treated as cut short. A plan's own top-N (LIMIT 5) is the answer, not truncation, and is never flagged. To answer such a question, ask something narrower (aggregate in the sub-query) or raise the datasource's row_limit.

docs.title: No anti-join: what "bought X but never Y" does here
docs.text:
CombineGroup.operation is one of standalone, compare, join and union. join and compare are both inner joins (how="inner" in PolarsDuckdbEngine.combine), and FilterSpec has no null or existence operator, so there is no way to express "present on the left and absent on the right". This is a capability gap in the plan language, not a bug in the engine.

Asked "Which customers bought jazz tracks but never rock?", the model decomposes it into the two sets and then reaches for a right-hand column to negate against — right.customer. That column does not exist: an inner join keyed on the shared column drops the right-hand copy, and the other right-hand columns are suffixed _right. Every tier 2 run has failed this question, and what reached the caller was polars' own unable to find column "right.customer"; valid columns: ["customer"].

Resolving the prefix away would be worse. right.customer would become customer, the filter would run against the intersection, and the answer would be the customers who bought both genres — wrong, and silently so. So the attribute check refuses the question and says why. The decomposer now makes this check first and asks the model once more with the same message; a second answer with the same problem ends the run in the decomposer with it, before any scan runs. A recording run also met the made-up variant, a filter on bought_rock, which the same check catches. The message reads:

Aggregator failed: Post-combine operation references 'right.customer', which
the combined result does not have. Available columns: customer. A column
qualified by side does not survive the combine: ... it cannot be expressed:
the plan language has no anti-join or set-difference operation ... so the
question is refused rather than answered with the intersection.

The same gap has a second shape: the decomposer sometimes emits the two sub-queries uncombined, and AggregationService.execute then returns two terminal result sets, which the run reports as "expected one result set, got 2" (2026-09-22_27cad30). Both are the same missing operation.

Closing it properly means adding an anti-join (or except) to CombineGroup.operation, the decomposer prompt, the DAG and the engine. That is a feature, not a fix, and is deliberately not done here.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: GraphState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • AggregatorResponse
  • ExecutionDAG

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Deterministic for a fixed DAG and artifact inputs.
  • Aggregation order follows DAG layers and ordered inputs.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • AGGREGATOR_FAILED
  • JOIN_KEY_UNCONVERTED, a warning: join-key values that did not convert to the key's type
  • RESULT_TRUNCATED, an error when a join/compare input hit its row cap, a warning when a union input did

Logs failures via logger.error.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• No internal retry logic.
  • Idempotent for a fixed DAG and artifacts.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• Scans Parquet artifacts lazily and executes joins/aggregations in polars; the combined result is streamed to its artifact (sink_parquet), and only the preview rows are collected into Python.
  • Cost grows with artifact size and DAG complexity. A join, sort or group-by may still need its inputs in memory as polars columns, never as Python rows.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: aggregator
  • Adds reasoning entries for success and failure.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• Uses PolarsDuckdbEngine.
  • settings.results.preview_rows: rows of each terminal result kept in terminal_results.
  • The combined result is written to the runtime's results store (ctx.artifact_store, <storage.path>/results/), as the sub-query artifacts are.

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Replace aggregation engine by modifying node to use a different AggregationService.
  • Replace node in build_graph() for alternate aggregation behavior.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Fails if required artifacts are missing.
  • Several post-combine ops on one combine group are siblings, not a chain: each reads the combine's output and is its own terminal result.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Delegates SQL execution to an executor service based on datasource capabilities.
  • Persists results via the artifact store and returns ExecutorResponse.
  • Sits after GeneratorNode in the SQL agent subgraph.
  • Class: ExecutorNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/executor/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Validate required execution inputs (SQL and datasource ID).
  • Gate execution on the datasource declaring supports_sql.
  • Build and submit ExecutorRequest.
  • Return executor response and propagate errors.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - GeneratorNode

Downstream: - Subgraph end (artifacts returned to control graph).

Trigger conditions: - Executed when SQL generation succeeds.

flowchart LR
    Generator[GeneratorNode] --> Executor[ExecutorNode] --> EndNode[SubgraphEnd]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From SubgraphExecutionState:

  • generator_response.sql_draft (required)
  • sub_query.datasource_id (required)
  • sub_query.schema_version (optional)
  • trace_id, subgraph_name, user_context

From Runtime:

  • ds_registry
  • tenant_id

Validation performed:

  • Missing SQL → MISSING_SQL
  • Missing datasource ID → MISSING_DATASOURCE_ID
  • No executor for datasource → INVALID_STATE

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to SubgraphExecutionState:

  • executor_response (ExecutorResponse)
  • errors and reasoning

Side effects:

  • Executes SQL against datasource via executor service.
  • Reads the result a batch at a time when the adapter has execute_batches (StreamingAdapterProtocol), settings.results.fetch_batch_size rows per batch, and writes each batch to the artifact as it arrives (ArtifactStore.write_batches); an adapter without it is called through execute and its one frame is written the same way. A failure the adapter reports between batches fails the sub-query as a failed execute would, and nothing is written (see artifact store). metrics.row_count and metrics.bytes_returned are summed over the batches.
  • SqlExecutorService also takes ExecutorRequest.parameters and max_rows, which this node never sets: generated SQL carries no parameters and its LIMIT is in the text. The curated matcher sets both for a verified query: the parameters reach the adapter in AdapterRequest.parameters and are bound, and the stream stops after max_rows rows, cutting the last batch and closing the adapter's stream.
  • Persists results to artifact store, one artifact per sub-query: the request's node_id (the sub-query id) is passed to the store as sub_query_id and dag_node_id, so two sub-queries of one run never write the same file (see artifact store). The ArtifactRef records it as sub_query_id.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Validate SQL and datasource ID.
  2. Check the adapter declares supports_sql; otherwise return INVALID_STATE.
  3. Build ExecutorRequest with trace/subgraph identifiers and schema version.
  4. Run execute.before (the cost rule's built-in policy.cost first, when policies.cost is set), execute the request, and run execute.after on the result's summary. The cost rule's estimate, when it asked for one, is returned as estimate and reaches SubQueryResult.estimate, even when the SQL was then stopped.
  5. After execute.after, run the answer sanity checks on the result (below), unless settings.pipeline.sanity_checks is false; a result a hook stopped is never checked.
  6. On exception, emit EXECUTOR_CRASH.

docs.title: Answer sanity checks
docs.text:
Cheap checks on each sub-query's result, before the aggregator, in pipeline/nodes/executor/sanity/: the filter values of an empty result (values.py), join fan-out (fanout.py) and all-null columns (nulls.py). Every probe is a sqlglot tree built from the plan and rendered by the adapter (render_sql), bounded, and never run on a table the caller's scope denies; a check that fails to run reports nothing, and a failure in the checks never fails the run. A verified query is not checked: it runs in the curated matcher, not through this node.

Probes and hooks. A probe (the value check's and the fan-out check's) is SQL the hooks never see: it runs outside execute.before and execute.after, and nothing publishes it. So when any hook is attached at execute.before (an operator gating the SQL that reaches the database), no probe runs; only the all-null check, which reads the saved result and sends nothing to the database. None runs either for a caller the cost rule gives a limit, since a probe would bypass it; a caller with no limit keeps them. settings.pipeline.sanity_checks: false turns every check off. A probe is bounded by the datasource's timeout; one that times out is skipped silently.

Check Runs on Code Then Missing filter value an empty result VALUE_NOT_FOUND A close value and a retry left: an ERROR, retried once. Otherwise a WARNING. Join fan-out a result with rows JOIN_FAN_OUT Under COUNT, confirmed, with a retry left: an ERROR, retried once. Under SUM or AVG, or with no retry left: a WARNING. All-null column a result with rows ALL_NULL_COLUMN Always a WARNING.

Each check retries at most once per sub-query, within settings.pipeline.retries.max, and a pinned plan (supplied, approved or chosen) is never retried, so its findings are warnings. Each finding carries details.attempt, which the SQL agent routes on, and publishes sanity.flagged (code, sub_query_id, retry; see Events). A warning reaches the result's warnings as a RunWarning, and the answer synthesizer says it (see AnswerSynthesizerNode).

docs.title: Join fan-out
docs.text:
Joining Customer to Invoice on Invoice.CustomerId repeats each customer once per invoice, so COUNT(c.CustomerId) counts invoices and SUM(c.Credit) adds each customer's credit several times. A table's rows are repeated when a join in the plan reaches, on its far side, a key that is not the far table's whole primary key (from the snapshot, through the sub-query's relevant_tables); every table on the near side of that join is repeated. One table joined to two others on their many side (a many-to-many sum: invoices and tickets of one customer) is the same case. A table with no known primary key is taken as unique, so it is never suspected: a warehouse that declares no keys (Snowflake or BigQuery often do not, nor do views) gets no fan-out check.

A suspected COUNT, SUM or AVG over a column of a repeated table (not already DISTINCT) is confirmed by one probe over the plan's own FROM, joins, WHERE and GROUP BY: does any group hold one row of that table more than once?

SELECT 1 FROM <the plan's FROM and joins>
WHERE <the plan's WHERE> AND NOT <alias>.<primary key> IS NULL
GROUP BY <the plan's groups>, <alias>.<primary key>
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 LIMIT 1

A row confirms it. The rows an outer join null-extends have no key, so they never count, and a row that appears once in each of several groups (which a grouped aggregate counts rightly) never counts either. The probe needs a single-column primary key and every table of the plan readable by the caller. The key keeps its case as reflected and is spelled as the generator spells a column, rendered by the adapter in its dialect.

Under COUNT the planner is told to count distinct values, which the plan can say (Expr.distinct). Under SUM or AVG the repair (aggregate the many side first) needs a derived table the plan cannot express, so it is a warning: "SUM(Customer.Credit) may count some Customer rows more than once: joining Invoice repeats them." Messages name tables and columns, never values.

docs.title: All-null columns
docs.text: A result with rows whose column holds only nulls (usually an outer join that matched nothing, or the wrong column) is a warning. It reads the saved result's null counts, never its values; there is no probe and no fix to suggest.

docs.title: An empty result's filter values
docs.text:
"Which customers bought Metal?" planned as Genre.Name = 'Metal' returns no rows because Chinook's genre is 'Heavy Metal'. Reported as is, the answer says nobody bought any. So when a query succeeds with zero rows, sanity/values.py's check_values() looks at every string literal the plan's WHERE compares a bare column to with =, IN or LIKE, through AND and OR only (a negated or != comparison, a column inside a function, and a number are left alone), at most five per sub-query:

  1. Does it exist? SELECT 1 FROM <table> WHERE <column> = '<value>' LIMIT 1 (LIKE for a pattern). If yes, nothing is said: the empty result stands.
  2. The closest values. From the column's sample values in the snapshot when one of them is close (a case-insensitive match, then by similarity), with no query. Otherwise a case-insensitive match first (LOWER(column) = LOWER('value'), DISTINCT, LIMIT 3); failing that, a bounded SELECT DISTINCT column ... LIMIT n (n is 500, or the adapter's row_limit if lower) and the three most similar by difflib (cutoff 0.6).
  3. What it reports, as VALUE_NOT_FOUND:
  4. With a close value and a retry left, an ERROR telling the planner which values exist: "No Genre.Name value is 'Jaz', so the query returned no rows. The closest existing values are 'Jazz'; use one of them if it is what the question means." The SQL agent sends it back through the refiner (see SQL agent). It is raised once per sub-query: an empty result after that retry is reported as a warning instead.
  5. Otherwise a WARNING: "There is no Genre with Name 'Polka'." (with "; the closest is ..." when there is one). The sub-query still succeeds with its empty result, and the answer synthesizer is told the value does not exist (see AnswerSynthesizerNode).

Every probe is a SELECT built with sqlglot and rendered by the adapter (render_sql), so no dialect is named here; each has a LIMIT no higher than the adapter's row cap. A table the role may not read (RBAC, as the logical validator checks it) is never probed, a probe the database refuses claims nothing, and a failure in the check never fails the run.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: SubgraphExecutionState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • ExecutorRequest
  • ExecutorResponse

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Deterministic request construction.
  • Execution results depend on external datasource state and are not deterministic.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • MISSING_SQL
  • MISSING_DATASOURCE_ID
  • INVALID_STATE
  • EXECUTION_FAILED: the database rejected the query as wrong (the adapter's retryable); the SQL agent sends it back to the refiner while retries remain
  • DB_EXECUTION_ERROR: the database refused or could not run the query (permission, timeout, connection); fatal
  • EXECUTOR_CRASH: an exception escaped the adapter
  • VALUE_NOT_FOUND: an empty result filtered on a value its column does not have; an ERROR (retried once) when a close value exists, a WARNING otherwise
  • JOIN_FAN_OUT: an aggregate over rows a join repeated, confirmed by the probe; an ERROR (retried once) under COUNT, a WARNING under SUM or AVG
  • ALL_NULL_COLUMN: a result column with no value; a WARNING

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• No internal retry logic. The SQL agent's check_execution routes a retryable EXECUTION_FAILED, and this attempt's VALUE_NOT_FOUND or JOIN_FAN_OUT ERROR, back to the refiner (see SQL agent).
  • Idempotency depends on datasource and query semantics.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• External I/O dominates (database execution).
  • Artifact persistence writes Parquet results.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: executor (and sanity, sanity.values, sanity.fanout for skipped checks)
  • sanity.flagged for each sanity finding
  • Propagates executor response reasoning and errors.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• tenant_id from settings.
  • settings.pipeline.sanity_checks (default true): false turns the sanity checks off.
  • Executor selection based on adapter capabilities.

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Extend SqlExecutorService to alter execution behavior.
  • Replace node in build_sql_agent_graph() to alter execution behavior.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Executes in‑process on the pipeline thread pool; there is no process sandbox (see ../../execution/isolation.md).
  • No built‑in retries on transient execution failures.
  • The fan-out check reads only the select list's COUNT, SUM and AVG of a plain column, and confirms with the plan's whole WHERE but no GROUP BY; a SUM or AVG fan-out is reported, not repaired.
  • The filter-value check covers string literals in WHERE only, not HAVING, and reads at most 500 distinct values to find a similar one, so on a high-cardinality column a near miss can go unsuggested (the value is then reported as missing).
