docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Converts the AST plan into SQL using sqlglot.
  • Enforces adapter row limits and dialect selection.
  • Sits between LogicalValidatorNode and ExecutorNode.
  • Class: GeneratorNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/generator/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Convert PlanModel expressions into sqlglot expressions.
  • Build a SQL query with ordered selects, joins, filters, groupings, and limits.
  • Apply adapter dialect and row limit.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - ClarifierNode, after LogicalValidatorNode passed the plan

Downstream: - ExecutorNode

Trigger conditions: - Executed when logical validation passes and the clarifier did not ask which reading was meant.

flowchart LR
    Validator[LogicalValidatorNode] --> Clarifier[ClarifierNode] --> Generator[GeneratorNode] --> Executor[ExecutorNode]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From SubgraphExecutionState:

  • ast_planner_response.plan (required)
  • sub_query.datasource_id (required)

From Runtime:

  • ds_registry (adapter dialect and row limits)

Validation performed:

  • Raises if datasource ID or plan is missing.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to SubgraphExecutionState:

  • generator_response (GeneratorResponse with sql_draft, and row_cap: the adapter's row_limit when it, not the plan's own LIMIT, bounds the query; None when the plan asked for that many rows or fewer). The aggregator uses it to tell a sub-query cut short by the cap from a complete one (see EngineAggregatorNode).
  • reasoning
  • errors on failure

Side effects:

  • Adapter registry access for dialect/limits.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Validate presence of datasource ID and plan.
  2. Resolve adapter and dialect.
  3. Compute effective limit from plan/adapter row limit: row_limit is the datasource's row_limit bounded by the settings.results.row_limit ceiling (100,000), or the ceiling when the datasource sets none; the limit is min(plan.limit or row_limit, row_limit). When the cap is what bounds the query, record it as row_cap.
  4. Traverse AST with SqlVisitor to build sqlglot expression tree.
  5. Every operator becomes the node sqlglot's parser would build (+ -> exp.Add, * -> exp.Mul, IS NOT -> NOT ... IS ..., and so on), wherever it is nested. An operator with no mapping raises; it is never rendered as a function named after the operator.
  6. An operand that is itself an operator is parenthesised, because sqlglot prints a hand-built tree without adding the parentheses its parser would have seen ((a + b) * c would otherwise print as a + b * c).
  7. / is sqlglot's true division, so on SQLite it renders as CAST(a AS REAL) / b rather than integer division.
  8. || is string concatenation, rendered as the dialect's own: a || b on SQLite and Postgres, CONCAT(a, b) on MySQL, a + b on T-SQL. A + with a string operand (a non-numeric string literal, or another concatenation) renders the same way, because on SQLite 'Jane' + ' ' is numeric addition and returns 0. A + between two columns stays addition: their types are not known here.
  9. Select aliases and column names are quoted, the dialect's way, only when they are not bare identifiers. The decomposer names result columns in plain words and the planner must use those names as aliases, so an alias such as sales support agent renders as AS "sales support agent" (and AS `sales support agent` on MySQL), in the select list and in the ORDER BY tie-breakers.
  10. A func expr with distinct: true wraps its arguments in exp.Distinct, so {"kind": "func", "func_name": "COUNT", "is_aggregate": true, "distinct": true, "args": [x]} renders as COUNT(DISTINCT x). PlanModel.distinct: true renders SELECT DISTINCT.
  11. A func expr is built with sqlglot.exp.func(name, *args), so a function sqlglot knows becomes its typed node and each dialect renders it its own way (LENGTH is LEN on T-SQL, COUNT is COUNT_BIG on T-SQL). A name sqlglot does not know (such as STRFTIME) stays as written; the logical validator has already limited names to ast_planner.functions.ALLOWED_FUNCTIONS. A function sqlglot builds as an operator (MOD(a, b) is a % b) keeps its operands' grouping.
  12. Dates are portable: DATE_PART(unit, x) becomes CAST(EXTRACT(unit FROM x) AS INT), an integer, and DATE_TRUNC(unit, x) becomes exp.TimeToStr(exp.TimestampTrunc(x, unit), '%Y-%m-%d'), a YYYY-MM-DD string, with unit year, quarter, month or day. YEAR(x), QUARTER(x), MONTH(x), DAY(x), EXTRACT(unit, x) and DATE_TRUNC(x, unit) written by a model are read the same way. The generator writes no dialect SQL for them: the adapter renders the tree (next step).
  13. Attach joins. The first table in plan.tables is the FROM table. left_alias/right_alias do not say which table is new: each join attaches whichever side is not yet in scope, taking the first listed join that touches a table already in scope, so joins may be listed in any order. When the new table is the join's left side, left/right outer joins are mirrored so the same table is preserved. Joined tables keep their schema_name/database qualifiers.
  14. Order the rows completely. The plan's ORDER BY terms come first, with their direction. Every other selected column follows as an ascending tie-breaker, in select order. With no ORDER BY in the plan, the query is ordered by every selected column. This does not change what the query means, but without it the LIMIT below could keep a different subset of rows on each run.
  15. An aliased item is ordered by its alias (ORDER BY genre, track_sales), which stays valid for aggregates under GROUP BY. Terms are never positions.
  16. A select item already used as an ORDER BY term, by expression or by alias, is not repeated.
  17. Constant items are skipped: they order nothing, and a bare number would be read as a position.
  18. Every term, the plan's own and the tie-breakers, keeps the dialect's default NULL placement for its direction, so no NULLS FIRST/NULLS LAST clause is rendered (nor, on T-SQL and MySQL, a CASE WHEN ... IS NULL emulation, which is invalid when the term is an alias). For example, a plan ordering by city ascending and c.Country descending renders ORDER BY city ASC, c.Country DESC, c.LastName on SQLite, Postgres, T-SQL and MySQL alike.
  19. The logical validator runs on the plan before this step and never sees the tie-breakers.
  20. Apply the effective limit, then the plan's offset when it is above zero: rows 11 to 20 are limit: 10, offset: 10. The limit is already capped, so a page is never longer than the row cap, and row_cap is reported exactly as without an offset. sqlglot renders the pair in each dialect's own form (LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10; OFFSET 10 ROWS FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY on T-SQL). An offset only means something in an order, so a plan with an offset and no order_by, or a negative offset, is refused here with a ValueError; the logical validator runs this builder, so the planner is asked to fix it before generation (see Buildability). The tie-breakers of step 6 then make the page the same on every run.
  21. Hand the finished tree to the adapter's render_sql(expression) (see the SDK). An adapter without the hook is rendered with query.sql(dialect=adapter.get_dialect()). The SQLite adapter rewrites the date nodes with STRFTIME/DATE(x, 'start of ...'); the others use sqlglot's rendering.
  22. Return GeneratorResponse with SQL and reasoning.
  23. On exception, emit SQL_GEN_FAILED.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: SubgraphExecutionState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • GeneratorResponse
  • PlanModel / Expr

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Deterministic for a fixed AST and adapter dialect.
  • Ordering is the plan's own list order: the first select item is the first column, the first table is the FROM table.
  • Row order is total: every selected column is an ORDER BY term (see step 6), so the same plan run against the same data returns the same rows in the same order, even when LIMIT truncates the result.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Emits PipelineError with:

  • SQL_GEN_FAILED

A malformed join graph is a planning error, not something to guess around. SQL_GEN_FAILED is raised when a join names an undeclared alias, when a join connects two tables that are both already in scope, when a join cannot be reached from the FROM table, or when a declared table is never joined.

In practice the planner should never see this. There is no retry edge after the generator, so a SQL_GEN_FAILED ends the sub-query. LogicalValidatorNode therefore runs _build_query() itself and reports the same ValueError as a retryable INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE one node earlier — see Buildability. The checks below stay where they are: they are the single definition of the rules, and the validator calling this code is what keeps the two in step. SUPPORTED_BINARY_OPS is exported for the same reason — it is the set SqlVisitor._visit_binary renders, and the validator rejects anything outside it before the plan gets here.

Logs exceptions via logger.exception.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Validates the AST plan (PlanModel) against schema and policies.
  • Exists to enforce correctness and security before SQL generation.
  • Sits between ASTPlannerNode and GeneratorNode in the SQL agent subgraph.
  • Class: LogicalValidatorNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/validator/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Validate aliases, joins, and column references.
  • Reject any plan the generator could not build (see Buildability below).
  • Enforce table access through the caller's Scope, with strict datasource namespacing.

Literal filter values are not validated against a column's sampled values. The adapter records every value of a text column with at most 50 distinct values, but only the five most frequent of a larger one: a retrieval hint, not the column's domain. Treating it as an allowlist rejected correct filters on any higher-cardinality column. Safety comes from the policy table allowlist and from schema resolution, neither of which depends on stats. A value that turns out not to exist is caught after execution instead, and only when the result is empty (see ExecutorNode).

docs.title: Buildability: the validator runs the generator
docs.text:
_validate_columns() resolves columns against a query in which every plan table is CROSS JOINed (_build_validation_query()). That is correct for column resolution — alias-to-column visibility does not depend on join structure — and it is exactly why the validator is blind to join topology.

The generator builds the real FROM clause and walks the join graph, so four structural mistakes used to pass validation CLEAN and fail one node later as a terminal SQL_GEN_FAILED: a declared table never joined to the FROM table, a plan with several tables and no joins at all, a join island that does not connect to the FROM table, and the same pair joined twice. GeneratorNode has no retry edge after it, so each of those ended the sub-query with no chance for the planner to fix it.

Rather than restate those four rules here and let the two drift apart, _validate_buildable() calls GeneratorNode._build_query() with the sub-query's own datasource dialect and discards the tree. Any ValueError becomes a retryable INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE, and the message is extended with the plan's tables and the foreign keys declared between them, written with the plan's own aliases — the same move _describe_column_failure() makes for columns:

Table alias(es) t3 are declared in the plan but never joined to the FROM table.
Plan tables: t1 = Artist, t2 = Album, t3 = Track.
Foreign keys between them: t2 (Album).ArtistId = t1 (Artist).ArtistId;
t3 (Track).AlbumId = t2 (Album).AlbumId.

It runs last, after every other static check, so each of those keeps its own error code and the generator's wording never replaces a more specific one. The cost is a second tree build, measured at ~2.4 ms against a ~3.4 s planner call.

test_logical_validator_generator_parity.py asserts the invariant directly: for each broken plan shape, the generator rejects it and so does the validator. The same route rejects an offset with no order_by, or a negative one (test_plan_offset.py): a page only means something in an order.

Column resolution is delegated to sqlglot's optimizer. The node converts the plan into a throw‑away sqlglot expression tree (reusing the generator's SqlVisitor) and runs sqlglot.optimizer.qualify.qualify() against a schema built from relevant_tables. The LLM contract is unchanged: the planner still emits a PlanModel, never SQL.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - ASTPlannerNode

Downstream: - ClarifierNode on success, which goes on to GeneratorNode unless it asks which reading was meant - retry_handler on retryable errors

Trigger conditions: - Executed when an AST plan is present.

flowchart LR
    Planner[ASTPlannerNode] --> Validator[LogicalValidatorNode] --> Clarifier[ClarifierNode] --> Generator[GeneratorNode]
    Validator --> RetryHandler[retry_handler]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From SubgraphExecutionState:

  • ast_planner_response.plan (required)
  • relevant_tables (required)
  • user_context (required for the policy check)
  • sub_query.datasource_id (required for namespacing)
  • sub_query.expected_schema (optional validation)

Validation performed:

  • Aliases must be unique.
  • Joins must match known relationships.
  • Column references must exist and be unambiguous.
  • Every binary operator must be one the generator can render.
  • The plan must build into a query at all.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to SubgraphExecutionState:

  • logical_validator_response (LogicalValidatorResponse, carrying errors, reasoning and checks)
  • errors and reasoning

checks is a List[ValidationCheck] (name, passed, message) recording what was validated, not only what failed. The names are fixed and always in this order:

name meaning plan_present A plan reached the validator. The only check emitted when it did not. structure_and_schema Tables, columns and joins resolve against the retrieved schema. policy Every table in the plan is allowed for the caller's role.

On failure the check's message is the first corresponding error's message.

Side effects:

  • None beyond in‑memory validation.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. If plan is missing, emit MISSING_PLAN and stop.
  2. Run _validate_static() for structural checks:
  3. _resolve_plan_tables() maps each plan alias to its schema columns and emits TABLE_NOT_FOUND for unknown tables. This stays hand-written because qualify() silently ignores relations absent from its schema.
  4. _distinct_function() rejects a func expr named DISTINCT with INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE: COUNT(DISTINCT x) is distinct: true on the COUNT expr, and SELECT DISTINCT is PlanModel.distinct.
  5. _unsupported_functions() rejects every other func name that is not a plain identifier (^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$) naming a function in ast_planner.functions.ALLOWED_FUNCTIONS (read-only aggregates and scalar functions, any case), with UNSUPPORTED_FUNCTION at ERROR severity, so the refiner retries with the list in the message. The list leaves out LEGACY_FUNCTIONS (STRFTIME), which older plans may still call but which the planner prompt never offers. func_name becomes the function's name in the SQL, so this is what keeps model text such as SELECT 1); DELETE FROM T; -- out of it.
  6. _date_operations() rejects a date function whose unit is not year, quarter, month or day, or whose shape is not (unit literal, date), with INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE; the message states the portable forms.
  7. _unsupported_operators() rejects a binary op the generator's SqlVisitor cannot render, with INVALID_PLAN_STRUCTURE. The schema's op Literal admits NOT, which belongs on a unary expression; every other member is in generator.node.SUPPORTED_BINARY_OPS. This runs before any check that walks the plan through the visitor, because an operator it cannot render makes all of them raise — which is how op: "NOT" used to surface as a VALIDATOR_CRASH.
  8. _validate_columns() builds the plan's sqlglot tree and runs qualify(..., validate_qualify_columns=True). On failure each distinct column reference is re-probed so every bad reference is reported, and _describe_column_failure() rewrites the optimizer's SQL-oriented text into plan-oriented feedback the refiner can act on. ORDER BY terms are wrapped in exp.Ordered first (generator.node.ordered()): sqlglot only wraps an argument it has to parse, and a bare function node in Order.expressions makes qualify() raise.
  9. join_key_type_errors() (validator/join_keys.py) checks each select item that is a join key (its alias names an expected_schema column the decomposer marked join_key) and a plain column reference: the column's type from the schema snapshot is parsed by sqlglot.exp.DataType.build in the datasource's dialect (the adapter's get_dialect()) and put in a category (number, text, temporal, boolean or other). A temporal column declared a number or a boolean, or a number or boolean column declared a date, is a retryable JOIN_KEY_TYPE_MISMATCH that asks for another column, never a cast (the plan has none): "The join key order_key is declared a date, but Orders.OrderKey is a number. Select a column that holds a date for this key." Every other pair is coerced by the aggregator; a type sqlglot cannot place, a column with no type and a computed select item are not checked (Wave A, D30).
  10. _validate_buildable() runs last and is the buildability check: it calls the generator's own _build_query() and throws the tree away. See below.
  11. Run _validate_policy() for policy enforcement. This always runs, even when static validation failed or raised — the security check is never skipped. It asks the caller's Scope (ctx.policy_engine.scope(user_context, datasource_id), the same one the schema retriever hid tables with) about every table in the plan. The schema retriever never showed the planner a denied table, so a plan that names one anyway is a model naming a table it was not given, and is refused here. The policy errors come first in the node's errors, before the static ones: such a table is also missing from the planner's schema (TABLE_NOT_FOUND), and the denial is the reason. Each forbidden table yields a CRITICAL SECURITY_VIOLATION whose message is "You do not have permission to see the data this question requires." (it names nothing), with details = {datasource_id, table, roles, rule} for the trace (rule is Scope.rule_for: the deny pattern, or the missing allow), and a warning log line. policies.refusal_names_tables: true puts the role and table in the message instead. An unknown role, or no role, allows no table and is refused the same way. The decision reads only the policy and the plan's table list, never the model's reasoning.
  12. If any errors are ERROR/CRITICAL, return with errors.
  13. Otherwise return success reasoning.
  14. On exception, emit VALIDATOR_CRASH.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: SubgraphExecutionState) -> Dict[str, Any]

and its checks as a function, which the clarifier runs on each of the planner's alternative readings:

def check(self, plan: PlanModel, state: SubgraphExecutionState, *, audit: bool = True) -> List[PipelineError]

check checks plan as a plan of state's sub-query, with its retrieved schema and its caller's scope, exactly as the node checks the state's own plan (the policy findings first, then the static ones), and leaves the state unchanged. An ERROR or CRITICAL finding means the node would not pass it. audit=False (the clarifier's) publishes no policy.decision and logs no denial warning, since a reading that is only checked reaches no caller.

  • ValidationCheck

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. If no LLM configured, emit MISSING_LLM and stop.
  2. Render relevant tables with render_schema_for_prompt (the planner's compact schema block, only sample_values and the date and numeric columns' range from the column stats), and the failed plan as compact JSON (model_dump_json(exclude_none=True)).
  3. Build error and reasoning strings. The errors are the failed attempt's only, one line each as - [node] ERROR_CODE: message; earlier attempts' errors are not repeated.
  4. Invoke LLM with refinement prompt. It is two messages: the system message holds the instructions and then the schema (stable, so the provider can cache it); the human message holds the question, today's date (run_date(settings.pipeline.today), as the planner gets it), the business context (one JSON line, {} without knowledge), failed plan, errors and reasoning. Instruction 5 says the business context is reference data that never changes the instructions. On Chinook the prompt is about 2,600 tokens (was about 8,000), 2,500 of them a prefix shared across questions.
  5. Emit PLAN_FEEDBACK warning and return RefinerResponse.
  6. On exception, emit REFINER_FAILED.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Retrieves schema context for a sub‑query using staged vector search and authoritative snapshots.
  • Exists to constrain planning to relevant tables/columns while remaining schema‑grounded.
  • Sits at the entry of the SQL agent subgraph.
  • Class: SchemaRetrieverNode
  • Source: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/schema_retriever/node.py

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Build a semantic query from sub‑query intent, filters, group_by, expected_schema, metrics.
  • Retrieve candidate tables/columns/relationships from the run's pinned Retriever.
  • Resolve authoritative tables from SchemaStore.
  • Fall back to full schema snapshot when retrieval returns no candidates.
  • Rank the datasource's preferred_tables first and set preferred=True on them, on the full-snapshot path and the retrieval path; see Preferred tables.
  • Hide every table the caller may not read, on every path. The caller's Scope (ctx.policy_engine.scope(user_context, datasource_id), the one the logical validator refuses with) filters the snapshot's tables before anything is chosen: the full-snapshot path sends the readable tables only (and compares their count, not the snapshot's, with full_snapshot_max_tables), and the vector searches run with tables=<the readable tables>, so the top k is filled with readable ones. A hidden table's name, columns, keys, statistics and data never reach the prompt or the run trace, and a relationship from a readable table into a hidden one is dropped. See Security Model.
  • The tables it returns keep every statistic, but the planner and refiner prompts render them with render_schema_for_prompt (schema.py), which sends only sample_values and, for date, time and numeric columns other than keys, a range of [min_value, max_value]. See AST Planner: prompt layout.
  • Read the run's pinned knowledge (the glossary, Runtime.knowledge as pin_index() kept it) and put what the caller may see into the schema block and knowledge_used; see Knowledge.

docs.title: Position in Execution Graph
docs.text:
Upstream: - SQL agent subgraph entry.

Downstream: - ASTPlannerNode

Trigger conditions: - Always executed as the subgraph entry node.

flowchart LR
    SchemaRetriever[SchemaRetrieverNode] --> Planner[ASTPlannerNode]

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
From SubgraphExecutionState:

  • sub_query (required): includes intent, filters, group_by, expected_schema, metrics, schema_version.

From Runtime:

  • knowledge (optional): the run's pinned Knowledge; none means no glossary
  • settings.knowledge: top_k and block_max_chars
  • vector_store (optional)
  • state (the state store; required for authoritative resolution)
  • ds_registry (optional): get_preferred_tables(datasource_id), get_dialect(datasource_id) (for derived date roles)

Validation performed:

  • If sub_query missing, returns empty relevant_tables.
  • If no candidates from vector store, falls back to full snapshot.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Mutations to SubgraphExecutionState:

  • relevant_tables (list of Table)
  • knowledge_used (KnowledgeUsed): the terms and rules sent as [BUSINESS_CONTEXT]; absent when none matched, and for a pinned plan
  • reasoning and warnings in fallback paths

Side effects:

  • Vector store queries.
  • Schema store reads.
  • None for knowledge: the planner publishes knowledge.used (an operator event, never on the caller's stream) on the sub-query's first prompt that carries knowledge_used. A plan-cache hit sends no prompt, so it publishes nothing, and the sub-query's result reports no knowledge_used.

docs.title: Internal Flow (Step-by-Step)
docs.text:
1. Build semantic query with _build_semantic_query().
  2. Retrieve table/metric chunks via retrieve_schema_context(), k = settings.retrieval.table_k (8).
  3. If no table chunks, retrieve columns via retrieve_column_candidates(), k = table_k.
  4. If tables are identified, retrieve columns/relationships via retrieve_planning_context(), k = settings.retrieval.planning_k (12).
  5. Resolve schema snapshot via _resolve_snapshot().
  6. Build Table objects with _build_tables_from_snapshot().
  7. If no tables were found, return full snapshot with warning.
  8. On exception, log error and return empty relevant_tables.

docs.title: Preferred tables
docs.text:
A datasource's preferred_tables (in datasources.yaml, see Datasources) are matched against snapshot tables by bare name or schema.table, case ignored.

  • Full snapshot: every preferred table is in the list, first.
  • Retrieval: preferred tables the tables search picked come first. A preferred table the search scored but did not pick is added (before the planning search, so its columns and relationships are fetched too) when its similarity is at least the least similar pick's minus PREFERRED_MARGIN (0.05).
  • Each preferred Table has preferred=True. render_schema_for_prompt sorts preferred tables first, then by name, and prints "preferred":true on them only; with no preferred tables the block is byte-identical to before. Planner instruction 14 tells the model to plan against a preferred table when it answers the question.
  • Being preferred never shows a hidden table: a preferred table the caller's scope denies is left out like any other.

docs.title: Knowledge
docs.text:
Wave B (K2, design). The datasource's merged knowledge is first filtered to the caller's scope with nl2sql.knowledge.scope.visible (an item naming a table the caller cannot read, or whose text mentions one, is left out), then resolved against the snapshot by schema_knowledge():

Field of the schema block What is sent A table's description The glossary's, else the database's comment (D38). Either is dropped when its text mentions a table the caller cannot read. A column's description The same rule A column's role The glossary's, else the one the snapshot proves: identifier for a primary or foreign key, date for a temporal type (D61) A column's unit, grain, values The glossary's, when it sets them (values on role: enum only) relationships The foreign keys into readable tables, plus each glossary join between two readable tables whose names resolve and whose types compare, with its cardinality and "source": "glossary" (D46). The logical validator's join check matches it as it matches a foreign key.

notes are never sent. knowledge_used (nl2sql/knowledge/match.py):

  • Terms whose name or a synonym appears, as whole words with case and punctuation ignored, in the sub-query's intent or the question: 1.0 for the name, 0.9 for a synonym, the best settings.knowledge.top_k (8). Two terms sharing a synonym are both sent; that is how the planner sees an ambiguity. A term the caller sees also matches when its knowledge.term index entry is at least settings.knowledge.match_floor (0.6) similar to the sub-query's intent (Retriever.retrieve_term_candidates), scoring that similarity; if the search fails, terms match by name only.
  • Rules whose tables is empty or names one of the tables sent.
  • The denied-name pattern is built once per sub-query, and only the readable tables' comments are checked against it.
  • The block is cut to settings.knowledge.block_max_chars (4,000) by fit_business_context (nl2sql/knowledge/render.py): the lowest-scored terms first, then rules from the last; dropped lists what was cut.

Both hold only items within the caller's scope, since SubQueryResult.knowledge_used is returned to the caller.

docs.title: Contracts & Interfaces
docs.text:
Implements a LangGraph node callable:

def __call__(self, state: SubgraphExecutionState) -> Dict[str, Any]

Key contracts:

  • Table / Column (node schema)
  • SchemaSnapshot (authoritative source)

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text:
• Deterministic snapshot resolution for a fixed schema_version.
  • Vector retrieval ranking may be non‑deterministic (MMR).

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
• Exceptions are caught and logged via logger.error.
  • Returns empty relevant_tables with error reasoning; no PipelineError is emitted.

docs.title: Retry + Idempotency
docs.text:
• No internal retry logic.
  • Idempotent for fixed vector retrieval output; vector ranking may vary.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• Depends on vector store retrieval latency and schema store reads.
  • In‑memory processing of candidates and snapshot tables.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logger: schema_retriever
  • Emits reasoning and warnings on fallback paths.
  • Returns a retrieval record in its update (not a state field, so LangGraph drops it; the run trace keeps it): the query text embedded, each search's pool with scores, the MMR picks in order and what was dropped, and the tables and columns sent to the planner; or, when the schema is small enough to send whole, skipped: true and why. Column entries of a table the role cannot read keep their name and rank but lose their scores (their embedded text holds sample values). See Debugging a run.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• settings.retrieval.full_snapshot_max_tables, table_k and planning_k (see Settings).
  • Vector store configuration is set in Runtime.

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Modify semantic query construction to include additional signals.
  • Replace node in build_sql_agent_graph() for alternative retrieval strategies.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• No tenant scoping in vector retrieval.
  • No caching of retrieved tables across retries.
  • Fallback to full schema can be expensive for large schemas.

docs.title: Related Code
docs.text:
• packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/schema_retriever/node.py
  • packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/indexing/retrieval.py

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Purpose: orchestrates the end-to-end NL2SQL pipeline as a LangGraph state machine.
  • Why it exists architecturally: central control plane that wires global nodes, subgraphs, and aggregation into a single execution DAG.
  • When it is invoked: via run_with_graph() runtime entry point.

Defining function: build_graph() Source file path: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/graph.py

docs.title: Boundary Definition
docs.text: This graph is the top-level orchestrator. It encapsulates datasource resolution, decomposition (which builds the execution DAG), routing to subgraphs, aggregation, and answer synthesis. It does NOT implement subgraph internals (SQL planning/execution), per-node business logic, or adapter-specific execution; those are delegated to nodes and registered subgraphs.

docs.title: Entry Conditions
docs.text:
Required state: - GraphState.user_query must be provided. - GraphState.trace_id is auto-generated if not provided.

Preconditions: - Runtime must be initialized with registries/services used by nodes (vector store, LLM registry, datasource registry, schema store, RBAC).

Triggering parent graph: - None. This is the root graph invoked by run_with_graph() in pipeline/runtime.py.

docs.title: Exit Conditions
docs.text:
Successful completion criteria: - Reaches END after answer_synthesizer when aggregation and synthesis finish without fatal interruptions.

Failure exits: - datasource_resolver can short-circuit to END via resolver_route when no datasource is resolved/allowed, or when its answerability check refuses the question (QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE); no other LLM call runs. - layer_router can return END if no execution_dag or layers are present. - layer_router returns END once every scan has run if none produced an artifact (every sub-query was denied or failed), and whenever the graph was built with execute=False. The aggregator and answer synthesizer are skipped, so the run's errors are the sub-queries' own -- for a policy denial, SECURITY_VIOLATION first -- and no LLM call is spent explaining an empty result. - layer_router raises PipelineExecutionError (an NL2SQLError carrying the PipelineError payload on .error) when no compatible subgraph exists for a datasource; this propagates as an exception from the router function. A conditional-edge router may only return routing decisions, so it cannot report the failure as a PipelineError value in state the way a node does.

Partial completion behavior: - If routing cannot schedule any scan-layer work but execution_dag exists and at least one scan produced an artifact, it routes to aggregator directly. If some scans produced artifacts and others did not, the aggregator still runs and reports the missing ones as AGGREGATOR_FAILED. - Errors added to GraphState.errors do not automatically stop the graph; the graph relies on routing logic and node behavior for termination. - aggregator_route ends the run when the aggregator failed (AggregatorResponse.errors is not empty), so the answer synthesizer never spends a model call on an empty result and AGGREGATOR_FAILED is the run's outcome.

docs.title: Internal Node Composition
docs.text:
Execution order (nominal path): - curated_matcher — CuratedMatcherNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/curated_matcher/node.py — only when curated answers are configured and the run executes: answer with a verified query (curated_route → verified → layer_router), or fall back (generated → datasource_resolver). Without curated answers the node is not in the graph and datasource_resolver is the entry point. - datasource_resolver — DatasourceResolverNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/datasource_resolver/node.py — resolve candidate datasources, RBAC, and the answerability check (an LLM call). - decomposer — DecomposerNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/decomposer/node.py — decompose query into sub-queries, and build the ExecutionDAG from them (decomposer/dag.py). - layer_router — inline lambda + routes.build_scan_layer_router — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/routes.py — route each scan layer to a subgraph or aggregator. - <subgraph nodes> — via wrap_subgraph() — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/graph_utils.py — invoke registered subgraphs per scan node. - aggregator — EngineAggregatorNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/aggregator/node.py — execute aggregation DAG. - answer_synthesizer — AnswerSynthesizerNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/answer_synthesizer/node.py — produce final answer.

Mermaid diagram (main pipeline only): 

flowchart TD
    curated_matcher -.->|verified| layer_router
    curated_matcher -.->|generated| datasource_resolver
    datasource_resolver -->|continue| decomposer
    datasource_resolver -->|end| END
    decomposer --> layer_router
    layer_router -->|subgraph| subgraph_exec
    subgraph_exec --> layer_router
    layer_router -->|aggregator| aggregator
    layer_router -->|end| END
    aggregator -->|ok| answer_synthesizer --> END
    aggregator -->|failed| END

The dotted edges exist only when curated answers are configured.

docs.title: State Contract
docs.text:
State model: GraphState (packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/state.py).

Field ownership, reducers, and lifecycle are defined in ../graph_state.md.

docs.title: Step-by-Step Execution Flow
docs.text:
1. With curated answers configured, curated_matcher runs first. On a verified hit it has already run the query and filled decomposer_response, execution_dag, artifact_refs and subgraph_outputs as for one sub-query, so layer_router finds the scan done and goes straight to step 7. Any fallback continues at step 1 with nothing in the state changed.
  2. datasource_resolver resolves candidate datasources (vector search only when more than one datasource is registered), filters them by RBAC, then asks the LLM whether any allowed datasource can answer the question.
  3. resolver_route decides:
  4. continue if allowed datasources exist and the question was judged answerable.
  5. end if none exist, the question is not answerable, or the response is missing.
  6. decomposer uses the LLM to produce SubQuery objects and combine groups, then builds a deterministic ExecutionDAG from them in code. The DAG is a pure function of that output, so it is not a node of its own; a DAG that cannot be built is reported as PLANNER_FAILED and the run ends at the router.
  7. layer_router inspects the DAG and current artifact_refs:
  8. If no DAG or layers, returns END.
  9. If next scan layer is empty, routes to aggregator -- or to END when no scan produced an artifact or execute is False.
  10. For each scan node, resolves a compatible subgraph and sends build_scan_payload.
  11. Each subgraph execution returns artifact_refs, subgraph_outputs, and errors to GraphState.
  12. layer_router is re-entered until all scan-layer nodes produce artifacts.
  13. aggregator executes the DAG using the stored artifact_refs.
  14. aggregator_route ends the run if aggregation failed; otherwise answer_synthesizer summarizes aggregated results into a final answer.
  15. Graph reaches END.

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text: Determinism guarantees and non-determinism sources are documented in ../determinism.md.

docs.title: Error Propagation
docs.text: Failure domains, retry scope, and recovery limitations are centralized in ../failure_recovery.md.

docs.title: Retry + Recovery
docs.text: See ../failure_recovery.md for retry scope and recovery behavior.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• Blocking calls include LLM requests in datasource_resolver, decomposer and answer_synthesizer.
  • The decomposer's DAG construction and the aggregator are CPU-bound.
  • Subgraph executions are dispatched per scan layer and can run in parallel via LangGraph routing.
  • Overall pipeline is executed on a single-worker thread pool created per run and guarded by settings.pipeline.timeout_s.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Each node uses nl2sql.common.logger.get_logger() with node-specific names.
  • GraphState.trace_id is propagated into subgraph IDs and executor requests, but no code binds it into logging context (trace_context is defined but not used).
  • run_with_graph() accepts LangGraph callbacks via config={"callbacks": callbacks}.
  • No explicit metrics or tracing spans are emitted in the graph code.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• settings.pipeline.timeout_s (default 60) controls total pipeline timeout. It is read from the runtime (ctx.settings), as is every setting the nodes use.
  • Subgraph selection is governed by datasource capabilities in the subgraph registry.

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Add new subgraphs by constructing them in build_graph() and extending resolve_subgraph() with their required capabilities.
  • Insert additional nodes in build_graph() by adding nodes/edges to the StateGraph.
  • Customize routing by replacing build_scan_layer_router() or resolver_route().

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• execute=False in build_graph() makes layer_router return END instead of dispatching the aggregator, and is passed to the SQL agent subgraph.
  • Errors accumulated in GraphState.errors do not alter routing unless explicit routes inspect them.
  • No trace/span propagation into logging context, despite trace context helpers existing.
  • Merge reducers for artifact_refs/subgraph_outputs overwrite on key conflicts without ordering guarantees.

  • packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/datasource_resolver/node.py

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
• Purpose: plan, validate, generate, and execute SQL for a single sub-query.
  • Why it exists architecturally: isolates SQL-capable execution into a reusable subgraph that can be scheduled per scan node in the global execution DAG.
  • When it is invoked: when layer_router resolves a datasource with SUPPORTS_SQL capability and sends a scan-layer payload.

Defining function: build_sql_agent_graph() Source file path: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/subgraphs/sql_agent.py

docs.title: Boundary Definition
docs.text: This subgraph encapsulates the SQL planning and execution loop for a single SubQuery. It does NOT perform cross-subquery aggregation, answer synthesis, or datasource resolution; those responsibilities are owned by the main pipeline graph and upstream nodes.

docs.title: Entry Conditions
docs.text:
Required state: - SubgraphExecutionState.trace_id - SubgraphExecutionState.sub_query (must include id, datasource_id, and intent)

Preconditions: - sub_query.datasource_id must map to a registered adapter/executor. - Schema store and vector store may be used if configured; otherwise schema retrieval falls back to full schema snapshot.

Triggering parent graph: - layer_router in the main pipeline graph sends build_scan_payload() to the subgraph via wrap_subgraph().

docs.title: Exit Conditions
docs.text:
Successful completion criteria: - Reaches END after executor and produces executor_response. - Or reaches END after clarifier, which asked which reading of the question was meant (NEEDS_CLARIFICATION, INFO): no SQL is generated or run, and the wrapper reports the sub-query with status needs_clarification.

Failure exits: - check_planner returns end when planner output is missing and retries are exhausted or errors are non-retryable. - check_logical_validation returns end when validation errors are non-retryable or retries are exhausted. - check_execution returns end after executor unless the database rejected the query as wrong (EXECUTION_FAILED) and retries remain: a success, a refusal (DB_EXECUTION_ERROR: permission, timeout, connection) and any other executor error all end the subgraph. - Cancellation forces end in router checks and in the retry handler. The run's CancellationToken is read from the RunnableConfig (configurable.cancellation_token); when no token is present the subgraph behaves as not cancelled.

Partial completion behavior: - If planner or logical validation errors are retryable and retry budget remains, execution loops via retry_handler → refiner → ast_planner. - So does a query the database rejected as wrong (an unknown column or table, a type mismatch, bad syntax): the adapter marks the error retryable and the executor reports it as EXECUTION_FAILED, with the database's own first line as the message.

docs.title: Internal Node Composition
docs.text:
Execution order (nominal path): - schema_retriever — SchemaRetrieverNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/schema_retriever/node.py — retrieve relevant schema tables/columns. - ast_planner — ASTPlannerNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/ast_planner/node.py — create SQL AST plan. - logical_validator — LogicalValidatorNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/validator/node.py — validate plan correctness and policy constraints. - clarifier — ClarifierNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/clarifier/node.py — validate the planner's alternative readings and, when two or three remain, end the sub-query by asking which was meant. See ClarifierNode. - generator — GeneratorNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/generator/node.py — generate SQL text from AST. - executor — ExecutorNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/executor/node.py — execute SQL and produce artifacts. - retry_handler — retry_node() — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/subgraphs/sql_agent.py — apply exponential backoff and increment retry count. - refiner — RefinerNode — packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/refiner/node.py — generate feedback for the planner.

Mermaid diagram (sql_agent only): 

flowchart TD
    schema_retriever --> ast_planner
    ast_planner -->|ok| logical_validator
    ast_planner -->|retry| retry_handler
    ast_planner -->|end| END
    logical_validator -->|ok| clarifier
    clarifier -->|ok| generator
    clarifier -->|end| END
    logical_validator -->|retry| retry_handler
    logical_validator -->|end| END
    retry_handler --> refiner --> ast_planner
    generator --> executor
    executor -->|retry| retry_handler
    executor -->|end| END

docs.title: State Contract
docs.text:
State model: SubgraphExecutionState (packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/state.py).

Field ownership, reducers, and lifecycle are defined in ../graph_state.md.

docs.title: Step-by-Step Execution Flow
docs.text:
1. schema_retriever builds a semantic query from sub_query and retrieves relevant schema context; if none found, it falls back to full schema snapshot.
  2. ast_planner runs an LLM planning chain to produce PlanModel.
  3. check_planner routes:
  4. ok if a plan exists.
  5. retry if errors are retryable and retry budget remains.
  6. end if errors are non-retryable or retries exhausted.
  7. logical_validator validates the plan for structural and policy compliance.
  8. check_logical_validation routes:
  9. ok when no blocking errors exist.
  10. retry when retryable errors exist and retry budget remains.
  11. end when errors are non-retryable or retries exhausted.
  12. clarifier passes straight through when the planner gave no alternative readings. Otherwise it runs each alternative through LogicalValidatorNode.check (the static checks and the caller's scope), drops those that fail, merges those that render to SQL another option has, and keeps the rest on ast_planner_response.alternatives. check_clarifier routes end when it asked (two or three options, a named phrase, state.clarify and settings.clarify.enabled on), else ok. Every path from the planner to the generator still passes the validator.
  13. generator converts the plan to SQL for the target datasource dialect.
  14. executor runs SQL via the datasource adapter and returns artifacts/errors. check_execution routes retry when every executor error is a retryable EXECUTION_FAILED and retry budget remains, otherwise end. It also routes retry when the query returned no rows on a filter value the column does not have but a close one exists (VALUE_NOT_FOUND ERROR, raised once per sub-query; see ExecutorNode), and when a COUNT counted rows a join repeated (JOIN_FAN_OUT ERROR, raised once per sub-query; see ExecutorNode). Only a finding of this attempt (its details.attempt) routes retry.
  15. If routed to retry: retry_handler waits with exponential backoff and jitter, then increments retry_count.
  16. refiner uses LLM feedback to enrich error context, then loops back to ast_planner. Both are told about the latest attempt only, as {node, error_code, message} (nl2sql.pipeline.retry_feedback): never an earlier attempt's errors again, never a stack trace or details.
  17. Subgraph terminates at END.

docs.title: Determinism Guarantees
docs.text: Determinism guarantees and non-determinism sources are documented in ../determinism.md.

docs.title: Error Propagation
docs.text: Failure domains, retry scope, and recovery limitations are centralized in ../failure_recovery.md.

docs.title: Retry + Recovery
docs.text: See ../failure_recovery.md for retry scope and recovery behavior.

docs.title: Performance Characteristics
docs.text:
• Blocking LLM calls: ASTPlannerNode and RefinerNode.
  • External I/O: vector store retrieval and schema store access in SchemaRetrieverNode; datasource execution in ExecutorNode.
  • CPU-bound steps: SQL generation via sqlglot in GeneratorNode.
  • Retry loop introduces sleep-based delays on failures.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Node-specific loggers are used (schema_retriever, planner, logical_validator, generator, executor, refiner).
  • trace_id is stored in state and forwarded to executor requests; logging context is not explicitly set.
  • No explicit metrics or tracing spans are emitted by the subgraph code.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Read from the runtime's settings.pipeline.retries when the subgraph is built:

  • max (default 3)
  • base_delay_s (default 1.0)
  • max_delay_s (default 10.0)
  • jitter_s (default 0.5)

docs.title: Extension Points
docs.text:
• Modify build_sql_agent_graph() to insert, remove, or rewire nodes and edges.
  • Add new subgraphs by constructing them in build_graph() and extending resolve_subgraph() with their required capabilities.
  • Replace node implementations via dependency injection in Runtime.

docs.title: Known Limitations
docs.text:
• Generator errors are not routed into the retry loop; a failure proceeds to executor, which reports MISSING_SQL, and terminates at END.
  • No subgraph-specific metrics or trace spans are emitted.
  • The executor retries only what the adapter marks retryable. An adapter that raises instead of returning a failed ResultFrame ends the sub-query with EXECUTOR_CRASH.

Because the generator has no retry edge, the invariant the loop depends on is that logical_validator rejects every plan generator would refuse to build. LogicalValidatorNode._validate_buildable() enforces it by running the generator's own _build_query() — see Buildability. Without it, a plan whose tables are not joined reached generator and ended the sub-query with a terminal SQL_GEN_FAILED.

docs.title: Charts
docs.text:
An answer's rows become a chart without a model call. engine.results.chart(result) reads the saved result and returns a ChartSpec: our own small typed chart (a line, a bar, a big number or a table), which to_vega_lite() exports for a browser. See Results API.

spec = engine.results.chart(result)          # a QueryResult, or a trace_id
spec.kind, spec.reason, spec.takeaway
vega = spec.to_vega_lite()                   # None for a table

docs.title: The spec
docs.text: Field Meaning kind line, bar, big_number or table title The question that ran (a run with one sub-query: its intent; a trace_id alone: Result) x, y, series, value Encodings (field, kind, a humanised title) the kind uses: x the time or category, y one or more measures, series a category split into lines, value the big number data ChartData: trace_id, result_id, columns, rows (at most charts.max_points), truncated takeaway One sentence from a template, or None for a table reason Why this kind, for example "one date column and 1 number"

docs.title: Column kinds
docs.text: The artifact writer records each column's kind in the run's manifest from the saved file's types: integer, decimal and float are number; date, time and timestamp temporal; string text; bool boolean; anything else other. When the run had one sub-query, its plan refines them: a DATE_TRUNC select item is temporal, a grouped DATE_PART('year', x) is temporal (a year axis), an aggregate is a measure, and a number that is grouped on is a dimension. In a plan that has an aggregate, a plain column that is not grouped on (an id) is a dimension too. With several sub-queries or no plan, every number is a measure and everything else a dimension.

docs.title: The five rules
docs.text:
First match wins.

# Shape of the result Chart 1 One row, one measure, at most one text column big_number 2 One temporal dimension, one to max_series measures, at least two rows line, x ascending 3 One temporal and one text dimension (at most max_series distinct values), one measure line with series 4 One text or boolean dimension, one to three measures, two to max_categories rows bar, in the plan's order if it ordered, else by the first measure descending 5 Anything else table

At most max_points rows are read. When the result has more, or was cut at the datasource row limit (ResultSummary.truncated), data.truncated is true and the chart is a table, so no point is dropped silently. kind= forces a kind the data can draw; any other is a ValueError naming the ones it can.

docs.title: Takeaways
docs.text:
Chart Sentence line "Revenue went from 100 in 2024-01-01 to 150 in 2024-03-01 (+50%)." For a series, the one with the largest last value. No change is given when an end is null or the start is zero. bar "Books has the highest sales: 50." (the category is written as the data has it) After a SUM or COUNT with no negative value: "..., 50% of the total shown." big_number "Total: 1,234.5." table none

Numbers have thousands separators and at most three digits after the point.

docs.title: Vega-Lite
docs.text: to_vega_lite() returns a Vega-Lite v5 spec with the rows inline (data.values): a line or bar mark, a temporal, ordinal (whole-number years, times of day) or nominal x, a quantitative y, several measures folded with a fold transform and told apart by a color field, and a color field for series. It sets no colour, scheme, font or size: the renderer's theme decides.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
# settings.yaml
charts:
  max_points: 1000
  max_categories: 20
  max_series: 5

docs.title: The chart chat tool
docs.text: In a conversation the chart tool charts the rows of an answer: turn (the latest turn with an answer when absent), step (the nth answer of the turn, from 1), result_id and kind. Its output is a chart whose body is the ChartSpec as JSON, titled with the question. It raises ToolNotApplicable when there is no answer with data, or its rows have expired.

docs.title: Diagrams
docs.text:
Arrives with K2 (Wave C, 0.9)

This page is a stub. engine.datasources.diagram exists with its final signature and raises NotImplementedError naming K2. The design is Wave C, section 4.

Two Mermaid views, written to read the same on a light or a dark page (no %%{init} line, no style, classDef or linkStyle):

  • The answer view, nl2sql.diagram_for(result): the tables each sub-query read, one edge per join.
  • The schema view, engine.datasources.diagram(datasource_id, *, user_context, tables=None): an erDiagram of the tables the caller's scope reaches. The caller is required.

docs.title: REST API (api)
docs.text:
The api section of nl2sql.yaml holds nl2sql-api's own settings. It is optional. The engine validates it like every other section (strict keys, ${env:...} references) and never reads it; nl2sql-api reads engine.config.api.

# nl2sql.yaml
api: { file: api.yaml }

# api.yaml
role_header: X-NL2SQL-Role      # a header a trusted proxy sets on every request
role: null                      # or one static role for every request
trust_body_role: false          # accept "role" in the request body (dev only)
cors_origins: [https://app.example.com]
Field Default Meaning role_header none The header a trusted, authenticating proxy sets with the caller's roles (comma-separated). Only configure it when the proxy overwrites that header on every request, or any client can pick its own role. role none One static role for every request, used when no header carries one. trust_body_role false Dev only: take user_context from the request body. Any client can then choose any role; the API logs a warning at startup. cors_origins [] Browser origins allowed to call the API. Empty, no cross-origin request is allowed.

The role sources are tried in that order: the header, then the static role, then the body (only with trust_body_role). A request with no role is a 401. See Caller role.

docs.title: Admin routes
docs.text:
The routes that change datasources, LLMs or the index need one of the roles in policies.admin_roles (default [admin]), which is a policy, so it lives in the policies section, not here. A request with another role is a 403.

Without any role source (role_header, role and trust_body_role all unset), admin routes answer loopback clients only, so a fresh local install still works and a published port does not hand out admin. See Admin routes.

docs.title: Starting nl2sql-api
docs.text:
nl2sql-api builds its engine from NL2SQL_CONFIG (else ./nl2sql.yaml), after loading the .env next to that file without overriding a variable already set. It calls engine.check() before it accepts requests: a required datasource that fails, or datasources configured and none ready, stops it with EngineNotReady; an optional one that fails leaves it serving the others. See Startup.

NL2SQL_CONFIG=/etc/nl2sql/nl2sql.yaml uvicorn nl2sql_api.main:app

The NL2SQL_API_* variables of 0.4 are not read; see From 0.4.

docs.title: Curated Answers (curated.yaml)
docs.text:
The curated section of nl2sql.yaml, usually its own curated.yaml, is where a data team writes verified queries: SQL they have already written and reviewed, with typed parameters, and the questions each query answers.

What works today

The section is loaded and checked (at startup and with nl2sql curated validate), every query can be run once with nl2sql curated test, its questions are indexed with nl2sql index, a question is matched to a verified query and answered by it (see What happens at question time), and the playground badges such an answer Verified. The demo ships six verified queries (In the demo). Preferred tables (below) and proposals from thumbs-up feedback (From feedback to verified queries) are built too. Business metrics are parsed but not used yet.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
# nl2sql.yaml
curated: { file: curated.yaml }

The section is optional. Present, curated answers are on; absent, they are off, and nothing else changes. To turn them off, remove the line from nl2sql.yaml (the file can stay). A file: that does not exist is an error, and so is a section that is broken: building the engine (NL2SQL(config), nl2sql run, the REST API, the playground) fails with a ConfigError that names every problem, as a broken datasource does.

The matching knobs are in the settings section:

Setting Default Meaning settings.curated.match_top_k 5 Verified query candidates a question's search returns and the model is shown, one per query. settings.curated.match_floor 0.6 Cosine similarity the best candidate must reach before the model is asked to choose one. Below it the question is answered as if there were no curated section, with no model call. Calibrated on the local embedding model; see the design.

docs.title: Writing the file
docs.text:
One section covers every datasource, keyed by the datasource id. This is one of the demo's verified queries (nl2sql init --demo writes all six):

# curated.yaml
datasources:
  chinook:
    verified_queries:
      - id: top_customers_by_revenue
        description: "Customers ranked by invoiced revenue in a calendar year"
        questions:
          - "Who are our top {n} customers by revenue in {year}?"
          - "Best {n} customers in {year}"
        params:
          n:    { type: int, default: 10, min: 1, max: 100 }
          year: { type: int, min: 2000, max: 2100, example: 2012 }
        sql: |
          SELECT c.CustomerId,
                 c.FirstName || ' ' || c.LastName AS customer,
                 c.Country,
                 ROUND(SUM(il.UnitPrice * il.Quantity), 2) AS revenue
          FROM Customer c
          JOIN Invoice i      ON i.CustomerId = c.CustomerId
          JOIN InvoiceLine il ON il.InvoiceId = i.InvoiceId
          WHERE CAST(strftime('%Y', i.InvoiceDate) AS INTEGER) = :year
          GROUP BY c.CustomerId, customer, c.Country
          ORDER BY revenue DESC, c.CustomerId
          LIMIT :n
    metrics: []

docs.title: A verified query
docs.text: Key Required Meaning id yes A slug: lower-case letters, digits and _, starting with a letter. Unique within its datasource. description yes What the query returns, in a sentence. questions yes, at least one Phrasings the query answers. {name} marks where a parameter goes. params no The parameters, by name. sql yes The query, in the datasource's own SQL dialect.

docs.title: A parameter
docs.text: Key Meaning type int, float, string or date (YYYY-MM-DD). default The value used when the question gives none. A param with no default is required. min, max Bounds, for int, float and date. choices The allowed values, for string. example A typical value, used where a value is needed and there is no default.

docs.title: The SQL
docs.text:
• Write it in the dialect of the datasource it belongs to: the SQLite example above uses strftime, a Postgres datasource would use EXTRACT. It is parsed with the dialect the datasource's adapter declares.
  • Exactly one statement, and a query: a SELECT, a set operation such as UNION, or a WITH around one. No INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, CREATE, DROP, ALTER, SELECT ... INTO or statements the parser cannot type (VACUUM, PRAGMA), anywhere in the tree, a CTE included.
  • Parameters are :name placeholders, and they are exactly the declared params: no placeholder without a param, no param the SQL does not use. Positional ? placeholders are refused. Values are always bound, never pasted into the text, so a value cannot change the shape of the query.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
metrics: (a list of name, description, expression, table) is accepted and checked for shape so the format is fixed, but nothing uses it yet.

Every key is checked: a misspelt one (descripton:) is an error, not ignored.

docs.title: Checking the file
docs.text:
nl2sql curated validate                              # ./nl2sql.yaml, or NL2SQL_CONFIG
nl2sql --config prod/nl2sql.yaml curated validate

Building the engine runs every startup check; a section that fails one exits 1 with the ConfigError. The command then adds the one that needs the index: every table a query reads (CTE names aside) is in its datasource's latest indexed schema, compared case-insensitively. A datasource that has not been indexed yet is skipped for that check, with a note. The command prints a table, one row per query, and exits 1 on any error, so it can run in CI:

                         Verified Queries
┏━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ Datasource ┃ Query                    ┃ Status ┃ Details                            ┃
┡━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ chinook    │ top_customers_by_revenue │ OK     │ Verified against the indexed schema │
└────────────┴──────────────────────────┴────────┴────────────────────────────────────┘
Check At startup curated validate YAML parses and every key is known yes yes Every datasource key is a configured datasource yes yes Query ids unique within a datasource yes yes Every {placeholder} in a question is a param, every param is in a question yes yes Defaults, examples, bounds and choices agree with the type yes yes SQL is one read-only query in the datasource's dialect yes yes SQL :name placeholders are exactly the params yes yes Tables the SQL reads are in the indexed schema no yes, when indexed

From Python, the same check is engine.curated, on the engine's own config:

from nl2sql import NL2SQL

engine = NL2SQL.from_config("nl2sql.yaml")
report = engine.curated.validate()
if not report.ok:
    for error in report.errors:
        print(error)
    for entry in report.entries:
        print(entry.datasource_id, entry.query_id, entry.status, entry.details)

docs.title: Testing the queries
docs.text:
validate reads the SQL; it does not run it, so a column renamed under a query passes it. nl2sql curated test runs every verified query once against its database:

nl2sql curated test
nl2sql --config prod/nl2sql.yaml curated test

It reads the same config as validate. Each param is bound to its default, else its example; a param with neither fails its query without running it, so give every required param an example. A query that fails the static checks (not read-only, placeholders that do not match the params) is never run. The rest run read-only through their datasource's adapter, the same path a matched question takes, with the values bound and only the first batch of rows fetched. It prints one row per query and exits 1 if any fails, so it can run in CI after a schema change:

                                     Verified Queries
┏━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ Datasource ┃ Query                    ┃ Status ┃ Params          ┃ Details                                      ┃
┡━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ chinook    │ top_customers_by_revenue │ PASS   │ n=10, year=2012 │ 10 rows in 0.00 s                            │
│ chinook    │ revenue_by_year          │ FAIL   │                 │ The database rejected the query: no such     │
│            │                          │        │                 │ column: Total                                │
└────────────┴──────────────────────────┴────────┴─────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

From Python it is engine.curated.test(), which returns a report like validate()'s: ok, errors, and one entry per query with its status (PASS or FAIL), params, row_count and details.

docs.title: Indexing the questions
docs.text:
nl2sql index embeds every phrasing of every verified query, and its description, beside the datasource's schema entries. Placeholders are filled first with the param's example, else its default: "Best {n} customers in {year}" is indexed as "Best 10 customers in 2012". The SQL is never indexed.

After editing the curated section, re-index its questions:

nl2sql index --refresh                       # every datasource
nl2sql index --refresh --datasource chinook  # one

--refresh writes the entries again from the stored snapshot and embeds only those whose text changed (here, the verified queries): it reads no schema and makes no model call, so it takes seconds. The datasource must have been indexed once with plain nl2sql index. A plain nl2sql index also picks up the file, and a schema re-index always keeps the verified queries.

Until you re-index, nl2sql doctor and the index status (engine.index.health(), GET /api/v1/index/status) warn:

Warning: curated.yaml changed for 'chinook' since it was indexed; run `nl2sql index --refresh --datasource chinook`.

It is a warning, not a failure: the index stays ok, because the stale entries still name queries that exist.

docs.title: What happens at question time
docs.text:
With the file loaded and at least one verified query in it, every question that executes starts at the curated matcher (node reference):

  1. It searches the indexed phrasings of the verified queries of the datasources the caller's role may read (only the pinned datasource when a request names one), and keeps the best settings.curated.match_top_k queries.
  2. If the best one's similarity is below settings.curated.match_floor, the question goes to the normal pipeline. No model call is made.
  3. Otherwise one model call sees those candidates: each one's datasource.id, description and params (type, bounds, choices, default). Never the SQL. The model picks the one that answers the whole question and gives its parameter values, or answers none_of_these.
  4. Code checks the values against the param specs. A param the question does not give takes its default; a required one missing, or a value out of bounds, sends the question to the normal pipeline.
  5. Every table the SQL reads must be allowed for the role by the policies section. If one is not, the question goes to the normal pipeline, which refuses it the way it always does. The user is never told a verified query exists.
  6. The SQL runs with the values bound by the driver, through the same executor as generated SQL. The row limit is the datasource's row_limit (capped by settings.results.row_limit): the executor stops reading there and marks the result cut, rather than adding a LIMIT to your SQL. The result is saved, paged and exported like any other, and the answer is written from it, told what the numbers mean by the query's description.

A verified answer costs two model calls (the choice and the answer). When anything above does not hold, the run continues as if there were no curated section, and the answer is generated.

Every answer says where it came from, in QueryResult.source (and the REST response):

{"type": "verified", "id": "top_customers_by_revenue", "datasource_id": "chinook", "params": {"n": 5, "year": 2012}}

or {"type": "generated", ...} with the other fields null. The sub-query of a verified answer has plan_source: "verified", its sql is your SQL with its :name placeholders, and its plan is null.

In the playground a verified answer carries a green Verified · top_customers_by_revenue label beside the question, with the bound values in its tooltip. The Plan station says no plan was written and lists the query and its values, the Checks station shows the matcher's three checks (read-only, params, role), and the SQL station shows your SQL as Verified SQL, with its placeholders. A generated answer looks as it always has.

Why a question was not matched is in the run trace: the curated_matcher node's curated_match record lists the candidates and their similarities, the floor, the model's choice and reason, the checked values, and one reason code: not_configured, no_candidates, below_floor, none_of_these, model_failed, unknown_query, param_invalid, param_missing, policy_denied, capability_missing or execution_failed. A verified query that fails to run also adds a warning to the result.

The model for the choice is the curated_matcher agent in the llm section, falling back to the top level.

Parameters are bound by the datasource's adapter. Every built-in adapter binds them; a third-party adapter has to declare SUPPORTS_BOUND_PARAMETERS (SDK), and a verified query with params on one that does not is never run (capability_missing).

docs.title: In the demo
docs.text:
nl2sql init --demo (which nl2sql demo runs the first time) writes curated.yaml with six verified queries on Chinook and includes it from nl2sql.yaml; nl2sql demo indexes their questions with the schema:

Query One of its phrasings Params top_customers_by_revenue "Who are our top {n} customers by revenue in {year}?" n (default 10), year (example 2012) revenue_by_year "What is the total revenue per year?" none monthly_revenue "What was the monthly revenue in {year}?" year (example 2013) sales_by_country "What are total sales by country?" none best_selling_genres "Which genre sells the most tracks?" n (default 5) top_artists_by_tracks_sold "Who are the top {n} artists by tracks sold?" n (default 10)

Two of the guided questions, "What is the total revenue per year?" and "Which genre sells the most tracks?", are phrasings of these, so with a key they come back verified. Check and run them with nl2sql --config nl2sql-demo/nl2sql.yaml curated validate and nl2sql --config nl2sql-demo/nl2sql.yaml curated test.

The keyless demo (a hosted Space with no key, or nl2sql demo replaying recordings) answers from recorded model answers, and those include the matcher's VerifiedQueryChoice for every guided question. So without a key, "What is the total revenue per year?", "Which genre sells the most tracks?", "How many customers do we have, by country?" and "How many purchases were there per month in 2013?" come back verified, and the rest generated.

docs.title: Preferred tables
docs.text: Preferred tables are not in the curated section: they are a preferred_tables list on a datasource, naming views or tables (built by the data team, never by the package) the planner should reach for first. See Datasources: preferred tables.

docs.title: From feedback to verified queries
docs.text:
A thumbs-up on a generated answer is a candidate verified query: a real question, and SQL a person said was right. engine.feedback.record(..., rating="up") files it in the review queue as a verified_query proposal; it reaches the curated section only when an admin accepts it.

nl2sql review list --kind verified_query --as admin
nl2sql review show <id> --as admin
nl2sql review accept <id> --as admin

The proposal's change is an entry in the curated section's shape, for the datasource the run used:

id: how_many_customers_are_in_brazil
description: 'TODO: say what this query returns. ...'
questions:
- How many customers are in Brazil?
sql: |
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM Customer WHERE Country = 'Brazil'
  • id comes from the question: lower case, words joined by _, at most 60 characters, q_ in front when it would start with a digit.
  • questions holds the question as it was asked, as the one phrasing.
  • sql is the run's generated SQL, exactly as it ran. Every value in it is literal ('Brazil' above): the proposal has no params.
  • description is a placeholder.

The same question and SQL is one proposal however often it is rated; a new SQL for the same question supersedes the open one. These file nothing: thumbs-down ratings, answers that came from a verified query already, runs that did not succeed, runs with no SQL or more than one statement, runs on more than one datasource, and ratings recorded before the feedback table kept the datasource (see Feedback and Signals).

Accepting is the approval. Before accepting, a reviewer checks the SQL answers the question and, with edits (or by editing the change in a review file), writes the description, turns the values a reader would change into {params} in the question and :params in the SQL with a params: entry, drops the row-cap LIMIT the generator added unless the question asks for it, and adds other phrasings. Accept then runs the curated checks on the edited section, rewrites the section's own file (curated: {file: curated.yaml}) in canonical form, swaps the engine's curated answers and refreshes that datasource's curated index entries, so the next question can match it. An inline section, or a config built in code, is never written: export the proposals and edit by hand. See The review queue.

Accept rewrites curated.yaml

The rewrite is canonical: keys in the models' order, datasources and params sorted by name, SQL as literal blocks, under a fixed header. Comments in curated.yaml are not kept; write remarks in a query's description. A file edited since the engine loaded it is never overwritten: accept refuses with FILE_CHANGED.

docs.title: Datasource Configuration
docs.text:
The datasources section of nl2sql.yaml lists the databases the engine can query. nl2sql init writes it as a folder, one file per datasource, so each team can own its own database's file:

# nl2sql.yaml
datasources: { file: datasources/ }

# datasources/sales.yaml   (the id defaults to the file name: "sales")
type: postgres
description: Orders, customers and revenue for the EU shop.
connection:
  host: db.internal
  port: 5432
  database: sales
  user: nl2sql
  password: "${env:SALES_DB_PASSWORD}"
limits: { row_limit: 1000, timeout_ms: 8000, max_bytes: 10485760 }
index:
  exclude_tables: ["*.*_audit"]
preferred_tables: [public.revenue_daily, v_monthly_sales]
domains: [revenue, customers, orders]
sample_questions:
  - What was revenue by region last quarter?
  - Which customers placed the most orders this year?
required: true

The section can also be a file holding the list (datasources: {file: datasources.yaml}), or the list written inline in nl2sql.yaml. An empty list is valid: the apps add datasources at runtime.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Field Default Meaning id the file name in a folder, otherwise required The datasource's id. In a folder, if it is given it must equal the file name. type required The adapter: sqlite, duckdb, postgres, mysql, mssql, or an adapter a plugin registers. A misspelt or uninstalled one is a ConfigError with "did you mean" and the install hint. description none What is in the database. The resolver's answerability check reads it, so write one. connection {} The adapter's connection settings, validated against its connection model; see Connection. Every value may be a ${provider:key} reference and keeps it until the adapter is built. A relative SQLite or DuckDB database is relative to nl2sql.yaml. limits none row_limit, timeout_ms, max_bytes; see Limits. index everything What of the database is indexed; see Index. preferred_tables [] Tables or views the planner should reach for first. See Preferred tables. sample_questions [] Questions the datasource answers. Each is indexed as an entry of its own (schema.datasource_example), one of the signals routing votes with. domains [] A routing hint written by people. Routing does not read it yet. required false engine.check() fails (EngineNotReady) when this datasource cannot connect, and the CLI, nl2sql-api and the demo refuse to start. See Startup.

In Python, Datasource(id=..., adapter=MyAdapter(...)) passes a built adapter object instead of type.

docs.title: Connection
docs.text:
Each adapter declares its connection keys in a connection model, and the keys are strict: a key the model does not have is an error when the engine is built, with the field it was probably meant to be.

datasources[0].connection: connection.hostname: unknown key 'hostname'. Did you mean 'host'?
Adapter Keys sqlite database (the file) duckdb database (the file, or :memory:) postgres host, port (5432), database, user, password, sslmode (disable, prefer (default), require, verify-full) mysql host, port (3306), database, user, password mssql host, port (1433), database, user, password, driver (the newest ODBC Driver N for SQL Server installed), trusted_connection (false), encrypt (true), trust_server_certificate (false)

postgres, mysql and mssql also take pool, the connection pool:

connection:
  host: db.internal
  # ...
  pool: { size: 5, max_overflow: 0, timeout_s: 30, recycle_s: 1800 }   # the defaults
Key Default Meaning size 5 Connections kept open max_overflow 0 Extra connections allowed under load timeout_s 30 How long a query waits for a free connection recycle_s 1800 A connection older than this is replaced

With no overflow, size is also the most queries NL2SQL runs against that database at once, so it cannot overload a production server. A SQLite or DuckDB file has no pool.

In Python, connection may also be the adapter's model, used as given:

from nl2sql.adapters.postgres.adapter import PostgresConnection

Datasource(id="sales", type="postgres",
           connection=PostgresConnection(host="db.internal", database="sales", user="nl2sql",
                                         password=os.environ["SALES_DB_PASSWORD"]))

The model's JSON Schema (PostgresConnection.model_json_schema()) describes the form for connecting that database; a password is "format": "password".

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
limits:
  row_limit: 1000       # the most rows one sub-query returns
  timeout_ms: 8000      # the longest one statement may run
  max_bytes: 10485760
  • timeout_ms: every built-in adapter enforces it (SQL Server rounds up to whole seconds; SQLite stops a statement with a progress handler). Every session is read-only where the database allows it, with no setting; SQL Server cannot, and check() warns. See each adapter page for how.
  • row_limit: unset, it is settings.results.row_limit (100,000); set higher, settings.results.row_limit still bounds it. A result that reaches it is flagged as truncated and the answer says so.
