engine.evals measures how well the engine answers your questions. You write cases (a question, what each role should get, and the SQL a person reviewed) in suite files. A run asks every case once per role and scores it with registered scorers, and the result is an EvalReport.

The package ships one suite, Chinook's 47 gold cases, and nl2sql init --demo copies it next to the demo's nl2sql.yaml. The format is in Cases and suites, and what makes a case pass is in Scorers. To build a suite for your own database, seed draft cases from its schema and review them (Benchmark your own database).

docs.title: Configuring it
docs.text:
evals.yaml is a config section, like curated.yaml. Its keys are strict and it is loaded with the config:

# nl2sql.yaml
evals: { file: evals.yaml }

# evals.yaml
suites: [evals/chinook.yaml]       # relative to nl2sql.yaml
scorers: [result_match, outcome, faithfulness, retrieval_recall, routing]   # the default: all five
curated: true                      # mode full: curated answers on (the default)
max_cost_usd: 5.00                 # mode full's dollar cap over a whole run; it needs one
gate: { max_regressions: 2, alpha: 0.05, max_cost_increase: 0.20 }

A suite file is data. It is read when a run asks for it, never when the engine starts, so a large suite does not slow down engine start. gate configures the regression gate, which compares a run with a baseline.

docs.title: The facade
docs.text:
from nl2sql import NL2SQL, load_config

engine = NL2SQL(load_config("nl2sql.yaml"))
report = engine.evals.run(mode="plans")          # no key, no cost
print(report.accuracy, report.accuracy_generated)
Method What it does engine.evals.load(path=None) The suites evals.yaml names, or the one file at path, as EvalSuites engine.evals.run(suites=None, *, mode="full", llm=None, cases=None, roles=None, scorers=None, curated=None, passes=1, max_cost_usd=None, on_case=None, clarify=False) Runs every approved case once per role in its outcome map, passes times, and returns an EvalReport engine.evals.gate(report, baseline) The regression gate: report against a baseline report, record or benchmarks/ folder, with evals.yaml's gate settings. Returns a GateResult (The gate) engine.evals.regenerate(path, *, allow_packaged=False) Runs each approved case's sql and alt_sql through its datasource's adapter and writes rows and alt_rows (Regenerating rows). A suite the package ships is refused unless allow_packaged engine.evals.seed(datasource_id, *, count=20, out, user_context, max_cost_usd=None) Drafts up to count cases from the datasource's schema, as user_context sees it, and appends them to out as status: draft. Returns a SeedReport (Benchmark your own database) engine.evals.scorers() The registered scorer names: the five built-ins and any plugin's

The run arguments:

  • cases narrows the run by case id or tag. A selector that matches nothing is an error.
  • roles narrows it by role.
  • An argument left as None takes its value from evals.yaml.

on_case(config, record, spent) is called after each case. It gets the config's name, the case's record and the dollars spent so far.

docs.title: The modes
docs.text:
Mode What runs Model calls Curated answers Plan cache full The whole pipeline, on the configured LLM or on each named config yes; needs max_cost_usd as curated says (on by default) off plans Each case's hand-written plan through the validator, generator and executor, on the gold-plan fake LLM none off as configured retrieval Datasource routing and schema retrieval only none (the configured embedder) off not used

Every mode runs on a runtime derived from the engine's (ctx.derive), so the engine serving traffic never changes. In each mode:

  • Refusals are generic. A refusal message never names a table (policies.refusal_names_tables is off for the run). The outcome scorer checks for the generic message.
  • Mode full turns the plan cache off. A second pass asks the planner again instead of replaying the first pass's plans.
  • Modes plans and retrieval turn curated answers off. The curated matcher makes a model call the gold-plan fake cannot answer, and a verified hit would skip the plan or the retrieval being measured.
  • Mode retrieval always runs the vector search. Its runtime sets settings.retrieval.full_snapshot_max_tables to 0, because Chinook's 11 tables are under the limit that would otherwise skip the search.

docs.title: Mode full: the configured model, priced and capped
docs.text:
llm takes one of three values:

  • None: the engine's own llm section, reported as default.
  • One LLM.
  • A mapping of names to LLM sections. Each one runs on its own derived runtime over the same cases, and the report compares them.

The named configs in nl2sql/evaluation/presets/ are llm sections too: load_llm_file(path) and model_config("gpt-5.4") in nl2sql.evaluation.presets build one.

Every call costs money, so mode full checks prices before it starts and checks the cap before every case:

  • Every model must have a price. Before any call, every model that any node of any config would use must have a price, in llm.prices or the engine's dated table (Prices). A missing price is an UnknownPriceError naming the config, the node and the model.
  • The run stops before it could pass the cap. Before each case, the run adds the most expensive case so far to its running total. If that could pass max_cost_usd, the run stops and the report says stopped: "max_cost".
  • The first case always runs. So a run can pass the cap by at most one case's cost.
  • An unknown cost is not counted as zero. A call that reported no token counts (a failed call) cannot be priced. The run goes on, leaves it out of spent (so spent is a lower bound), counts it in the report's unknown_cost_calls, and logs one warning.

Each call is priced by the model its node is configured with, and the dollars are in report.spent and each record's cost.

docs.title: Curated answers in mode full
docs.text:
curated: true is the default. Each case record says where its answer came from in source (verified or generated).

A case that a verified query answered is run a second time with curated answers off, and that second run is scored as the case's generated answer (in the record's generated). Only the cases a verified query answered pay for the second run.

The report gives two accuracies:

Accuracy What it measures accuracy What users see accuracy_generated Every case on the generated path: the model's own skill, comparable across configs

Both are also split by source.

docs.title: Clarification
docs.text: A case may expect the engine to ask the caller to narrow the question (outcome clarify). Evals run with clarify=False, the default, so every other case measures the most likely reading: the clarify role runs are left out and counted in report.skipped. With clarify=True they run, and the outcome scorer passes them when the run's status is needs_clarification. The clarify suite holds such cases.

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
EvalReport has:

  • mode and suites (each suite's name, path and SHA-256 digest).
  • roles, passes, curated, clarify, max_cost_usd, spent, stopped, skipped and settings (mode retrieval's retrieval settings).
  • database: the datasource, engine and schema fingerprint of the datasources the suites name.
  • configs: one board per LLM config. Mode plans reports one board named plans, and mode retrieval one named retrieval.
  • comparison, when there are several configs.

report.accuracy and report.accuracy_generated read the first config's board.

Two accuracies, on purpose. accuracy.overall counts a case as passed only when every scorer that applies passes. In mode full with the default scorers, that includes faithfulness, retrieval_recall at 1.0 and routing. So it is stricter than the accuracy 0.6's tier 2 published. accuracy.execution is that older measure alone: result_match and outcome passed, no other scorer counted. Compare it, not overall, with the runs published before 0.7 (docs/benchmarks.md).

A board holds:

Field What it is accuracy overall (what users see), lenient, generated and execution, each with a 95% Wilson interval; pass_k over several passes; and the rates by_tag, by_difficulty, by_source and generated_by_source summary pass, fail, error and skip counts per role and in total scores Per scorer: how many cases it applied to, passed, failed and errored on, and its mean value retrieval The mean table and column recall over the cases retrieval_recall scored, how many were perfect, and how much was sent answerability, faithfulness, tokens_by_node, cost, latency, retries, errors_by_code, determinism As for a single run, summed or averaged over the cases models, planned_cases, completed_cases The config's model per node, and the cases the run would make and made results One record per case run: its status and reason, every scorer's score, the SQL, the answer, the plans, source and generated

Accuracy over 47 cases has an interval about 14 points wide, so two runs are compared case by case, not headline to headline. The statistics are in the Chinook suite.

docs.title: Events
docs.text: Each case runs under its own run scope (QueryAPI.open_scope and close_scope), so it publishes run.started and run.finished like any question. This includes mode retrieval, where no graph runs: its scope closes with an empty result. Every finished case also publishes eval.case on the engine's bus, with the suite, case, role, whether it passed, the answer's source, each scorer's verdict and its cost. The end of the run publishes eval.finished, with the suites, the number of cases, both accuracies and the dollars spent.

docs.title: The regression gate
docs.text:
engine.evals.gate(report, baseline) compares a run with a baseline and returns a GateResult:

Field What it is ok True only when the runs were compared and nothing regressed regressions One line per problem: too many cases flipped to fail, a significant drop, or a cost rise series_break Why nothing was compared: another suite digest, another mode, or no config in common compared Per config and measure: the cases that flipped each way, McNemar's p-value, both accuracies and both costs per case

The baseline is an EvalReport (or the JSON nl2sql eval run writes), a record from benchmarks/, or a path to either. A path to a benchmarks/ folder means its newest record of the run's mode, database and config.

Only the same suite and mode compare. Two runs are compared only when the suites' digests match and the mode is the same. Anything else is a series break: ok is false and nothing is compared.

The gate reads execution accuracy. A case passes when result_match and outcome pass; no other scorer counts. That is accuracy.execution, the measure 0.6's tier 2 published, so a run compares with the history published before 0.7 and a faithfulness verdict alone is never a regression. A kind: routing case has no rows to check and is left out of it. With curated answers on, it is checked twice: as users see it, and on the generated path. Mode retrieval has no execution, so its cases are read by their status.

For each config both runs have, the gate fails when:

  • more cases passed in the baseline and fail now than are allowed. Mode full allows max_regressions (2 by default), because the model is noisy. Modes plans and retrieval run no model, so they allow none: any flip is a real break;
  • in mode full, more cases were lost than gained and McNemar's exact two-sided p-value on the flips is under alpha; or
  • cost per case rose by more than max_cost_increase.

Comparable means what the history page means by it (records.series_key): the same mode, suite digest and schema fingerprint and, in mode full, the same roles and curated answers. Both runs must also have run the same roles, so a role left out cannot quietly shrink the comparison.

The statistics are in the Chinook suite.

docs.title: The CLI
docs.text:
Command What it does nl2sql eval run [--suite PATH ...] [--mode full\|plans\|retrieval] [--llm SPEC ...] [--cases ID/TAG ...] [--passes N] [--max-cost USD] [--baseline PATH] [--out FILE] engine.evals.run, then engine.evals.gate with --baseline nl2sql eval regenerate PATH engine.evals.regenerate; exits 1 when a case's SQL failed nl2sql eval seed --datasource ID --out PATH [--count N] [--role R] [--max-cost USD] engine.evals.seed, as --role (else policies.default_role); exits 2 on a refusal, 3 at the cost cap or the call limit, and refuses to run when CI is set (Benchmark your own database) nl2sql eval publish [REPORT ...] [--note TEXT] [--from DIR ...] Records each report under benchmarks/, then rebuilds the results page and the README block. Run from the repo root

--llm names an LLM config to compare in mode full, and repeats:

  • gpt-5.4, mini-helpers or claude-planner: a preset from nl2sql/evaluation/presets/, named by itself;
  • mine.yaml: a file holding an llm section, named by its stem;
  • NAME=PRESET or NAME=FILE: either, under a name you choose.

Without it, the config's own llm section runs as default.

nl2sql eval run writes the report to --out, by default eval_<mode>.json next to nl2sql.yaml, with a run stamp: when it ran, and the engine version and commit. nl2sql eval publish records that stamp, not the time it publishes.

Exit code When 0 The run finished, and nothing regressed against --baseline 1 A regression against --baseline 2 A usage error: a bad --llm, a run the engine refuses (no cost cap, an unpriced model), mode full with CI set (whatever its value, CI=false included), a missing or unreadable baseline, or one that cannot be compared 3 The cost cap stopped mode full early: the report is partial 
# From a demo folder: the key-free gate CI runs, against the repo's records
nl2sql eval run --mode plans --baseline ../benchmarks
# A paid run comparing two configs, under a $10 cap
nl2sql eval run --mode full --llm gpt-5.4 --llm mini=mini-helpers --max-cost 10
# From the repo root: record it and rebuild the results page
nl2sql eval publish demo/eval_full.json --note "slim prompts"

docs.title: In CI
docs.text:
The key-free eval-gates job (parallel to the integration tests) runs the eval gate on the demo's Chinook suite and on the routing suite, after indexing them:

nl2sql --config demo-ci/nl2sql.yaml eval run --mode plans --baseline benchmarks
nl2sql --config demo-ci/nl2sql.yaml eval run --mode retrieval --baseline benchmarks
nl2sql --config demo-ci/nl2sql.yaml eval run --mode retrieval --suite evals/routing.yaml \
  --baseline benchmarks --out demo-ci/eval_routing.json

Each run is gated against the newest record of its mode and database in benchmarks/ (plans/chinook/, retrieval/chinook/ and retrieval/chinook-support-webanalytics/). The three reports are uploaded as the eval-reports artifact whether the gate passed or not. On the routing suite, a case that loses its routing top-1 or a shortlisted datasource is a flip, and mode retrieval allows none. A changed suite or schema starts a new series, so the gate exits 2 until the baselines are recorded again. The integration job also runs tests/e2e/test_evals_plans.py, where every case must pass for every role.

docs.title: Re-recording CI's baselines
docs.text:
CI's plans and retrieval baselines are recorded on CI's own runner (ubuntu-latest, Python 3.12), never on a laptop: retrieval recall passes a case only at 100% column recall, which near-tie rankings of the local ONNX embedder can move between platforms.

  1. Push the change. The eval-gates job's "Eval gate" steps run the three gates and upload eval_plans.json, eval_retrieval.json and eval_routing.json as the eval-reports artifact, pass or fail.
  2. Download them: gh run download <run id> -n eval-reports -D eval-reports.
  3. From the repo root, record the ones the change moved, naming where they came from: nl2sql eval publish eval-reports/eval_retrieval.json eval-reports/eval_routing.json --note "CI baseline: ubuntu-latest, Python 3.12, https://github.com/nadeem4/nl2sql/actions/runs/<run id>".
  4. Commit the records and the regenerated pages in the same PR, and push. The next run gates against them.

Never edit a record by hand, engine_version included. A change that moves the gate on purpose (a suite change, routing or retrieval work) re-records the baselines it moves this way, in the PR that makes the change.

Mode full spends a key: nl2sql eval run --mode full refuses to start when CI is set. The owner runs it before a release (Releasing).

docs.title: Cases and suites
docs.text:
A suite is a YAML file of cases. Each case is a question and what each role should get. An answerable case also has the SQL a person reviewed and the rows that SQL returns. nl2sql.evaluation.suite holds the model (EvalCase, EvalSuite), the loader and the writer.

version: 1
cases:

- id: chinook_001
  question: How many customers do we have, by country?
  datasources: [chinook]
  status: approved                  # draft | approved | retired; only approved cases run
  origin: hand                      # hand | seeded | feedback
  difficulty: easy
  tags: [aggregation, rbac-denial]
  outcome: {admin: allowed, analyst: allowed, viewer: refused}
  tables: [Customer]
  columns: [Customer.Country, Customer.CustomerId]
  order_matters: false
  sql: |
    SELECT Country, COUNT(CustomerId) AS customer_count
    FROM Customer
    GROUP BY Country
    ORDER BY customer_count DESC, Country
  rows:                             # written by regenerate, never by hand
  - {Country: USA, customer_count: 13}
  - ...
  plan: {...}                       # optional: the hand-written plan, for mode plans
Field Meaning id Unique in the suite question The natural-language question datasources The datasources the question is about. The routing scorer checks a run used exactly these. A case with sql names one status draft, approved or retired. Only approved cases run kind answer (the default, left out of the file) or routing: a case that says only where a question goes. A routing case has no sql, gets no result_match verdict and is left out of execution accuracy in every mode. An approved answer case that a role may answer must have sql; the loader rejects it otherwise origin hand (written by a person), seeded (drafted from a datasource's schema) or feedback (exported from a thumbs-up run) difficulty Optional: easy, medium or hard tags Free categories. A run can be narrowed to them, and the report gives accuracy per tag paraphrase_group Optional. Cases with the same intent share it and the same rows outcome Per role: allowed, refused, unanswerable or clarify. The case runs once per role named here tables, columns The tables the SQL reads, and the Table.Column names the answer needs. retrieval_recall scores against them order_matters Whether row order counts when rows are compared sql The reviewed SQL, in the datasource's dialect; null for an unanswerable case and for a kind: routing case rows The rows sql returns, as {column: value} maps. Written by regenerate, never typed by hand alt_sql, alt_rows Reviewed alternative answers and their rows plan Optional. A PlanModel written as data, which mode plans serves through its fake LLM. Mode plans needs one for every answerable case

The outcomes:

Outcome What the role should get allowed An answer. result_match then checks its rows refused The validator's refusal, with the generic message and no rows unanswerable The resolver's QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE clarify A request to narrow the question (status needs_clarification). This runs only with engine.evals.run(clarify=True); the outcome scorer passes it when the run asks and returns no rows

An approved case must have one alt_rows entry per alt_sql. An unanswerable case cannot have an alternative.

docs.title: Where suites live
docs.text:
evals.yaml names suites by path, relative to nl2sql.yaml. The suites the package ships are in nl2sql/evaluation/suites/, and nl2sql init --demo copies them into the demo's evals/ folder. engine.evals.load(path) and engine.evals.run([path]) also take a suite file directly.

The Chinook suite (suites/chinook.yaml) is 0.6's gold set (chinook_gold.yaml and chinook_gold_plans.yaml) with its keys renamed and nothing else changed:

Was Now datasource datasources expected outcome needed_tables, needed_columns tables, columns gold_sql, gold_result, alt_gold_sql, alt_gold_result sql, rows, alt_sql, alt_rows plans in chinook_gold_plans.yaml plan on each case

test_chinook_suite_holds_the_gold_data_unchanged pins a SHA-256 of every case's question, SQL, rows, alternatives, outcomes, tables, columns and plan, taken from the old files with the old loader. The Chinook suite describes it.

docs.title: The routing suite
docs.text:
suites/routing.yaml asks which of the demo's three databases (chinook, support, webanalytics) a question belongs to. Every case is approved, origin: hand, asked as admin, and names the datasources a right answer needs. None names tables, so in mode retrieval the routing scorer alone decides it. Its tags say where each case came from:

Tag Cases gold The Chinook suite's 43 answerable questions. Their answers are checked in chinook.yaml; here a recall miss cannot hide a routing one sample Each demo datasource's sample questions, as nl2sql init --demo writes them paraphrase, hand Questions written for routing and read against each datasource's schema, most about support and webanalytics. Ten carry reviewed SQL, with rows written by regenerate, so mode full checks those answers too

Every case without SQL is kind: routing, so mode full's execution accuracy is over the ten answered cases only. The suite's header names the cases with two defensible answers (support holds the same customers as Chinook), which a routing change may flip on purpose. | cross-database | Three questions that need two databases |

Every case also carries the names of the datasources it needs as tags, so --cases support runs every case about support, cross-database ones included. Mode plans cannot run the suite, since its cases have no plans. So the demo's evals.yaml names only chinook.yaml, and the routing suite is run by name:

nl2sql eval run --mode retrieval --suite evals/routing.yaml --out eval_routing.json   # no key: CI's gate
nl2sql eval run --mode full --suite evals/routing.yaml --max-cost 5                   # the release check

In mode retrieval a case passes when routing ranks one of its datasources first and shortlists all of them (settings.routing.candidates, cut at max_datasources). A few cases fail today; the baseline records where routing misses, and the gate allows no other case to start failing. The test bed's 1,200-table wide schema has routing cases of its own in the realdb job (tests/realdb/test_routing_wide.py), since they need the test bed's databases.

docs.title: The clarify suite
docs.text:
suites/clarify.yaml holds five approved cases about "sales", which the demo glossary leaves open: two terms list it as a synonym, revenue and invoiced total, so a planner that sees both names the phrase and the run ends needs_clarification. Each case expects clarify from admin and has no SQL: what the asker picks next is a person's choice, not a gold answer. The suite is copied by nl2sql init --demo but not named in evals.yaml, since its cases run only with clarification on:

engine.evals.run(suites=["evals/clarify.yaml"], clarify=True)

docs.title: Regenerating rows
docs.text:
rows and alt_rows are never typed by hand. After you add or edit a case, an alternative or any SQL, run:

engine.evals.regenerate("evals/mine.yaml")

For each approved case with SQL, regenerate asks the case's datasource adapter to run sql and every alt_sql. It goes through the engine's DatasourceRegistry, read-only and within the datasource's limits: the expected rows come from the same adapter questions run on. The rows are written back in the order the SQL returns them.

The returned RegenerateReport counts the result sets written, and lists in failed each case left unchanged and why:

  • the SQL failed;
  • the result was cut at the datasource's row limit;
  • a case with SQL names more than one datasource.

A suite the package ships (nl2sql/evaluation/suites/) is refused unless you pass allow_packaged=True. In an installed package it is not yours to rewrite: copy it into your project, as nl2sql init --demo does. The repo's own workflow passes the flag, from a checkout, after a reviewed alt_sql is added to suites/chinook.yaml.

The other cases are still written. The file keeps its leading comment lines and its layout, and the committed Chinook suite is byte for byte what regenerate writes.

docs.title: Drafts
docs.text:
A case that a machine wrote starts as a draft, and a draft never runs. nl2sql eval seed (engine.evals.seed) drafts cases from a datasource's schema, with origin: seeded (Benchmark your own database). nl2sql feedback export --good (engine.feedback.export(path)) writes each thumbs-up run as a draft case to a suite file of its own, with origin: feedback, the run's SQL, the datasources it read, and the rating role allowed.

To promote a draft:

  1. Check that the SQL answers the question.
  2. Fill in difficulty, tags, tables, columns and the outcome for each role.
  3. Set status: approved.
  4. Run regenerate to write its rows.

Drafts never replace reviewed cases. Seeding and export refuse these paths:

  • a suite the package ships;
  • a suite evals.yaml names;
  • any existing file that holds an approved case.

A file of drafts may be written again.

docs.title: Scorers
docs.text:
A scorer decides whether one case run passed. It is a registry kind: the built-ins and any plugin's are listed the same way and named in evals.yaml's scorers.

Kind Entry point group Interface Version Built-ins scorer nl2sql.scorers nl2sql.evaluation.scorers.Scorer 1 result_match, outcome, retrieval_recall, faithfulness, routing

docs.title: The built-ins
docs.text:
Scorer Passes when Applies to Modes result_match The rows match the case's rows or any alt_rows an allowed role on a case with sql full, plans outcome The role got what the case says: an answer (allowed), the generic refusal (refused), QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE (unanswerable) or status needs_clarification (clarify) every role full, plans retrieval_recall The schema retriever sent every one of the case's tables and columns; the value is the column recall an allowed role with tables full, retrieval faithfulness Every number and quoted name the answer states is in the result or its counts a run that wrote an answer full routing Mode full: the run used exactly the case's datasources. Mode retrieval: routing ranked one of them first (top1), and all of them are among the datasources it ranked, up to settings.routing.max_datasources (shortlist) an allowed role full, retrieval

In mode retrieval, routing passes a case only on both top1 and shortlist. Its detail keeps each, with the ranking (routed) and the datasources it missed, and the board's routing gives the share of cases for each. The gate allows no flip in mode retrieval, so it fails when either drops. A kind: routing case (which says where a question goes, not what it returns) gets no result_match verdict and is left out of execution accuracy.

A scorer that does not apply to a case returns no verdict. A scorer that cannot score the run's mode is left out of that run.

A case passes when every scorer that applies to it passes. A scorer that raises scores the case as an error: its passed is None and the message is in detail["error"]. The run goes on, and the report counts errors apart from failures.

result_match compares rows strictly:

  • column names are ignored, and column order counts;
  • numbers match within half a cent;
  • row order counts only when order_matters.

It also keeps the lenient reading in detail["lenient"], which accepts reordered and a few extra columns, and period labels against dates. The report gives the strict and lenient accuracy side by side. The rules, and faithfulness's, are in the Chinook suite.

In mode full, retrieval_recall reads what the run's schema retriever sent. In mode retrieval, the runner runs the retriever itself, with the question as the query.

docs.title: The interface
docs.text:
# nl2sql/evaluation/scorers/__init__.py (engine side: a scorer sees a QueryResult)
class Score(BaseModel):
    value: float | None        # 0..1; None when the scorer does not apply to this case
    passed: bool | None
    detail: dict[str, Any] = {}

class CaseRun(BaseModel):      # what a scorer is given
    case: EvalCase
    role: str
    mode: str                  # "full", "plans" or "retrieval"
    result: QueryResult        # every row, not the capped sample a caller sees
    rows: list[list[Any]] | None     # the first result set's rows
    columns: list[str]
    retrieval: dict[str, list[str]] | None   # table -> columns the retriever sent
    routed: list[str] | None                 # mode retrieval: datasources, best first

class Scorer(Protocol):
    interface_version: ClassVar[int]          # 1
    config_model: ClassVar[type[BaseModel]]
    modes: ClassVar[frozenset[str]]           # the modes it can score
    @classmethod
    def from_config(cls, cfg: BaseModel) -> "Scorer": ...
    def score(self, run: CaseRun) -> Score: ...

CaseRun.expected is the case's outcome for the run's role. Each scorer is built once per run, from its config_model's defaults.

docs.title: Writing your own
docs.text:
A scorer that fails any answer slower than five seconds:

from nl2sql import NL2SQL, Registry, Score
from nl2sql.evaluation.scorers import NoConfig


class Fast:
    interface_version = 1
    config_model = NoConfig
    modes = frozenset({"full"})

    @classmethod
    def from_config(cls, cfg):
        return cls()

    def score(self, run):
        if run.expected != "allowed":
            return Score()                        # does not apply
        seconds = sum(run.result.timings.values())
        return Score(value=1.0 if seconds <= 5 else 0.0, passed=seconds <= 5,
                     detail={"seconds": seconds, "reason": f"took {seconds:.1f} s"})


registry = Registry.default()
registry.add_scorer("fast", Fast)
engine = NL2SQL(config, registry=registry)
engine.evals.run(scorers=["result_match", "outcome", "fast"], max_cost_usd=2)

A plugin package declares it as an entry point instead:

[project.entry-points."nl2sql.scorers"]
fast = "my_package.scorers:Fast"

Put a reason in detail when a case fails. The report shows the first failing scorer's reason for the case.

docs.title: Benchmark your own database
docs.text:
Chinook's suite measures the engine on Chinook. To measure it on your own data you need cases for your own schema, and writing forty of them by hand is the slow part. engine.evals.seed drafts them: a model proposes questions, the engine checks and runs each one, and you review what survives.

from nl2sql import NL2SQL, UserContext, load_config

engine = NL2SQL(load_config("nl2sql.yaml"))
report = engine.evals.seed("sales", count=20, out="evals/sales.yaml",
                           user_context=UserContext(roles=["analyst"]), max_cost_usd=0.50)
print(report.written, report.dropped_invalid, report.stopped_at_cost_cap)

nl2sql eval seed --datasource sales --count 20 --role analyst --max-cost 0.50 --out evals/sales.yaml

Every seeded case is a draft. A draft never runs in an eval: a person reads it, fixes it, and approves it (Drafts).

docs.title: How a case is seeded
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  S["The caller's tables<br/>(the live index build)"] --> M["eval_seeder<br/>5 questions + typed plans"]
  M --> V["Logical validator<br/>and generator"]
  V -->|refused| DI["dropped_invalid"]
  V --> H["execute.before and<br/>execute.after hooks"]
  H -->|"deny, failure,<br/>approval"| DH["dropped_hooked"]
  H --> X["The adapter runs the SQL<br/>read-only"]
  X -->|fails| DF["dropped_failed"]
  X -->|no rows| DE["dropped_empty"]
  X --> W["Appended as a draft"]
  1. The model sees what the caller may read. The eval_seeder agent is shown the datasource's live index build exactly as the planner would show it to the caller: tables, columns, keys, descriptions, and sample values where the datasource collects them (index.sample_values). A table the caller's role may not read never reaches the model.
  2. It writes questions and plans, never SQL. Each call asks for five questions of mixed difficulty, each with a typed plan in the planner's own format. Five keeps one structured answer small enough to parse, and one bad plan costs only its batch. Each call goes through parse-and-retry, like every structured call.
  3. The engine validates each plan before any SQL exists. The plan runs as a pinned plan under the caller's scope: the plan.after hooks, the logical validator and the generator, with no model call. A plan the validator refuses, a table the role may not read included, is dropped and counted. When a plan.after hook changes the plan, the draft keeps the changed plan: the one that produced its SQL.
  4. The SQL passes the execute hooks. The SQL is model-proposed, so it goes through execute.before and execute.after exactly as a question's SQL does: an approval hook or a cost guard sees it. A deny, a hook failure or a NeedsApproval drops the case (dropped_hooked); nothing is queued for approval. regenerate is different on purpose: it runs SQL a person reviewed and approved, and calls no hook (Hooks).
  5. The SQL runs read-only. The generated SQL runs through the datasource's adapter: a read-only session, the datasource's timeout, and the row limit the generator wrote into the SQL. Only the first row is read (execute_batches(request, 1) where the adapter streams), which is enough to know the query returns rows. A query that fails or returns no rows is dropped. No row is kept.
  6. Survivors are appended as drafts. Each one is written with status: draft, origin: seeded, the question, the engine's SQL, the plan, the tables and columns the plan reads, and an outcome. A question already in the file is skipped and counted as a duplicate. rows stay empty.

docs.title: Who it seeds as
docs.text:
Seeding needs a caller, and it fails closed:

  • With no user_context, or one with no role, it refuses before anything is asked.
  • A role whose scope does not reach the datasource, or reaches none of its tables, is refused. So is a role the policies do not define.
  • nl2sql eval seed asks as --role, else policies.default_role. With neither, it exits 2.

The drafts hold only what the caller may read. A draft's outcome marks allowed each of the caller's roles whose own scope reads every table of the plan; a role that reads only some of them (a caller's scope is the union of its roles) gets no entry. Add the outcome for every other role when you review them.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
Seeding is not a question, so the per-question caps in settings.pipeline do not apply. It runs under a budget of its own:

  • A dollar cap, always. max_cost_usd, by default evals.yaml's. With neither, seeding refuses to start.
  • A priced model. The eval_seeder agent's model must have a price, in llm.prices or the engine's dated table (Prices); otherwise seeding raises UnknownPriceError before any call.
  • At most three calls per batch of five, parse retries included, so a model that keeps answering nothing usable stops on its own.
  • A prompt that does not grow with the file. Each call is told how many questions are already written and shown only the newest ten, so it does not repeat them.

The budget is checked before each call. When either limit is reached, the next call is never sent, the drafts so far are written, and the report says which: stopped_at_cost_cap or stopped_at_call_limit. The eval_seeder agent runs on the top-level llm unless llm.agents.eval_seeder names another model (Agents).

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
SeedReport:

Field What it counts path The suite file written written Drafts appended dropped_invalid Plans the validator or a plan.after hook refused, questions that read as SQL, and the questions of a call whose answer never parsed dropped_hooked SQL an execute.before or execute.after hook denied, failed on, or asked approval for dropped_failed Queries the database rejected dropped_empty Queries that returned no rows dropped_duplicate Questions already in the file, or proposed twice stopped_at_cost_cap Whether the dollar cap stopped seeding early stopped_at_call_limit Whether the three-calls-per-batch limit stopped it early usage The model calls, tokens and dollars spent

nl2sql eval seed prints the counts and the dollars, exits 2 on a refusal (no role, an unreadable datasource, no cost cap, an unpriced model, a refused --out) and 3 when the cost cap or the call limit stopped it. Like mode full, it refuses to run when CI is set.

docs.title: Where drafts may go
docs.text:
out is relative to nl2sql.yaml, or absolute. Seeding appends to it and keeps its leading comment lines; a new file starts with a short header saying what the file is. Like feedback export, seeding never writes into:

  • a suite the package ships;
  • a suite evals.yaml names;
  • a file that holds an approved case.

Keep drafts in a file of their own, and move each case into a configured suite once it is approved.

docs.title: Reviewing the drafts
docs.text:
1. Read each question and its SQL. Fix the wording, or the SQL, or delete the case.
  2. Fill in tags, and the outcome for each other role (allowed, refused or unanswerable).
  3. Set status: approved and move the case into a suite evals.yaml names.
  4. Run nl2sql eval regenerate on that suite to write the expected rows.

From then on the case runs in nl2sql eval run, and the regression gate holds it.

docs.title: Execution Isolation and Concurrency
docs.text: This page describes how a pipeline run is bounded, cancelled, and protected in the current implementation. It is deliberately explicit about what the engine does not do, because the boundaries matter when you reason about failure.

docs.title: There is no process sandbox
docs.text:
The engine runs entirely in one process. run_with_graph() dispatches the graph onto a single-worker concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor (pipeline/runtime.py) created per run, so the caller's thread stays free to enforce GLOBAL_TIMEOUT_SEC. Concurrency across runs is the caller's to provide (a web server's own worker pool, for instance), not a setting of this engine. Threads share one interpreter and one address space.

Two consequences follow, and neither is a sandbox property:

  • A hard crash in a database driver (segfault, abort()) terminates the whole process, including the orchestrator. There is no disposable worker to absorb it.
  • Memory is shared. A run cannot be isolated from another run by the runtime.

docs.title: Validation before SQL exists
docs.text:
This is the engine's real safety property, and it holds. The LLM emits an Abstract Syntax Tree, never SQL text. The AST passes through LogicalValidatorNode (pipeline/nodes/validator/node.py) before the generator is reached. That node:

  • resolves every column against the retrieved schema snapshot using sqlglot.optimizer.qualify;
  • enforces the table policy through the caller's Scope (policies/scope.py), failing closed when no datasource ID is present.

An unvalidated plan never becomes SQL, so it never reaches an adapter. This is a correctness and authorization gate, not a containment boundary: it prevents bad SQL from being generated, it does not contain a driver that misbehaves on SQL that passed.

docs.title: Per-run cancellation
docs.text:
Each invocation constructs its own CancellationToken (common/cancellation.py) and threads it to nodes through config={"configurable": {"cancellation_token": token}}. Because the token is per-run, cancelling one run never affects another.

Nodes observe the token and unwind cooperatively, so a cancelled run returns a normal result carrying a CANCELLED PipelineError rather than raising. run_with_graph() cancels the token on SIGINT/SIGTERM, and on Windows interactive terminals also on Ctrl+X.

Cancellation is cooperative: a node blocked inside a driver call does not abandon that call. The token is checked between and within nodes, not inside third-party I/O.

docs.title: Global timeout
docs.text:
settings.global_timeout_sec (GLOBAL_TIMEOUT_SEC, default 60) is enforced by future.result(timeout=...) in run_with_graph(). On expiry the run's CancellationToken is cancelled and the caller gets a PIPELINE_TIMEOUT error and a user-facing message, within about a second of the limit.

The timeout bounds how long the caller waits, not how long the work runs. The underlying thread is not killed; it winds down in the background once its nodes observe the cancelled token, or once its current I/O completes.

docs.title: One circuit breaker
docs.text:
VECTOR_BREAKER (common/resilience.py) is the only breaker the system defines (fail_max=5, reset_timeout=30). It wraps vector-store retrieval in indexing/retrieval.py only.

LLM calls and SQL execution are not breaker-guarded. Their failures surface as PipelineError values in graph state; see Error Handling.

docs.title: Adapter-level limits
docs.text:
row_limit is real and is enforced where it cannot be talked around: the generator bakes min(plan.limit, row_limit) into the SQL it renders, where row_limit is the datasource's own bounded by RESULT_ROW_LIMIT (100,000) (pipeline/nodes/generator/node.py).

max_bytes is not enforced. It is read from datasource options, stored on the adapter and reported by the datasource API, and nothing ever compares it to anything. The adapter does estimate a result's size (average row size from a 50-row sample) and reports it as ResultFrame.bytes, but that number is only copied into metrics; no threshold is applied, nothing is truncated and no error is raised. Treat max_bytes as documentation of intent, not a limit.

Neither is isolation in any case.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Mechanism Module What it bounds AST validation + policies pipeline/nodes/validator/node.py What SQL may be generated at all CancellationToken common/cancellation.py One run, cooperatively global_timeout_sec pipeline/runtime.py How long the caller waits VECTOR_BREAKER common/resilience.py Vector retrieval only ThreadPoolExecutor pipeline/runtime.py One worker per run, so the caller can time out; not isolation

If you need blast-radius containment against driver-level crashes, run the engine in a process you are willing to lose (a per-request worker, a container replica) and rely on your supervisor to restart it. The engine does not provide that boundary itself.

docs.title: Adding a New Adapter
docs.text: This guide describes how to add a new datasource adapter and make it available to NL2SQL.

docs.title: 1. Implement the adapter contract
docs.text:
All adapters implement DatasourceAdapter, version 2, and declare a connection_model. See ../adapters/sdk.md for the authoritative contract and required fields/methods.

If you are building a SQL adapter, extend SQLAlchemyAdapter from nl2sql_sdk.sqlalchemy (pip install "nl2sql-sdk[sqlalchemy]"): it connects, executes, reads the schema the datasource's index scope wants with catalog row estimates and type-aware statistics, and reports what it could not read as issues. You implement url and get_dialect, and override system_schemas, row_estimates or column_profile where your database differs. See SQLAlchemy adapters and the complete example in Building adapters.

docs.title: 2. Register it
docs.text:
The engine finds an adapter by its type name in the registry. There are two ways to put a name there.

From a package, declare an entry point in the nl2sql.adapters group of your pyproject.toml:

[project.entry-points."nl2sql.adapters"]
snowflake = "nl2sql_snowflake.adapter:SnowflakeAdapter"

Registry.default() lists every installed entry point by name and imports none of them. An adapter is imported when a datasource uses its type.

In your own code, register the class on a registry you build:

from nl2sql.registry import Registry

registry = Registry.default()

@registry.adapter("snowflake")
class SnowflakeAdapter: ...

# or: registry.add_adapter("snowflake", SnowflakeAdapter)

A registration belongs to that registry only, so two engines or two tests never see each other's. Adding a name that is already there, including a built-in, raises unless you pass replace=True.

When the adapter is loaded, the registry checks three things and stops with a message that says how to fix each:

Check Fails with interface_version is the version this engine needs (2) nl2sql-snowflake implements adapter interface 1; this engine needs 2. every module in driver_modules is installed (importlib.util.find_spec, without importing it) the missing modules and your install_hint only one installed package declares the name both package names

An unknown type suggests the closest registered name. nl2sql list-adapters shows every registered adapter and whether it can be loaded.

docs.title: 3. Configure the datasource
docs.text:
Add a datasource to the datasources section of nl2sql.yaml, for example as its own file in datasources/:

# datasources/sales_db.yaml
type: postgres
description: "Sales warehouse"
connection:
  host: "${env:PG_HOST}"
  database: sales
  user: "${env:PG_USER}"
  password: "${env:PG_PASSWORD}"

References under connection are resolved by the engine's SecretManager when the adapter is built, and the block is then validated against the adapter's connection_model: an unknown key is an error.

docs.title: 4. Validate capabilities
docs.text:
Ensure capabilities() advertises the correct set for routing and execution:

  • supports_sql if SQL execution is supported.
  • supports_bound_parameters if execute (and execute_batches) bind AdapterRequest.parameters by name to :name placeholders through the driver. Without it, a verified query with parameters is never sent to the adapter. Adapters built on SQLAlchemyAdapter inherit both the binding and the capability.
  • enforces_read_only and enforces_timeout only when the session cannot write, and a statement past limits.timeout_ms is stopped, on a real server.

docs.title: 5. Optional: let scan() find it
docs.text:
engine.datasources.scan() offers the databases it finds in a connection URL, in files under a folder and on the default ports of 127.0.0.1. It finds an adapter only if the adapter declares how, with the four members of DiscoverableAdapter:

from nl2sql_sdk.discovery import Found

class SnowflakeAdapter:
    file_suffixes = ()
    default_ports = ()
    url_schemes = ("snowflake",)

    @classmethod
    def connection_for(cls, found: Found) -> dict | None:
        if found.kind != "url":
            return None
        ...  # parse found.value into the fields of SnowflakeConnection; never connect

An adapter without them still works; it is just chosen by name instead of found.

docs.title: Source references
docs.text:
• Adapter protocol: packages/sdk/src/nl2sql_sdk/protocols.py
  • Registry: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/registry.py
  • Datasource registry: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/datasources/registry.py
  • SQLAlchemy base adapter: packages/sdk/src/nl2sql_sdk/sqlalchemy/adapter.py

docs.title: Adding New Chunk Types
docs.text: Chunking is the backbone of retrieval. This guide explains how to add new schema chunk types.

docs.title: 1. Add a new chunk model
docs.text:
Define a new chunk class in nl2sql.indexing.models:

  • Inherit from BaseChunk.
  • Provide a stable, deterministic ID.
  • Implement get_page_content() and metadata via get_metadata().

docs.title: 2. Extend the chunk builder
docs.text:
Update SchemaChunkBuilder to emit the new chunk type:

  • Add a _build_*_chunks() method.
  • Include it in build() alongside existing chunk builders.

docs.title: 3. Update retrieval filters
docs.text:
If your chunk type should be retrievable:

  • Add it to the appropriate Retriever.retrieve_* filters. Its metadata must be scalars (an index entry holds nothing else).
  • Update SchemaRetrieverNode logic if new chunk types influence planning.

docs.title: 4. Update planner/validator (if required)
docs.text:
If the chunk type carries new semantics, ensure:

  • ASTPlannerNode prompt includes the relevant context.
  • LogicalValidatorNode can enforce any new constraints.

docs.title: Source references
docs.text:
• Chunk models: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/indexing/models.py
  • Chunk builder: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/indexing/chunk_builder.py
  • Retrieval: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/indexing/retrieval.py
  • Schema retriever: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/schema_retriever/node.py

docs.title: Adding an Execution Backend
docs.text: SqlExecutorService is the only execution backend. ExecutorNode constructs it directly and gates it on the datasource declaring supports_sql.

docs.title: 1. Implement the executor service
docs.text:
Create a class that implements:

  • validate_request(request) -> list[PipelineError]
  • execute(request) -> ExecutorResponse

Use ExecutorRequest/ExecutorResponse as the contract.

docs.title: 2. Wire the executor
docs.text: Construct the executor in ExecutorNode.__init__ and select it in __call__ based on the datasource's capabilities, asked through DatasourceRegistry.supports(). ExecutorNode._supports_sql() shows the existing check: a datasource whose adapter does not declare the required capability must get no executor rather than being run anyway.

docs.title: 3. Update routing (if needed)
docs.text:
If a new subgraph is required for the backend, add it as a node in:

  • packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/graph.py

and extend resolve_subgraph() in packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/graph_utils.py so the capabilities it requires match the adapter's advertised capabilities.

docs.title: 4. Artifact handling
docs.text:
If the backend returns tabular results:

  • Return a ResultFrame.
  • Persist it via ArtifactStore to produce an ArtifactRef.

docs.title: Source references
docs.text:
• SQL executor: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/execution/executor/sql_executor.py
  • Executor node: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/executor/node.py
  • Executor contracts: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/execution/contracts.py

docs.title: Extending the Planner
docs.text: The planner generates a structured AST (PlanModel) which is validated and compiled into SQL. Extending planner logic typically requires changes to schema models, prompts, validator, and generator.

docs.title: 1. Update AST schemas
docs.text:
Modify PlanModel or related AST models in:

  • packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/ast_planner/schemas.py

Keep these rules in mind:

  • Models are strict (extra="forbid").
  • Expression kinds must pass model_post_init validation.

docs.title: 2. Update planner prompt
docs.text:
Update the prompt and examples in:

  • packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/ast_planner/prompts.py

PLANNER_PROMPT is a chat template of two messages. PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT holds what is the same for every question (instructions, PLANNER_EXAMPLES, the schema) and PLANNER_HUMAN_PROMPT holds what changes per call (expected schema, feedback, the question). Keep per-question text out of the system message, or the provider's prompt cache stops hitting. See AST Planner: prompt layout.

Ensure structured output still matches PlanModel.

docs.title: 3. Update validator logic
docs.text:
The logical validator enforces:

  • query type (READ-only)
  • table/column existence
  • alias uniqueness
  • join relationships
  • expected schema alignment

Update LogicalValidatorNode to recognize any new AST constructs.

docs.title: 4. Update SQL generator
docs.text:
GeneratorNode and SqlVisitor translate the AST into sqlglot expressions:

  • Extend SqlVisitor to handle new expression kinds or operators.
  • Update GeneratorNode._generate_sql() if new clauses are added.

docs.title: Source references
docs.text:
• AST schemas: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/ast_planner/schemas.py
  • Planner node: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/ast_planner/node.py
  • Logical validator: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/validator/node.py
  • SQL generator: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/pipeline/nodes/generator/node.py

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
NL2SQL supports three ways to get started. Choose the guide that matches how you want to use the platform:

  • PyPI (Python API): Install nl2sql-engine and use it programmatically.
  • Docker (REST API): Run the API service and integrate over HTTP.
  • From Source (Development): Clone the repo for local development and contributions.

docs.title: Choose your path
docs.text:
• PyPI (Python API)
  • Docker (REST API)
  • From Source (Development)
  • Demo Data (CLI-first)
  • MCP server: serve the engine to a desktop assistant or an IDE with nl2sql mcp

docs.title: One config: nl2sql.yaml
docs.text: Every path reads the same config, nl2sql.yaml, and the files it includes. The CLI takes it from --config PATH, then the NL2SQL_CONFIG variable, then ./nl2sql.yaml; nl2sql-api from NL2SQL_CONFIG, then ./nl2sql.yaml; Python from NL2SQL.from_config(path). The sections, their fields and every 0.4 file and variable they replace are in Configuration.

docs.title: Start a config with nl2sql init
docs.text:
nl2sql init my-project                       # writes my-project/nl2sql.yaml and its files
nl2sql init my-project --provider anthropic  # llm.yaml names Anthropic and its default model
nl2sql init my-demo --demo                   # the demo: three sample databases, roles, verified queries

init asks no questions. It writes nl2sql.yaml as a table of contents and each section in its own file:

nl2sql.yaml            # the table of contents
datasources/
  example.yaml         # a sqlite example     (--demo: chinook.yaml, support.yaml, webanalytics.yaml)
llm.yaml               # provider and model; no key
embeddings.yaml        # provider: local
policies.yaml          # allow_all: true      (--demo: admin, analyst and viewer roles)
storage.yaml           # path: .nl2sql
knowledge.yaml         # one yaml knowledge source: glossary.yaml
glossary.yaml          # what people know about the data (--demo: the Chinook glossary)
curated.yaml           # --demo only: the demo's verified queries
settings.yaml          # --demo only: a 300 s timeout and a trace for every run
data/                  # --demo only: the three sample SQLite files
.gitignore             # .nl2sql/ and .env are added to it
  • No key is written. llm.yaml names no api_key, so the provider's standard variable (OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY) is read. Put it in your environment or in a .env file next to nl2sql.yaml: the CLI, nl2sql-api and nl2sql demo load that file at startup and never let it override a variable that is already set. To read another variable, write api_key: "${env:MY_KEY}".
  • Nothing is overwritten unless you pass --force. If any file init would write already exists, it names the files and writes nothing. .gitignore is never replaced; the lines it lacks are added.
  • The result is checked. init loads what it wrote with load_config before it reports success, then prints the next steps.
  • --provider is openai (the default), anthropic or openrouter.

Then point datasources/example.yaml at your database (or rename it: the file name is the datasource id), and build the index:

cd my-project
nl2sql index                                 # or, from elsewhere: nl2sql --config my-project/nl2sql.yaml index
nl2sql run "How many customers are there?"

nl2sql index and nl2sql run first call engine.check(): each datasource connects, or is reported and left out. A datasource with required: true that cannot connect stops the command. nl2sql doctor prints the same report without running anything.

When a question can be read more than one way, nl2sql run numbers the readings. On a terminal it asks which one and runs the question again with your choice; with no terminal (a script, a pipe) it prints them and exits 4. Asking again is the same step for code.

docs.title: Set up what the engine knows: connect, index, profile, review
docs.text:
After the first index, let the engine suggest what it cannot read from the schema, and decide what to keep:

nl2sql index                              # connect and index (--profile --as admin also profiles)
nl2sql profile --as admin                 # joins the database does not declare, column roles
nl2sql review list --as admin             # what the profiler found, with its evidence
nl2sql review accept --all --kind column --as admin   # writes glossary.yaml once

The profiler is deterministic and bounded (Schema Profiler); nothing it proposes reaches a prompt or the index until an admin accepts it (Review Queue).

From Python, nl2sql.config.init_project(folder, demo=..., provider=..., force=...) writes the same files, and nl2sql.config.demo_config() builds the demo's Config in code, with the databases opened read-only from the installed package.

docs.title: Demo Data (CLI-first)
docs.text:
The demo is three SQLite databases, registered as three datasources. Chinook, a small digital music store, leads; it is vendored in the wheel (MIT, v1.4.5, 1.02 MB). Beside it are support, a help-desk ticketing system (about 232 KiB), and webanalytics, website traffic (about 284 KiB). Both hold synthetic data generated by this repository from a fixed seed (scripts/generate_demo_datasets.py), so a regeneration reproduces exactly what is committed and no third-party data is involved in either. All three are shipped in the wheel and copied into your project by the CLI, so no data is downloaded or built when you set the demo up. The tables, columns and row counts are in Demo datasets.

To see it before installing anything, the same playground runs at https://nl2sql.codewithnk.com, where you bring your own model key.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
After pip install "nl2sql-engine[demo]" and nl2sql demo:

  1. No questions at the terminal. The command does not prompt. It looks for a model key -- --api-key, then OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, then a key saved in the project's .env, then an Ollama daemon on localhost:11434 -- and says which mode it chose: Live mode with the provider, or Replay mode when it finds none.
  2. A project folder and an index. The first time, it writes ./nl2sql-demo (--dir changes it) with nl2sql init --demo, which copies in the three databases above; every start then builds the engine, calls engine.check(), and indexes the schemas on your machine when the index is missing, empty or out of date. The first run downloads a ~79 MB embedding model; indexing needs no key.
  3. A local page. It prints Playground ready at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ and opens that address in your browser (--no-browser skips it, --port changes it). Ctrl+C stops it.
  4. No key yet? Paste an OpenAI or Anthropic key (or an OpenRouter one) into the Settings page; the running demo switches to live without a restart.
  5. Ask. Pick one of twenty guided questions or type your own, as admin, analyst or viewer. A run shows the answer first, then the plan the model wrote, the checks, the generated SQL, the rows, and cost and time. Debug opens each step's model calls, prompts and responses, and the Pipeline page lists every step and which a model decides.

The demo command and the [demo] extra arrive on PyPI with 0.2.0. If pip says nl2sql-engine has no demo extra, you have an earlier release: install from a clone with pip install -e packages/sdk -e "packages/nl2sql[demo]".

docs.title: 1. Install the CLI
docs.text:
# Install from PyPI. Add the `demo` extra if you also want the browser
# playground that `nl2sql demo` serves; `[all]` covers drivers only.
pip install nl2sql-engine
pip install "nl2sql-engine[demo]"

# Or install from source (dev)
pip install -e "packages/nl2sql[all,demo]"

docs.title: 2. Write the demo project
docs.text:
nl2sql init --demo nl2sql-demo
nl2sql --config nl2sql-demo/nl2sql.yaml index

init --demo writes a complete config, relative to the folder you name:

nl2sql.yaml            # the table of contents
datasources/
  chinook.yaml         # each with its description, read-only connection,
  support.yaml         # 10,000-row limit and sample questions
  webanalytics.yaml
llm.yaml               # the provider and model; no key
embeddings.yaml        # provider: local
policies.yaml          # the admin, analyst and viewer roles below
storage.yaml           # path: .nl2sql (index, state.db, traces, results)
knowledge.yaml         # one yaml knowledge source: glossary.yaml
glossary.yaml          # the Chinook glossary: descriptions, roles, terms, a rule
curated.yaml           # six verified queries on Chinook
settings.yaml          # a 300 s timeout and a trace for every run
data/                  # chinook.sqlite, support.sqlite, webanalytics.sqlite
.gitignore             # .nl2sql/ and .env

It is the same config nl2sql.config.demo_config() (and NL2SQL.demo()) builds in code.

The glossary describes Chinook's invoices, its money and enum columns, the terms "revenue" and "invoiced total", and a rule. "Sales" is a synonym of both terms on purpose: the demo carries one real ambiguity. After nl2sql index, see what the engine makes of it, as a role:

nl2sql --config nl2sql-demo/nl2sql.yaml knowledge show --as analyst
nl2sql --config nl2sql-demo/nl2sql.yaml knowledge show --as viewer   # the catalog only: no invoice terms

Each item is labelled with its origin (knowledge, database or derived); see Knowledge. nl2sql index then builds the index, and exits 1 if any datasource fails. See Start a config with nl2sql init.

For the browser playground instead of the CLI, nl2sql demo does both steps in ./nl2sql-demo the first time (and adds a nl2sql-demo.json stamp recording which engine version wrote the folder; see Old demo folders), then serves a page over it. See the README for its flags, and the Settings page for entering a key and choosing models from the page.

docs.title: The schemas
docs.text:
Chinook is eleven tables with real declared foreign keys: Artist, Album, Track, Genre, MediaType, Playlist, PlaylistTrack, Customer, Employee, Invoice and InvoiceLine. support adds four - agents, customers, tickets and ticket_messages - and webanalytics five - devices, referrers, sessions, page_views and conversions. All three declare their foreign keys, which matters: LogicalValidatorNode checks every join in a plan against a declared relationship, so a dataset without them cannot answer a join question at all.

The three share their people. Both generated databases carry a customer_email column and a customer_id matching Chinook's Customer.CustomerId, so the same 59 customers appear in all three, and every timestamp in them falls inside Chinook's invoice window, 2009-01-01 to 2013-12-22. That does not make a question spanning two databases answerable: the engine plans each sub-query against a single datasource, so it cannot join across them. The shared columns are groundwork for when it can.

Three registered datasources also change how a question is routed. With one, the resolver took the only datasource and skipped the vector search; with three, the datasource search and the LLM answerability judge run on every question, so the demo exercises the part of the pipeline a single-dataset demo never reached. Indexing all three writes 186 entries - 111 for chinook (24 of them the verified queries' phrasings and descriptions), 36 for support and 39 for webanalytics - and nl2sql index takes about seven or eight seconds once the embedding model is cached; the first run on a machine still downloads the model.

docs.title: Verified answers
docs.text:
curated.yaml holds six verified queries on Chinook: SQL written and reviewed in advance, with typed params, and the questions each answers (top customers by revenue in a year, revenue by year, monthly revenue in a year, sales by country, best-selling genres, top artists by tracks sold). nl2sql.yaml includes it as the curated section, so curated answers are on, and indexing embeds their questions beside the schema. A question one of them answers runs its SQL with the values bound instead of a generated plan, and the playground labels the answer Verified · and the query's id. "What is the total revenue per year?" and "Which genre sells the most tracks?" among the guided questions are two of them. See Curated answers.

The keyless replay includes the matcher's recorded choices, so the badge appears without a key too, on the guided questions a verified query answers.

docs.title: The roles
docs.text:
policies.yaml is written with three roles, spanning all three datasources, so the policy check is visible without editing anything:

Role Patterns May read admin allow: ["*"] every table in every demo database analyst allow: [chinook, support, webanalytics], deny: [chinook.main.Employee, support.main.agents] everything except employee and support-agent records viewer allow: the seven Chinook catalog tables and webanalytics.main.devices, webanalytics.main.page_views, webanalytics.main.referrers no customer, invoice or ticket-message data, and no access to support at all

Ask the viewer role about customers and no model ever sees the Customer or Invoice tables: they are hidden from the planner, so the answer is that the connected data cannot answer the question. A plan that names a hidden table anyway is refused by the logical validator with a SECURITY_VIOLATION before any SQL is generated. policies.yaml sets refusal_names_tables: true, so the demo's refusal names the role and table; outside the demo the message is the generic "You do not have permission to see the data this question requires." See Security Model. The playground's schema panel follows the Ask as role too: it lists only the tables that role may read (engine.datasources.schema(..., user_context=)).

docs.title: API keys in the demo
docs.text:
embeddings.yaml says provider: local, so schema chunks are embedded with the key-free ONNX all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model bundled with chromadb instead of the OpenAI embeddings API. The first indexing run downloads roughly 79 MB of model files into a local cache, which can take a few minutes.

This covers the embedding step only. The demo is not key-free end to end:

  • nl2sql run "..." calls a chat model, so it needs a working LLM key (OPENAI_API_KEY, or an OpenRouter key with llm.yaml pointed at provider: openrouter). Keep it in the environment, or in a .env file next to nl2sql.yaml, which the CLI loads without overriding a variable already set.
  • The demo's model is gpt-5.4 with temperature: 0.0. It replaced gpt-4o, whose 30,000 tokens-per-minute limit on the owner's account was below one question with a single retry; gpt-5.4 had 500,000 and accepts temperature: 0. To use a model that rejects it (gpt-5.5, gpt-5-mini), set temperature: null in llm.yaml - see LLM configuration â†’ Temperature. With an OpenRouter key or Ollama, change model to one that provider serves: live mode switches the provider, not the model name.
  • Indexing calls no model: the demo's own indexing (the first run, the startup repair and the playground's Rebuild) reads the schema and the glossary and embeds them, with the local embedding model by default. Descriptions a model drafts are proposals for review, not part of the index.
  • nl2sql demo --api-key <key> takes the key on the command line and writes it into the project's .env, never into a YAML file. The provider follows the key's shape: a key beginning sk-or- is OpenRouter and is stored as OPENROUTER_API_KEY with provider: openrouter; a key beginning sk-ant- is Anthropic and is stored as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY with provider: anthropic, model claude-opus-5 and temperature: null (install nl2sql-engine[anthropic]); anything else is OpenAI. llm.yaml names no key: the running engine is given it in memory, ahead of any key exported for the same provider, and later runs read it from .env. The process environment is never written. .env is covered by .gitignore, but a key passed on the command line is visible in shell history and to ps, so the environment variable remains the more private route.
  • So nl2sql init --demo and nl2sql index complete with no chat key at all, and nl2sql index exits 0. It exits 1 if any datasource actually fails to index, which is safe to rely on in a script. A missing key surfaces when a chat model is first called (nl2sql doctor names it before that).
  • Pointing llm.yaml at provider: ollama removes the chat key requirement, but a local model's ability to satisfy the pipeline's structured output is model-dependent - see LLM configuration â†’ Ollama.

Sharing the demo with other people is the one case where none of this applies: nl2sql demo --hosted serves the playground with no key on the server at all, and each visitor pastes their own into the page; a visitor without one can replay the guided questions from recorded runs. It refuses to start when OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set. See Hosted demo.

Each project keeps its index under its own storage.path (the demo's is nl2sql-demo/.nl2sql/index), with one namespace per embedding model. If you change the embeddings section of an existing project, run nl2sql index: the new model's namespace starts empty, and the old one stays until nl2sql index prune.

Column statistics are read when a datasource is indexed, so a change to what indexing records reaches an existing demo folder only when it is indexed again. After 0.2.2, a text column with at most 50 distinct values keeps all of them rather than five. nl2sql demo does not re-index a folder whose index is healthy, so run nl2sql index in the folder, or start a fresh one with nl2sql demo --dir <new folder>. The hosted image builds its index with nl2sql init --demo and nl2sql index, so a new image picks the change up.

docs.title: Index health and repair
docs.text:
The playground's schema panel reads the schema snapshot, for whichever database its Showing switcher names; the resolver, which picks the database for every question when more than one is registered, reads the separate vector index, and with three registered it searches on every question. After a run the answer header names the database it picked. The two can disagree: a folder once had its snapshot intact and 0 entries in its index, so the page looked fine while every question failed with SCHEMA_RETRIEVAL_FAILED. Three things now guard against that:

  • Startup repair. Every nl2sql demo start calls engine.check(), which reports what the index contains: the demo rebuilds it when it is missing or empty, or a datasource has no live build. A failed rebuild is reported (the playground still starts, and offers Rebuild) rather than ignored.
  • Rebuilds never leave an empty index. A datasource's new entries are written beside its current ones and switched in only when all are written; a failure keeps the previous entries answering questions. See Indexing.
  • Actionable errors. With an empty index the resolver says "The vector index is empty ... Re-index with nl2sql index", and nl2sql doctor prints the engine's check, the index status included.

docs.title: The search index panel
docs.text:
The playground's left rail opens with the Database panel, and with the demo's three databases it carries a switcher for which of them to read: a segmented control while there are four or fewer, a Showing select beyond that. At the foot of the rail, Search index is one line when all is well -- "Search index fresh. 186 entries, built 3 minutes ago." -- that opens to entries by type (datasource, tables, columns, relationships), the schema version they were built from, and when. One index holds every database, so with the demo's three the line inside says which they are -- "Covers chinook, support and webanalytics". With a single database both panels name it instead, and there is no switcher. When the index is empty, missing or out of date, or a rebuild is running or failed, the panel opens itself, a warning under the top bar says what that means for a question, and the panel's Rebuild the index button becomes the rail's one filled button. Rebuild is also always available on demand.

  • Rebuild re-reads one database's schema into a new snapshot and rebuilds its entries beside the current ones; questions keep using the current entries until the new ones are complete, and a question in flight finishes on the entries it started with. That database is the demo's own, named in the button's help; nl2sql index rebuilds all three.
  • It shows each step as it runs. The first run downloads the 79 MB embedding model, so it can take a few minutes.
  • Write descriptions with the LLM is off by default because it spends tokens on your key; it is unavailable in replay mode.
  • It has the Settings page's guardrails (so does the Retrieval inspector): local only unless --allow-settings, and only from the playground page itself.
  • On the hosted demo there is no button at all. The panel says instead that the index was built before the demo started and which databases it covers, and prints the server's own reason where the button would be: rebuilding writes to disk, and the sample data never changes.

docs.title: Old demo folders
docs.text: Demo folders are not upgraded in place: a folder written by an older engine keeps that engine's defaults (for example an older default model). A folder written by a 0.4 engine (configs/, .env.demo) has no nl2sql.yaml and cannot be read by 0.5: start a new --dir. New folders get a nl2sql-demo.json stamp; when nl2sql demo starts in a folder stamped by an older engine, or in one with no stamp at all, it warns and suggests a fresh --dir. The playground's index panel repeats the warning.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
The playground is five pages, named across the top of every one of them: Home, Ask, Pipeline, Settings and Retrieval. Each is a route in the address bar -- #/, #/ask, #/pipeline, #/settings and #/retrieval -- so a reload stays where you were, a link can be pasted to someone else, and Back and Forward walk the pages you visited. A route nobody serves lands on Home.

Home says what the engine does and shows it: the five steps a question travels (Question, Plan, Check, SQL, Rows, marked by whether a model or code decides each), then a short clip of Ask, Pipeline and Retrieval with a link into each. Try a sample question opens Ask and asks a guided question; on the hosted demo it picks one with a recorded answer, so it works before you add a key. The nav marks the page you are on, and marks Settings or Retrieval when the server has it off; the page itself then says why. Moving between pages keeps the question, the answer and the Debug choice: they belong to the visit, not to the page.

At the right of the top bar a status pill says which mode the page is in -- Live, Replay mode with how many guided questions it has recordings for, or on the hosted demo whether this tab has a key yet. Hover it, or let a screen reader read it, for the full sentence: how replay answers, or whose key answers and the hosted limits.

docs.title: The Ask page
docs.text:
Ask is the question box, then the run, answer first:

  • Suggestions. Under the question box, a row of chips offers three or four guided questions for the database the rail is showing, and N more opens every pile, one per database. On a phone the row is a strip you swipe sideways. The run sits right below the box.
  • The answer leads. Once a run is back, its first block is the answer: the question and the role it was asked as, the answer sentence in the largest type on the page, and a strip such as 10 rows / 3 of 3 checks / 2 plans / 5.04 s / $0.0187. Each item in the strip moves the keyboard to its station below. A refusal gets the same block: Refused at the checks. No SQL was written.
  • The stations. Plan, Checks, SQL, Rows and Cost & time follow, each with a small heading, a tag for who decides it (Model Â· gpt-5.4, from the run's usage, or Code) and the step's time. On the spine a round mark is a model step and a square one is code; filled with a tick is done, an outline is waiting and a dashed outline was not reached.
  • Every sub-query. When a question is split into several sub-queries, the Plan and SQL stations show each one under its own head (Sub-query 1 of 2, its intent and its database).
  • Rows, at any size. The Rows station reads the run's saved results, not the sample the answer model saw. Its head gives the whole result's row count, and a result cut at its row ceiling says so: Cut at 1,000 rows, so some are missing. Narrow the question to get them all. The table shows 100 rows at a time, fetched from the server, with Previous, Next and Rows 101â€“200 of 3,340. A run with several results gets one tab per result. Download CSV streams the whole result from the server, every row.
  • The gate. The Checks station shows the plans the checks saw (Plan 1 refused, then Plan 2 passed when the first was sent back), why, in one sentence, and each check as a tile with a tick or a cross.
  • While it runs. The run streams (POST /api/ask/stream, Server-Sent Events): each station lights as its step finishes, with its time, and the next one goes live; the rest wait, faded. The Rows station loads its first page as soon as the result is saved, before the answer is written. The answer sentence then appears as the model writes it, a shade lighter until the run is back, when the plan, the checks and the SQL fill in. A recorded run on the hosted demo streams its recorded answer the same way, a word at a time. Where the stream cannot be used (an older server, a proxy that cuts it, a browser that cannot read a streamed reply), the page asks POST /api/ask instead and the first station stays lit until the whole run is back. A counter beside the button reads Running Â· 3.4 s, and after a moment Ask becomes Stop, which cancels the request: the run then says Stopped and every station is marked not reached. The server notices the dropped request within a quarter of a second and cancels the run: no further step starts and no further model call is sent, though the one already in flight finishes (and is billed by the provider). On the hosted demo a stopped question still counts toward both limits, because it is charged when it arrives, before it runs.
  • When it fails. A provider's refusal is said in words with the next step, for example OpenAI rejected this key. with Replace the key, which opens Settings. The provider's own reply is folded under Provider response.
  • On a phone, once a run is on the page, a bar at the bottom, Ask another question, takes you back to the question box. It hides while the box is in view.

docs.title: The Pipeline page
docs.text:
Pipeline lists every step a question passes through, in the order a run takes them, and marks which of them a model decides. Five do: the answerability check, the question splitter, the query planner, the plan repair and the answer writer. The other eight are ordinary code -- the layer router, the SQL agent, the schema search, the plan checks, the retry bookkeeping, the SQL writer, the executor and the result combiner -- which is the point: the model plans, and deterministic code writes the SQL, checks it against the real schema and this role's policy, and runs it.

The steps are grouped into three phases: Understand the question, Answer each sub-query (the SQL agent and its own steps, in a bracket, because they repeat per sub-query and again when the checks refuse a plan) and Combine and explain. A step a model decides is a raised row with a round mark and its model in a chip; a code step is a compact row with a square mark. A legend reads: asks a model, code, did not run, skipped.
