docs.title: Schema Profiler
docs.text:
After a datasource is indexed, the profiler reads its live snapshot, asks the database a bounded number of cheap questions through the adapter, and files what it finds as proposals. It is deterministic: no model runs unless you ask for drafted descriptions (draft=True, or nl2sql profile --draft). Nothing it finds or drafts reaches a prompt, the index or a file until a person with an admin role accepts it.

nl2sql index                        # the profiler reads the live build's snapshot
nl2sql profile --as admin           # file joins and column roles for review
nl2sql profile --as admin --draft --max-cost 0.25   # also draft descriptions with the model
nl2sql review list --as admin
nl2sql review accept --all --kind column --as admin   # writes glossary.yaml once

nl2sql index --profile --as admin indexes and then profiles the same datasources. From Python:

reports = engine.knowledge.profile(user_context=UserContext(roles=["admin"]))

profile(datasource_ids=None, *, user_context, draft=False, max_cost_usd=None) returns one ProfileReport per datasource the caller reaches:

Field Meaning datasource_id, schema_version What was profiled; the proposals carry the same schema_version proposals Proposals created or updated, by kind (join, column, table) probes Overlap probes run skipped_by_budget Join candidates proposed without a probe because a bound was reached drafted Descriptions the model drafted (draft=True only) cost What the drafting calls cost in USD; None when nothing was drafted stopped_by done, max_probes, time_budget, or cost_cap (drafting reached max_cost_usd) issues A probe that failed, a draft that could not be used, no model for drafting, an unavailable datasource, or "not indexed yet" seconds How long it took

max_cost_usd (--max-cost) without draft=True (--draft) is a ValueError.

The caller is required and has no default. The profiler reads and probes only the tables the caller's scope reaches, so a table the role denies is never probed and is named in no proposal. A datasource that was never indexed is reported with an issue and skipped: the profiler never reflects on its own. Each finished profile publishes profile.finished (counts only).

docs.title: What it proposes
docs.text: Nothing is proposed for what the glossary already says, what the database already declares (a foreign key is not proposed as a join), or what the schema proves. A primary or foreign key is an identifier and a temporal type a date: those roles are derived when the knowledge is shown, with origin derived, and never filed.

docs.title: Joins
docs.text:
For each column that is not part of a foreign key, the profiler looks for a single-column primary key (or the only column named id) in another table that it may point to. A pair of tables with a declared foreign key between them, or a column pair the glossary already joins, is skipped.

  1. Names. The column's name equals the key's (not when the key is a bare id), or it is the key table's name, singular or plural, followed by id or key. Case and underscores are ignored: customer_id finds customers.id, CustomerId finds Customer.CustomerId.
  2. Types. Both columns fall in the same category: number, text, temporal or boolean. A mismatch drops the candidate, and a type the profiler cannot place never matches. This is stricter than the query-time join-key check, which coerces a number against text: a proposed join should hold without coercion.
  3. Overlap. probe_overlap takes up to profiler.sample_rows distinct non-null values of the left column and counts how many exist in the key column. An overlap under profiler.min_overlap (0.9), or an empty sample, drops the candidate.
  4. Cardinality. many-to-one when the key is a primary key, else unknown. Two primary keys of one name (film.film_id, film_text.film_id) are one one-to-one pair, not two.

A join proposal's change is the glossary's join (from, to, cardinality) and its evidence is the name rule that matched (same_name or table_name_key), both types, the shared category, and sampled, matched and overlap (counts, never values). A candidate the budget did not reach, and one on an adapter without probe_overlap (the five built-ins have it), is proposed with overlap: null. A probe that fails (a timeout, a driver error) is an issue on the report, and its candidate is proposed with overlap: null too. An accepted join is a relationship: the schema retriever lists it beside the foreign keys, so the validator accepts a plan that uses it.

docs.title: Column roles
docs.text:
Proposed When enum A text or integer column, not an identifier and not named like a key (..._id), with at most profiler.enum_max_distinct (50) distinct values. values lists them with empty meanings for the reviewer to fill, only when the snapshot holds all of them (index.sample_values on) money A decimal column named like price, amount, total, cost, revenue, salary, fee or balance; unit from a _usd, _eur or _gbp suffix quantity An integer or decimal column named like qty, quantity, count or units, or with a _kg, _ms or _pct suffix, which is the unit date on text A text column whose smallest and largest values are ISO dates (SQLite keeps dates as text) A refined grain month or year when every value of a date column is the first of a month or of a year (needs all the column's values in the snapshot)

A role, unit, grain or set of values the glossary already has is not proposed again. The word lists are English only. The rules are one table in nl2sql/profiler/roles.py, with a test per row. On a wide schema (every key and temporal column is derived) this is a few hundred proposals at most, and nl2sql review accept --all --kind column --datasource ID --as admin writes the glossary once.

docs.title: Drafted descriptions
docs.text:
draft=True has the profiler agent (see Per-node models) describe what nobody has: a table or column with no description in the glossary (or a knowledge source) and none from the database. It is asked about those items only, one call per table the caller reaches, and shown that table's evidence (types, statistics, sample values, foreign keys). It never sees a table the caller's scope denies. Each answer is cleaned (unknown tables and columns dropped, text trimmed, duplicates removed), and a draft longer than knowledge.item_max_chars is dropped with an issue, since the glossary would refuse it on accept.

  • A table's draft is a table proposal (change: {description}).
  • A column's draft is merged with its role: one column proposal per column carries role, unit, values and the drafted description and synonyms together, because the queue keeps one open proposal per target. Its origin is draft when it carries a description, profiler when it carries only a role.
  • Nothing drafted is written into the schema snapshot or the index. It reaches a prompt only after a person accepts it into the glossary.
  • An item with an open drafted description in the queue counts as described: a repeat draft=True run does not ask the model about it again or replace the row. A run that finds only the same role for such a column (a plain profile, a run stopped at the cost cap) leaves the open row alone; a changed role still files and supersedes it.
  • A foreign key to a table the caller's scope denies is left out of the evidence, so the model never sees that table's name.

Cost. Drafting is capped at max_cost_usd for the whole call, across datasources (the argument, else profiler.max_cost_usd, 0.50). A model with no price in llm.prices is refused before any call (UnknownPriceError). A run that reaches the cap stops, files what it drafted so far, and reports stopped_by: cost_cap. With no model configured for the agent, nothing is drafted and the report says so in issues; the joins and roles are still filed.

docs.title: Bounds
docs.text:
# settings.yaml
profiler:
  sample_rows: 1000     # distinct values one overlap probe reads
  max_probes: 200       # overlap probes per datasource
  time_budget_s: 60     # per datasource; no probe starts after it
  min_overlap: 0.9
  enum_max_distinct: 50
  max_cost_usd: 0.50    # drafting, per profile call (profile(draft=True), --draft)

Probes run one at a time, strongest candidate first (an exact key-name match before a table-name match), each under the datasource's timeout_ms. The limit caps the sample, not the read: DISTINCT usually reads the whole column first, so on a large table the timeout is what bounds a probe. When max_probes or time_budget_s is reached the remaining candidates are proposed with overlap: null and the report says which bound stopped it.

A probe that measures an overlap under min_overlap also supersedes the profiler's own earlier open proposal for that join (one filed with overlap: null when a bound stopped the probes), so a reviewer cannot accept a join the profiler has since found wrong.

docs.title: Proposals are idempotent
docs.text: A proposal's id hashes its kind, datasource, target and change, so profiling twice updates the same open rows' evidence rather than adding rows. A rejected change is never proposed again, and an accepted one is in the glossary, which the next profile reads.

docs.title: Schema & Metadata Layer
docs.text:
The schema layer provides authoritative, versioned snapshots and structured retrieval to ground planning. It is split into:

  • Schema contracts: structural schema (tables, columns, foreign keys).
  • Schema metadata: the database's own comments and statistics.
  • The state store: immutable, versioned snapshots, and the diffs between them, kept by storage.state.
  • Schema retrieval: staged lookup via schema chunks.

docs.title: Schema contracts and metadata
docs.text:
Schema contracts are defined in nl2sql_sdk.schema:

  • SchemaContract: datasource_id, engine_type, tables
  • TableContract: table ref, column contracts, foreign keys
  • ColumnContract: name, type, nullability, primary key flag
  • ForeignKeyContract: constrained/referred columns, cardinality, business meaning

Metadata complements contracts:

  • SchemaMetadata: datasource description/domains, table metadata
  • TableMetadata: table description, row_count, column metadata
  • ColumnMetadata: description, stats, synonyms, PII flag
  • ColumnStatistics: distinct counts, min/max, sample values (for a text column: every distinct value when there are at most 50, else the five most frequent; most frequent first, ties by value). A column the adapter could not profile has no statistics and an index issue; values are kept only with the datasource's index.sample_values. See Reading a schema

docs.title: The state store
docs.text: Snapshots are kept by the engine's state store, the storage.state slot (see Storage). The built-in one is sqlite, a file at <storage.path>/state.db; any store implementing nl2sql_sdk.stores.StateStore can take its place. The same store holds the plan cache, the playground's answer ratings, the review queue, conversations, workspaces, dashboards with their last chart results, API keys and the index build lock. The interface is version 4.

docs.title: Snapshots are immutable
docs.text:
put_snapshot(snapshot) stores a snapshot as a new row and returns its schema_version, YYYYMMDDhhmmss_<hash8> (the time it was stored, and a hash of its contract and metadata). A stored snapshot is never changed: in the sqlite store a trigger refuses any UPDATE of the schema_snapshots table.

  • Storing a snapshot whose contract and metadata are identical to a stored one returns that version, and writes nothing.
  • A snapshot with the same structure but new metadata (statistics, descriptions) is a new version. A run that pinned the old version keeps reading exactly the snapshot its index build was made from.

The structural fingerprint (nl2sql.schema.generate_schema_fingerprint: datasource ID, engine type, sorted tables, columns and foreign keys) is still stored beside each row, and eval reports and records use it to identify a database.

docs.title: Schema diffs
docs.text: When a build stores a snapshot whose structure differs from the version it replaces, the orchestrator stores the diff between them beside the new version (put_schema_diff(diff), keyed by datasource and diff.to_version; get_schema_diff(datasource_id, schema_version) reads it back) and publishes schema.drifted. A version whose statistics alone changed gets no diff. The diff (nl2sql_sdk.schema.SchemaDiff) and how to read it are in Schema Drift. These two methods are why the store interface is version 2.

docs.title: Which snapshots are kept
docs.text:
After each build of a datasource, indexing calls keep_snapshots(datasource_id, keep), which deletes every other snapshot of the datasource, the plans cached on them and their diffs. keep is:

  • every version a build pointer names, in every index namespace, so switching back to an earlier embedding model still finds its snapshot;
  • the version the build just replaced, which runs in flight may have pinned;
  • the newest settings.schema.max_versions (default 3).

Nothing else deletes a snapshot; there is no age limit.

docs.title: The plan cache and feedback
docs.text:
The plan cache holds validated, executed plans keyed by (normalised sub-query intent, run date, planner model and knowledge digest, datasource_id, schema_version) (get_plan, put_plan). Deleting a snapshot deletes its cached plans; nl2sql cache clear (engine.clear_plan_cache()) deletes them all and keeps the snapshots. See Determinism → The plan cache.

The playground's answer ratings are kept too (add_feedback, list_feedback, clear_feedback): one row per rated run, questions and SQL, never rows. nl2sql feedback clear empties them and nothing else. See Feedback and Signals.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text: The sqlite store records each migration it has applied in a nl2sql_meta table, and the engine applies the pending ones when it starts (StateStore.migrate()). Migration 1 creates 0.5's three tables (schema_snapshots, plan_cache, feedback) if they are missing, so a 0.5 state.db is adopted as it is; migration 2 adds the feedback columns that came later; migration 3 adds the immutability trigger and the locks table; migration 4 adds the schema_diffs table; migration 5 adds the proposals table, the review queue (release 0.8, Wave B); migration 6 adds Wave C's five tables, below. A 0.8 state.db is migrated in place and keeps its rows.

docs.title: Conversations, dashboards and API keys
docs.text:
Release 0.9 (Wave C). StateStore version 4 adds these methods. Each takes and returns a plain JSON document (dict), because the SDK holds none of the engine's models; the document carries the fields the store filters on. The engine methods that use them arrive in C1 and D1 to D4.

Table (migration 6) Methods Filtered on Notes conversations put_conversation, get_conversation, list_conversations(tenant_id, user_id, limit), delete_conversation, purge_conversations(older_than) owner, updated_at One document per conversation, rewritten each turn, read whole. Stored without result rows. None is an owner of its own in list_*, not a wildcard. workspaces put_workspace, get_workspace, list_workspaces(tenant_id, user_id), delete_workspace owner, created_at Listed oldest first. A put on an existing id keeps its created_at, so renaming a workspace does not move it. dashboards put_dashboard, get_dashboard, list_dashboards(tenant_id, user_id), delete_dashboard, purge_dashboards(drafts_older_than), list_scheduled_dashboards() owner, status, updated_at, whether it has a schedule purge_dashboards deletes drafts only; saved dashboards are never purged. list_scheduled_dashboards serves the scheduler across owners. tile_runs put_tile_runs(dashboard_id, docs), get_tile_runs(dashboard_id), delete_tile_runs(dashboard_id, tile_ids) dashboard, chart (tile_id), at The last result of each chart, rows included. put_tile_runs replaces only the charts it lists and delete_tile_runs deletes only those it lists (an edit that changes what a chart shows discards its result). Deleted with the dashboard. api_keys add_api_key, revoke_api_key(key_id, revoked_at), get_api_key, list_api_keys id, hash, revoked_at A hash, never a secret. add_api_key is a plain insert and raises ValueError when the id exists, so a clash never replaces another holder's key. revoke_api_key sets revoked_at and nothing else; it returns False for an unknown id.

Stored chart results hold rows, so they sit in the owner's private state store and open only after the access check.

Each document's timestamps are ISO 8601; a stamp with no zone is read as UTC.

docs.title: The lock
docs.text:
lock(name, ttl_s) is a lease held for a with block: in the sqlite store, a locks row taken in a BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction, with an expiry. Every engine.index.build() holds the index lock, so nl2sql index is safe to run while nl2sql-api serves the same storage.path: a second build started meanwhile fails at once and says until when the lease runs. The lease expires after an hour, so a build that died cannot block forever.

The sqlite store opens its file on first use, never when it is built, and is safe to share between threads: each use of its one connection holds a lock.

docs.title: Which version is live
docs.text: There is no "latest snapshot" to read. Indexing stores a datasource's snapshot first and its index entries second; the index store's BuildPointer for the datasource then records the schema_version the live build was made from, and switching that pointer is the commit. The pointer also records the curated_hash and the knowledge_hash the build was made with, so health can tell that curated.yaml or the glossary has changed since. A snapshot holds only what the database said: model-drafted descriptions are proposals, and a person's words live in the glossary (see Indexing). Every reader (the resolver, the schema retriever, the curated matcher, engine.datasources.schema(), engine.curated.validate()) resolves the version through the pointer and reads get_snapshot(datasource_id, schema_version). A run reads the pointers once, when it starts. A snapshot stored by a build that then failed is named by no pointer, so nothing reads it. See Indexing → The build pointer is the commit.

docs.title: Retrieval and authority
docs.text:
Schema retrieval resolves authoritative tables/columns from the state store, not from the index. Index entries are only used to identify candidates; final schema is resolved via the snapshot the live pointer names. If retrieval yields no candidates, the retriever falls back to the full snapshot. The entries and the snapshot come from the same build, so their versions cannot disagree.

See ../architecture/indexing.md for retrieval stages, chunk types, and vector store behavior.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
An API key authenticates a client of MCP over HTTP (arriving with Wave C's M2). It carries the user, tenant and roles its holder runs as, so a key per person or per app is the unit of revocation. Nothing is inferred from the client. The design is Wave C, section 9.

nl2sql keys create --as admin --user ana --role analyst --tenant acme --label laptop
nl2sql keys list --as admin
nl2sql keys revoke <id> --as admin

On a project with policies.allow_all (the starter, nl2sql launch) no roles exist: leave out --as and --role, as in nl2sql keys create --user ana. Any --as or --role is refused as an unknown role.

create prints the token once. Keep it in the client's secret store: only its hash is kept here, so a lost token is replaced by a new key, not recovered.

docs.title: The token
docs.text: nl2sql_<id>_<secret>: id is 8 hex characters, shown in lists, logs and events; secret is 32 random bytes, URL-safe (43 characters). The state store keeps sha256(secret) and the key's fields, never the token. SHA-256 with no salt is deliberate: the secret is 256 bits of randomness, so there is nothing to guess and a slow hash would only cost time on every request. The comparison uses hmac.compare_digest.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
from nl2sql import NL2SQL, UserContext

admin = UserContext(user_id="root", roles=["admin"])

key, token = engine.api_keys.create(user_id="ana", roles=["analyst"], by=admin, tenant_id="acme", label="laptop")
engine.api_keys.list(by=admin)            # [ApiKey, ...], newest first, revoked ones included; no secret
engine.api_keys.revoke(key.id, by=admin)  # stops verifying at once
engine.api_keys.verify(token)             # UserContext(user_id="ana", tenant_id="acme", roles=["analyst"]) or None
Method Behaviour create(*, user_id, roles, by, tenant_id=None, label="") Returns the ApiKey and its token, once. roles must be configured in policies.roles; user_id must not be empty. An id that is already taken is retried with a new one and never replaces another key. Publishes api_key.created. list(*, by) Every key, newest first. ApiKey has no secret and no hash. revoke(key_id, *, by) Sets revoked_at; revoking a revoked key changes nothing. An unknown id is a ValueError. Publishes api_key.revoked. verify(token) The key's UserContext, or None for a malformed, unknown or revoked token, or a wrong secret. It takes no caller: it is how a caller is found.

by is required and has no default. A call without one is a TypeError, a by that is not a UserContext is a TypeError, and a by holding none of policies.admin_roles is a PermissionError. Under policies.allow_all every caller is an admin, as for the rest of the engine, but a key still cannot carry a role name: with no roles defined, roles=[] is the only value, and a role name is a ValueError. Keys outlive the policy, so an admin key minted under allow_all would become a real admin key once roles are configured. A key with no roles reads everything under allow_all and nothing once roles are configured; create new keys then.

docs.title: Events and logs
docs.text: api_key.created and api_key.revoked carry key_id, user_id, tenant_id, roles and by, and the audit observer keeps both. Neither the token nor any part of the secret appears in an event, a log line or an error. See Events.

docs.title: What a key does and does not give
docs.text: A key proves that the holder has the token; it does not prove who the holder is, and it does not expire. Revoke a key when a person leaves or a token leaks. A key's roles are checked against the policies at every request, so removing a role from policies.roles stops what the key can read, though not the key.

docs.title: Security Model
docs.text: Authorization is enforced at planning time, by the logical validator, before any SQL exists. That is the one security property this engine provides. It is not authentication, it is not containment, and it is not row- or column-level security.

docs.title: The role is supplied by the caller
docs.text:
There is no authentication in the query path; the engine believes the UserContext it is given. The one exception is an API key, which a transport may verify to find that context. Where the role comes from depends on the client:

  • CLI: nl2sql run --role <id>, defaulting to admin.
  • Python API: UserContext(roles=[...]), whatever the calling code passes.

  • REST API: the get_user_context dependency (packages/api/src/nl2sql_api/auth.py). It reads a header set by a trusted proxy (api.role_header in nl2sql.yaml) or a static role (api.role), and answers HTTP 401 when neither gives one. The body's user_context counts only with the dev flag api.trust_body_role: true, which logs a warning at startup. See Caller role. The routes that change datasources, LLMs or the index also need one of the roles in policies.admin_roles (default [admin]), else HTTP 403; with no role source configured they answer loopback clients only. See Admin routes.

  • API keys: engine.api_keys makes bearer tokens that each carry the user, tenant and roles their holder runs as, and verify(token) turns a token back into that UserContext. This is the one place the engine itself checks who is asking; MCP over HTTP is the first transport to use it, and the other clients above still do not. See API keys.

  • Playground: the page sends the role chosen in "Ask as" with each request (/api/ask, and /api/retrieval for the Retrieval inspector), and the server believes it. The inspector shows a role only the entries that role may read, but anyone who can reach the playground can ask as any role; it is a local demo, off beyond loopback unless --allow-settings.

The REST API still does not verify who the caller is. If you expose this service, put your own authentication in a proxy in front of it, derive the role from that, and have the proxy overwrite the role header on every request; otherwise any client can send the header itself. An empty roles list denies everything, which is the correct default for an unauthenticated caller.

A role name that is not present in the policy file grants nothing, exactly like an empty roles list. It grants nothing, so the caller is refused with a normal SECURITY_VIOLATION, not a crash: through the pipeline the datasource resolver refuses first (no datasource is reachable), and the validator on its own refuses every table with its policy check failed. An unknown name listed beside a known one is ignored, and the known role's permissions still apply.

docs.title: Hidden tables and strict refusal
docs.text:
Every access decision asks one Scope: what the caller may read in one datasource, from the roles' allow and deny patterns and, when one is configured, a policy check's grant (see Policies). A run builds each datasource's scope once, so every step decides the same way.

  • Denied tables are hidden from the planner. The schema retriever searches only the tables the scope allows, on both the full-snapshot path and the vector-retrieval path, so a denied table's name, columns, keys, relationships, statistics and sample values never reach the prompt, the LLM provider or the run trace. The answerability judge and the decomposer see only the readable table names. A question that needs only denied tables gets "no data for that question" from the planner rather than a refusal. (For tables the role can read, the prompt carries sample_values and, for a date, time or numeric column, its [min, max] as range; the other statistics stay in the snapshot.)
  • A plan naming a hidden table is refused. The logical validator asks the same scope for every table in the plan and refuses a denied one with SECURITY_VIOLATION before any SQL exists. The run ends there.
  • A generic message for the user. The refusal the caller sees is "You do not have permission to see the data this question requires." It names no table, because naming one tells an unauthorised user that it exists. The table, the role and the rule that denied it are logged as a warning and recorded in the error's details (datasource_id, table, roles, rule), which the run trace keeps and the QueryResult error summary does not carry. The validator's policy check is still present with passed: false, so a UI can show the gate firing.
  • Naming tables is an opt-in. Set policies.refusal_names_tables: true to put the role and table in the user-facing message ("Role 'viewer' denied access to 'chinook.Customer'."). The demo's config (nl2sql init --demo) sets it, because showing the refusal is the demo's point.
  • The decision is deterministic code. Only the scope decides, from the policy and the plan's table list. Nothing the model writes (its reasoning, a claim that the role is allowed) is read by the policy check, so a crafted prompt cannot turn a refusal into an allow.

Knowledge is data. The glossary (Wave B) reaches the planner and the refiner only as JSON values, in the schema block and in [BUSINESS_CONTEXT], capped per item and per block, and filtered by the caller's scope: an item naming a denied table, or whose text (or a database comment) mentions one, is never sent, returned on knowledge_used or named in the explanation. The prompt tells the model the block is reference data, but that is not what the guarantee rests on: a plan written under any glossary is validated with the caller's scope like every other, so hostile knowledge cannot widen access. A paraphrase of a hidden table's name is not caught by the filter; the validator still refuses a plan on the table. See Knowledge Is Data.

This is table-level access control. It is not column masking and not row-level security: a role that may read a table reads every column and every row of it. A downloaded trace of a permitted run holds real rows, and the playground serves any trace by id with no login, so restricting a trace to the user who produced it is left to a multi-user deployment.

docs.title: Security controls
docs.text:
• Policies: the policies section of nl2sql.yaml, evaluated by PolicyEngine into a Scope. A role allows and denies tables with patterns over datasource.schema.table (each part a glob, case ignored) — nothing finer. There is no column masking and no row-level security.
  • Policy check (optional): a plugin that asks an outside service (IAM, OPA, Cedar) what the caller may read, once per caller and datasource per run. Its grant is intersected with the roles, so neither can widen the other, and it fails closed: an exception denies the datasource for the run and is logged with the check's name. See A policy check.
  • Logical validation enforces schema constraints and policy-based table access.
  • Hooks (optional): your code at six points of every run, on the generated and the verified path. A hook may change the question, narrow the datasources or change the plan only before the validator, so a changed plan is validated (policies included) like any other, and a narrowed list of datasources is checked against the role again. After the validator a hook may only stop the run. Hooks fail closed: an exception denies with HOOK_FAILED unless that hook is configured on_error: open. See Hooks. A run a hook ended is withheld: its returned result is blank and its saved results are unreadable by trace id (engine.results and the REST results routes raise ResultNotFound). Every read goes through the run's manifest, which is written only once no hook can end the run any more (after answer.after allowed, while a hook sits there), so a deny cannot be bypassed by paging the run's files, during the run or after it. See What withholding guarantees.
  • Cost rule (optional, policies.cost): the built-in policy.cost hook asks the database for the rows a query is estimated to read, before it runs, and allows it, asks a person to approve it or refuses it (COST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, never retried) when it is over the caller's limit. It applies on every path that runs a question's SQL (generated, verified, a correction's check), under allow_all too, and a failed estimate follows the rule's unknown action (default allow). It limits cost, not access. See Policies → Cost.
  • Approval (a hook's NeedsApproval): the engine, not the hook, checks an Approval on the re-run: the request unedited, the same question and asker, the hash of the SQL generated again, and an approver holding one of the hook's configured roles. An Approval is not signed: it is trusted as far as the user_context the caller passes. See Query API → Approval.
  • A supplied plan (run_query(plan=...)) skips planning, not checking: its datasource is scope-checked, and the plan passes plan.after and the logical validator under the caller's role like any other.
  • API keys (engine.api_keys): the token is shown once and only the SHA-256 of its 256-bit secret is stored; verify compares in constant time and answers None for a malformed, unknown or revoked token. Managing keys needs a policies.admin_roles caller, a key's roles must be configured roles, and neither an event nor a log line carries the token. See API keys.
  • Audit logging records llm.changed events only: each engine.llm.replace (the Python API, PUT /api/v1/settings/llm, the playground's model switch), with who made it and each agent's old and new model, never a key. Queries are not audited. See ../observability/stack.md.
  • Bounded execution: a global timeout and a per-run cancellation token cap each run. There is no process sandbox — the engine runs in-process (see ../execution/isolation.md).

docs.title: What keeps the SQL read-only
docs.text:
The model never writes SQL. It emits a typed plan whose query_type is Literal["READ"] — pydantic rejects anything else before a node sees the plan, which is the whole enforcement — and the generator renders that plan with sqlglot starting from exp.select(). A statement that is not a SELECT therefore cannot be produced, and free text from the model is never executed.

Below that, the session itself is read-only wherever the database allows it. There is no setting: the engine never writes, so every built-in adapter makes each new connection read-only when it can, and declares ENFORCES_READ_ONLY only where it does:

Adapter Read-only session ENFORCES_READ_ONLY PostgreSQL SET default_transaction_read_only = on yes MySQL SET SESSION TRANSACTION READ ONLY yes SQL Server none: the database has no such session setting no DuckDB read_only=True on the file yes (not for :memory:) SQLite mode=ro yes

engine.check() warns about each datasource whose adapter does not declare it ("this adapter cannot make the session read-only"), and still routes to it. For those, the login is the third guard: on SQL Server, a login whose only role is db_datareader (see the adapter). The executor has no statement-kind or statement-count gate of its own. Grant the engine a read-only database user anyway: a read-only session stops writes, not reads of tables you did not mean to expose.

flowchart TD
    User[UserContext] --> Scope[PolicyEngine.scope]
    Check[PolicyCheck.grant, optional] --> Scope
    Scope --> Retriever[SchemaRetrieverNode: hides denied tables]
    Scope --> Validator[LogicalValidatorNode: refuses denied tables]
    Validator --> Executor[ExecutorNode]
    Executor --> Audit[audit observer: storage.path/audit/]

docs.title: Policy enforcement details
docs.text:
LogicalValidatorNode enforces strict namespacing through the Scope:

  • A table is read in a schema: the plan's, or the adapter's default schema. An allow of sales.public.orders does not allow sales.audit.orders. Patterns have one part or three; a two-part pattern is rejected when the config loads (see Policies).
  • Matching ignores case, so a deny cannot be dodged by Orders against orders.
  • Deny beats allow within a role; across roles a table is readable when some role allows it and that same role does not deny it.
  • If no datasource ID is present, validation fails closed.
  • With a policy check, a table must also be allowed, and not denied, by the check's grant; a check that failed allows nothing in that datasource.
  • An unknown role, or no role, allows nothing and is refused like any denial.
  • One SECURITY_VIOLATION per forbidden table, with the generic message unless policies.refusal_names_tables is set, and details naming the table, the roles and the rule.

docs.title: Validation gates
docs.text: Validation rules are enforced by LogicalValidatorNode and documented in ../architecture/invariants.md and ../architecture/nodes/logical_validator_node.md.

docs.title: Multi-Tenant Isolation Model
docs.text: Multi-tenancy is enforced through context propagation, artifact partitioning, and policy filtering. Tenant identity originates from Settings.tenant_id and is passed through execution requests and artifact paths.

docs.title: Tenant context propagation
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Settings[Settings.tenant_id] --> Context[Runtime.tenant_id]
    Context --> Executor[ExecutorNode/ExecutorRequest]
    Executor --> Artifacts[ArtifactStore.create_artifact_ref]

docs.title: Storage isolation
docs.text:
Artifacts are persisted under a tenant-partitioned path on every backend, driven by RESULT_ARTIFACT_PATH_TEMPLATE (default <tenant_id>/<request_id>/<sub_query_id>.parquet):

<backend root>/<tenant_id>/<request_id>/<sub_query_id>.parquet

This ensures per-tenant isolation for artifacts, and downstream aggregation only reads referenced artifacts from the current request.

Tenant isolation is not applied to indexing; the vector store and schema store are global in the current implementation (see ../architecture/indexing.md).

docs.title: Authorization model
docs.text: PolicyEngine turns UserContext.roles and the policies section of nl2sql.yaml into a Scope per datasource. The schema retriever hides denied tables from the planner, and the validator enforces the scope at planning time.

docs.title: Source references
docs.text:
• Tenant settings: settings.tenant_id in packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/config/models.py
  • Context initialization: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/runtime.py
  • Artifact paths: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/execution/artifacts/store.py
  • Policies: packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/policies/scope.py

docs.title: Artifact Store Architecture
docs.text:
Execution results are persisted as artifacts. The engine's ArtifactStore writes each result as Parquet, and the run's manifest as JSON, through the results store in storage.results (a ResultStore, see Storage), and emits ArtifactRef metadata used by aggregation and downstream consumers. Each sub-query's result is one artifact, and the run's combined result is another, beside them.

The engine makes the bytes; the store only keeps them under a key. The built-in local store keeps them as files in <storage.path>/results/. There is no built-in S3 or ADLS store: a remote store is four methods (see A results store of your own).

docs.title: Storage lifecycle
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Adapter[Adapter: execute_batches or execute] --> Batches[ResultFrame batches]
    Batches --> Store[ArtifactStore.write_batches]
    Store --> Parquet[Sub-query Parquet object]
    Parquet --> Ref[ArtifactRef]
    Ref --> Aggregation[EngineAggregatorNode: polars scan]
    Aggregation --> Combined[ArtifactStore.write_lazy]
    Combined --> Result[Combined result Parquet object]
    Result --> Computed[AggregatorResponse.computed_artifacts]
    Combined --> Manifest[manifest.json beside the results]
    Manifest --> Reader[ResultReader: page or CSV by request id]
    Result --> Reader

docs.title: Batched writes
docs.text:
A result is written a batch at a time, so a large one is never held whole as Python rows. The executor reads it from the adapter's execute_batches when the adapter has one (the SDK's optional StreamingAdapterProtocol; every SQLAlchemy adapter does) in batches of settings.results.fetch_batch_size rows (default 10,000), and from execute, as one batch, when it does not.

ArtifactStore.write_batches writes a single batch straight to the artifact, exactly as before. From the second batch on, each batch is written to its own part file in a temporary folder as it arrives, and polars then streams the parts into the artifact (sink_parquet), concatenated with vertical_relaxed so a column that is empty in one batch and text in the next is text. At most one batch is in memory at a time. If the adapter reports a failure between batches, nothing is written, the parts are removed, and the sub-query fails as it would have from execute. create_artifact_ref(frame, metadata) is write_batches([frame], metadata).

docs.title: The combined result
docs.text:
The aggregator reads each sub-query's artifact as a polars scan (ArtifactStore.scan_parquet), so combines and post-combine operations build one lazy plan, and writes each terminal result of the DAG to its own artifact with ArtifactStore.write_lazy, which streams the plan into the file and reads the row count and columns back from the file's metadata. It is rendered from the same template as the sub-query artifacts, with result_<node_id> as sub_query_id and dag_node_id, so the default template puts it in the run's folder:

<tenant_id>/<request_id>/result_<node_id>.parquet

A combined result has no subgraph or schema version of its own: a template that names <subgraph_name> or <schema_version> gets aggregator and result. Its ArtifactRef (with sub_query_id unset) is recorded in AggregatorResponse.computed_artifacts under the terminal node's id, and its row_count is the whole result's. AggregatorResponse.terminal_results holds only the first settings.results.preview_rows rows of it, read from the saved file, for the answer model.

docs.title: The result manifest
docs.text:
After saving a run's results the aggregator writes a manifest beside them with ArtifactStore.write_manifest: which results the run produced, never their rows. While a hook is attached at answer.after, it is written later, once those hooks allowed (see Withheld runs below).

{"request_id": "0f1c...", "results": [
  {"node_id": "combine_g1", "columns": ["genre_name"], "row_count": 25, "truncated": false, "column_kinds": {"genre_name": "text"}}]}

column_kinds is each column's type category, read from the saved parquet file's schema: integer, decimal and float are number; date, time and timestamp temporal; string text; bool boolean; anything else other.

truncated is true when a sub-query upstream of that node in the DAG was cut at its row cap. The same entries are AggregatorResponse.results and QueryResult.result_manifest.

Its path is the artifact template rendered like a saved result's, with manifest as the name and .json for .parquet, so the default template puts it at:

<tenant_id>/<request_id>/manifest.json

A template without <sub_query_id> or <dag_node_id> gets -manifest added, as any file of the run would (see One artifact per sub-query), so a flat template still gives each run its own manifest.

docs.title: Reading a result back
docs.text:
ResultReader (execution/artifacts/results.py), behind engine.results (manifest, page and csv) (see Query API), reads one tenant's results by request id:

  1. The request id and the result id must be plain tokens (letters, digits, _, -; up to 128 characters). Anything else is ResultNotFound, before any path is built.
  2. The manifest is read from the key rendered for the reader's tenant and that request id (ArtifactStore.read_manifest). No such key in the results store is ResultNotFound, so another tenant's run is not found, not refused. A run a hook ended has no manifest, so it is not found either (below).
  3. The result id must be a node_id the manifest lists. The parquet key is then rendered from the template, exactly as the aggregator wrote it (ArtifactStore.scan_result); the manifest never supplies a key.
  4. A page is scan.slice(offset, limit).collect() on a polars scan, so only that slice is read. A CSV export collects one CSV_CHUNK_ROWS (10,000) slice at a time and yields it as CSV text, header first.

docs.title: Withheld runs
docs.text:
Every read goes through the manifest (step 2), so a run's results are readable exactly when its manifest exists. A run a hook ended (HOOK_DENIED, HOOK_FAILED, NEEDS_APPROVAL, COST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED) never has one:

  • While a hook is attached at answer.after, the aggregator saves the parquet files but not the manifest. The node that asks answer.after (answer_synthesizer, or answer_gate for a run with no answer) writes it once the hooks allowed (release_results). Until then nothing is readable, not even from inside the run; a deny, or a run that crashes first, leaves no manifest. A failed write fails the run.
  • Without such a hook, no hook can end the run after the aggregator, which writes the manifest as soon as the results are saved, with no extra write.
  • A hook that ends the run at an earlier point ends it before the aggregator runs.

The parquet files are not deleted, because the ResultStore protocol has no delete; retention purges them with the rest of the run's folder. Since the manifest is written in the graph, every caller that runs it is covered: run_query, stream_query, nl2sql eval and trace replay. See What withholding guarantees.

docs.title: Where the files go
docs.text:
An artifact's key is the rendered path template, with / between its parts: <tenant_id>/<request_id>/<sub_query_id>.parquet by default. That key is the ArtifactRef's uri. Each Parquet file is written to a temporary folder first and handed to the results store in 1 MiB chunks (ResultStore.write); the manifest is handed over in one piece.

The local store keeps a key as a file under its folder, <storage.path>/results/, so the default template gives:

<storage.path>/results/<tenant_id>/<request_id>/<sub_query_id>.parquet

It writes each file to a temporary name and renames it, and refuses a key that is absolute or contains ...

Reading goes through ResultStore.open. When the store opens a local file, as local does, polars scans that file in place, so a page or a CSV slice reads only what it needs. Any other store's stream is read into memory first, because a scan outlives the call that opened it.

The store is exercised by real read/write round-trip tests (packages/nl2sql/tests/unit/test_artifact_store.py, test_trace_result_stores.py).

docs.title: Retention
docs.text:
The local store takes max_age_days (default 7):

# storage.yaml
results: { type: local, max_age_days: 30 }

engine.storage.purge() deletes every result file last written more than max_age_days ago, then the run folders it emptied, and returns how many files went. nl2sql storage purge calls it, and nl2sql-api calls it at startup and once a day. A result past its age is gone: its page and CSV routes then answer ResultNotFound, as for an unknown run.

docs.title: A results store of your own
docs.text:
There is no built-in S3 or ADLS store (owner decision 6 in the Phase 2 design). A results store is the ResultStore protocol from nl2sql_sdk.stores: bytes in, bytes out, no Parquet knowledge. A sketch on S3 with boto3:

from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path
from typing import BinaryIO, ClassVar, Iterable

import boto3
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field


class S3ResultsConfig(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")
    bucket: str
    prefix: str = "nl2sql/results/"
    max_age_days: int = Field(7, ge=1)


class S3Results:
    interface_version: ClassVar[int] = 4
    slot: ClassVar[str] = "results"
    config_model: ClassVar[type] = S3ResultsConfig

    def __init__(self, cfg: S3ResultsConfig) -> None:
        self.bucket, self.prefix, self.max_age_days = cfg.bucket, cfg.prefix, cfg.max_age_days
        self.s3 = boto3.client("s3")

    @classmethod
    def from_config(cls, cfg: S3ResultsConfig, *, folder: Path) -> "S3Results":
        return cls(cfg)

    def write(self, key: str, chunks: Iterable[bytes]) -> int:
        body = b"".join(chunks)          # or a multipart upload for large results
        self.s3.put_object(Bucket=self.bucket, Key=self.prefix + key, Body=body)
        return len(body)

    def open(self, key: str) -> BinaryIO:
        return self.s3.get_object(Bucket=self.bucket, Key=self.prefix + key)["Body"]

    def exists(self, key: str) -> bool:
        try:
            self.s3.head_object(Bucket=self.bucket, Key=self.prefix + key)
            return True
        except self.s3.exceptions.ClientError:
            return False

    def purge(self, older_than: datetime) -> int:
        deleted = 0
        for page in self.s3.get_paginator("list_objects_v2").paginate(Bucket=self.bucket, Prefix=self.prefix):
            for item in page.get("Contents", []):
                if item["LastModified"] < older_than:
                    self.s3.delete_object(Bucket=self.bucket, Key=item["Key"])
                    deleted += 1
        return deleted

Register it (registry.add_store("s3", S3Results), or the nl2sql.stores entry point group) and name it: results: { type: s3, bucket: my-results }. Or pass an object: Storage(path=".nl2sql", results=S3Results(...)). engine.storage.purge() purges a store that has a max_age_days attribute; one without it is left alone, for a bucket with its own lifecycle rule. A sketch like this one is not tested here; test yours against your bucket.

docs.title: ArtifactRef fields
docs.text:
ArtifactRef contains:

  • uri, the result's key in the results store, and format (parquet)
  • row_count, columns, bytes
  • content_hash, created_at
  • optional schema_version
  • optional sub_query_id, the sub-query whose result this is
  • path_template, the template actually rendered (see One artifact per sub-query)

docs.title: Path templating
docs.text:
The path template defines the artifact path relative to the results folder. It defaults to:

<tenant_id>/<request_id>/<sub_query_id>.parquet

Each <key> placeholder is substituted from the metadata the executor passes to write_batches. The SQL executor supplies these keys:

  • tenant_id
  • request_id (the trace ID, shared by every sub-query of a run)
  • sub_query_id (the sub-query's id, which is also its scan node's id)
  • dag_node_id (the same value as sub_query_id)
  • subgraph_name
  • schema_version

A template referencing any other placeholder raises a ValueError naming the placeholder that could not be filled. A path is never written with an unrendered placeholder in it. Adding placeholders therefore requires threading the corresponding metadata through the executor first.

docs.title: One artifact per sub-query
docs.text:
A question that decomposes into several sub-queries runs them under one trace ID, often side by side, and each must write its own file. When they shared <tenant_id>/<request_id>.parquet, concurrent writes produced one corrupt Parquet file (AGGREGATOR_FAILED: parquet: File out of specification), and sequential writes kept only the last sub-query's rows, so a join combined a result with itself and returned a wrong answer with no error.

A template that names neither <sub_query_id> nor <dag_node_id> is therefore made unique rather than rejected: the store adds -<sub_query_id> to the end of the file name, before its extension, so <tenant_id>/<request_id>.parquet writes <tenant_id>/<request_id>-<sub_query_id>.parquet. The ArtifactRef records the template actually rendered in path_template and the sub-query in sub_query_id. A store used directly, with no sub_query_id in its metadata, renders the template as written.

docs.title: Tenant-aware paths
docs.text:
Because the default template starts with <tenant_id>, artifacts are partitioned per tenant:

<results folder>/<tenant_id>/<request_id>/<sub_query_id>.parquet

docs.title: Testing Architecture
docs.text: Tests are organized by scope and live under packages/**/tests. The core engine has unit, integration, and end-to-end tests.

docs.title: Test layout
docs.text:
packages/nl2sql/tests/
  unit/             # Node-level tests, registries, stores
  integration/      # Pipeline components with real data
  e2e/              # End-to-end flows
  cli/              # CLI command tests
  adapters/         # Cross-dialect adapter contract tests
  sqlalchemy_base/  # tests of the SDK's SQLAlchemy base (nl2sql_sdk.sqlalchemy)
  realdb/           # Against real PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server (the test bed)
packages/api/tests/ # FastAPI route and service tests (stubbed engine)

pytest.ini is the single source of truth for pytest configuration - test paths, markers, and addopts. Do not add a [tool.pytest.ini_options] table to pyproject.toml: pytest reads only one config file, and pytest.ini wins, so such a table is silently ignored. Dev/test tooling lives in the root pyproject.toml under [dependency-groups] dev (pip install --group dev).

docs.title: Markers and what CI runs
docs.text:
Three independent things can make a test unrunnable in the fast job, so they are three markers. A test may carry more than one.

Marker Means Provided by integration Needs external resources: the demo's SQLite databases - vendored Chinook and the generated support and webanalytics, read from the installed package (nl2sql.testing.config.make_demo_config) - or the downloaded ONNX embedding model. The package; tests/e2e writes its own project with nl2sql init --demo llm Needs a real OPENAI_API_KEY. Costs money per run. Nothing in CI - never selected. realdb Needs a real PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQL Server: the test bed. testbed/docker-compose.yml, in the realdb workflow

Everything under packages/nl2sql/tests/integration/ is marked integration automatically by packages/nl2sql/tests/conftest.py, and everything under packages/nl2sql/tests/realdb/ is marked realdb the same way. The llm marker is declared per module, next to a comment saying which call needs the key. Only four modules carry it - test_ast_planner_real_data.py, test_decomposer_real_data.py, test_logical_validator_real_data.py and test_answer_synthesizer_real_data.py - all of them nodes that call a chat model directly. Nothing else in the directory needs a key: indexing calls no model, so tests that index real data run key-free.

.github/workflows/test.yml has three test jobs over the source tree:

  • test runs pytest -m "not integration and not realdb" across Python 3.12 and 3.13. This is the fast job and must stay fast.
  • integration runs pytest -m "integration and not llm" on one Python version, after writing and indexing a demo project (nl2sql init --demo demo-ci and nl2sql --config demo-ci/nl2sql.yaml index), key-free with the local embedder. The ONNX model is cached across runs. That subset covers schema indexing, datasource resolution, schema retrieval, aggregation and the local embedder against the real Chinook database; run it with --collect-only -q for the current list.
  • eval-gates runs in parallel with integration: the same demo project and model cache, then the three key-free eval gates (plans, retrieval, routing; see Evals) and the upload of their reports.

integration and eval-gates are skipped, and count as passing, on a pull request that changes only documentation (docs/** or Markdown files); the code-changes job decides.

A separate workflow, .github/workflows/realdb.yml, runs pytest -m realdb against the test bed on GitHub's runners: on pull requests that change database-facing code, nightly on main, and on demand before a release. Its realdb-gate job always runs and is the required check.

Three more jobs test the package rather than the source tree:

  • api-image builds packages/api/Dockerfile from the repository root, the image the release pushes to GHCR, without pushing it, and imports nl2sql_api.main inside it. tests/unit/test_docker_images.py separately checks that every Dockerfile's FROM python:X.Y satisfies every package's requires-python.

  • build builds the three wheels and sdists, installs them into a clean virtualenv and runs import nl2sql and nl2sql --help.

  • fresh-install takes those wheels and installs them the way a user does, pip install "nl2sql-engine[demo]", into an empty virtualenv outside the checkout. It then boots nl2sql demo --hosted (the command the Hugging Face Space runs) with no API key, and passes only when the playground page, /api/meta, /api/schema and /api/index all answer from that install. It is what catches a wheel that imports but ships without the built playground, the sample databases or a dependency the demo extra forgot. scripts/fresh_install_check.py is the whole check, so it runs the same on a laptop:

    pip install build
python scripts/fresh_install_check.py --build   # builds into dist/ first

Any *_API_KEY in your environment is dropped for the run, so a key you exported cannot make it pass where CI would fail. The decisions it makes are unit-tested in tests/unit/test_fresh_install_check.py. After a release the same script runs twice more, from publish_pypi.yaml: with --pypi X.Y.Z to install the published version from PyPI itself, and with --url https://nadeem4nk-nl2sql-demo.hf.space --expect-version X.Y.Z to wait for the live Space to serve it, then once more with its custom domain as --url (see Releasing).

Nothing selects llm. Those tests are run by hand with a key:

OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... pytest -m integration

Collection is not enough to keep these honest. Every test in the directory imports cleanly even when it calls a method that no longer exists, so rot shows up only at call time - which is the point of running the key-free subset in CI rather than gating on --collect-only. The subset is worth keeping wide: every test that can run without a key should, because the ones that cannot are never run by CI at all.

tests/e2e builds one demo project per session (demo_project), indexes it, then moves its .nl2sql aside and leaves a file of that name, so no test can open the shared index or state store. Each test runs on its own copy: private_storage(demo_project, tmp_path / "store") as project_config's storage, or copy_demo(demo_project, tmp_path / "demo") for a whole project. When tests shared the one state.db, engines left open by one test, copies taken while it was open and CLI runs writing it all met in the same file, and CI failed with disk I/O error in whichever test pytest-randomly ran next.

docs.title: Randomised test order
docs.text: pytest-randomly shuffles the order of tests on every run, which turns order-dependent tests - shared class-level caches, leaked globals, fixtures that do not unwind - into loud local failures rather than intermittent CI ones. Each run prints the seed it used; reproduce a failure with pytest -p randomly --randomly-seed=<seed>.

docs.title: Settings in tests
docs.text:
The engine reads its settings from its runtime, not from a process global (configuration v2, section 8), so a test sets them on the runtime it builds:

  • One node or service: nl2sql.testing.runtime.fake_runtime(settings=..., policies=..., traces_dir=..., **attrs) builds a stand-in runtime with a real config, a local results store and a files trace store on traces_dir (pass traces= for another trace store). Settings are written as in YAML: settings={"traces": {"mode": "always"}}.
  • A whole engine: Runtime.from_config(make_config(tmp_path, ...)). An Embeddings(instance=FakeEmbeddings(size=8)) keeps it free of any model.
  • One run with different settings: ctx.derive({"settings.pipeline.plan_cache": True}) returns a run-scoped runtime with a derived config, its own curated answers and its own LLMSet, sharing the stores and the engine's LLM client cache. Evaluation and trace replay use it the same way; the runtime it came from never changes. tests/unit/test_run_scoped_runtime.py pins that down.

There is no process-global settings object to monkeypatch, and no module writes os.environ: a test sets what it needs in the config it builds. The architecture tests keep it that way (An Engine Owns Its Config).

flowchart TD
    Unit[Unit Tests] --> Core[Core Components]
    Integration[Integration Tests] --> Pipeline[Pipeline Nodes]
    E2E[End-to-end Tests] --> Orchestration[Full Orchestration]

docs.title: Runtime coverage targets
docs.text:
• Pipeline nodes (test_node_*.py)
  • Subgraph orchestration (test_sql_agent_subgraph.py)
  • DAG layering (test_graph_layers.py)
  • Registry and store behavior (test_*_registry.py, test_state_store.py)
  • REST contract (packages/api/tests/) via FastAPI TestClient with the get_engine dependency overridden, so no datasource, LLM or network is needed

docs.title: Deterministic validation
docs.text:
Tests enforce deterministic behavior by:

  • using structured output schemas for planner/decomposer
  • validating stable IDs and DAG layering
  • running logical validator checks for expected schema alignment

docs.text: The SDK includes testing utilities to validate schema introspection and result contracts for new adapters.
