  • Core tests: packages/nl2sql/tests/
  • API tests: packages/api/tests/

docs.title: The Chinook Suite
docs.text:
The Chinook suite holds 47 cases about the vendored Chinook database (nl2sql/datasets/chinook.sqlite). Each case has hand-written SQL, the rows that SQL returns, and a hand-written plan. Evaluations compare the engine's answers against it. It is a suite in the eval case format and runs through engine.evals.

File What it holds packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/suites/chinook.yaml The suite: the cases, their rows and their plans packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/suite.py EvalCase, EvalSuite, the loader and the writer packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/regenerate.py regenerate: the rows, through the datasource's adapter packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/run.py The three modes, prices and the cost cap packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/gold_llm.py The gold-plan fake LLM that mode plans runs on packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/scorers/ The scorer interface and the five built-ins packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/evaluator.py Row comparison (compare_results, compare_results_lenient), which result_match reads packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/faithfulness.py Answer faithfulness: the written answer's numbers and names against the rows packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/report.py The report's boards: accuracy, intervals, pass^k, cost, latency packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/gate.py The regression gate's statistics: flips, McNemar's test, the checks packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/llm/prices.py The dated price table every call, mode full's included, is billed from packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/records.py Result records, comparable runs and the published pages packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/evaluation/presets/ Named LLM configs to compare (*.yaml, shipped in the wheel) benchmarks/<kind>/<database>/ Committed result records (layout) packages/nl2sql/tests/unit/test_chinook_suite.py Key-free checks, part of the normal unit suite

docs.title: The cases
docs.text:
The fields are described in Cases and suites. For this suite:

  • The tags. tags come from a fixed list: single-table, filter, join, multi-join, aggregation, having, order-limit, offset, ties, date, paraphrase, keyword-in-question, keyword-in-value, data-range and value-matching. data-range marks a case that needs to know where the data ends ("the most recent month in the data"), and value-matching one that names a stored value in other words ("heavy metal" for 'Heavy Metal').
  • rbac-denial and unanswerable. rbac-denial marks exactly the cases some role is refused, and unanswerable the four the database cannot answer.
  • Every case is approved and hand written, about chinook. So the run is scored, and identified, by Chinook, whatever else the demo registers.
  • The outcomes follow the demo policy. outcome follows CHINOOK_POLICIES in nl2sql/datasets/chinook.py: a role gets refused when its scope does not allow one of tables, and allowed otherwise. An unanswerable case is unanswerable for every role.
  • Ties are broken on a key. Where ORDER BY has ties, sql breaks them on a key (CustomerId, Country and so on) so the result is deterministic, and the case carries the ties tag. When the tie is only about order, order_matters is false.

The data never changes. The suite was moved from 0.6's chinook_gold.yaml and chinook_gold_plans.yaml with only its keys renamed. test_chinook_suite_holds_the_gold_data_unchanged pins a SHA-256 of every case's question, SQL, rows, alternatives, outcomes, tables, columns and plan. A new accepted answer is a reviewed alternative, followed by regenerate; never an edit to the gold data.

docs.title: What the tests check
docs.text:
pytest packages/nl2sql/tests/unit/test_chinook_suite.py runs without an API key and checks that:

  • the data hashes to the pinned digest;
  • every case is approved and hand, on chinook;
  • ids are unique, and paraphrase groups share one result;
  • every table and column exists, and tables equals the tables in sql;
  • every role in outcome exists in the demo policy, and each outcome follows from it;
  • every answerable case has a plan, and no other case does. Each plan is a PlanModel that reads exactly tables and selects as many columns as rows has;
  • every alt_sql reads no table outside tables, returns between one and twenty-five rows, and is not the gold answer written again;
  • Chinook's twelve guided questions (CHINOOK_QUESTIONS) are included verbatim. The demo offers twenty in all; the other eight ask about support and webanalytics, which this suite does not cover.

tests/unit/test_eval_regenerate.py runs regenerate through the sqlite adapter and checks that the committed file is byte for byte what it writes.

docs.title: How a run is scored
docs.text:
Each case runs once per role in its outcome map, and each run is scored by the scorers. For result_match and outcome:

Outcome Passes when allowed Status success, one result set, and its rows equal rows or any alternative refused Status error, a SECURITY_VIOLATION whose message is the generic refusal (it names no table), and no rows unanswerable Status error, a QUESTION_NOT_ANSWERABLE from the datasource resolver's answerability check, and no rows

Rows are compared by value, in selected column order:

  • Names don't count, order does. Column names and aliases are ignored, so SELECT Country AS c matches a gold Country column, but a swapped column order does not.
  • Numbers match within 0.005, because gold values are rounded to two decimals.
  • A number matches a string that spells it, within the same tolerance, so '2009' is 2009: databases differ in which of the two they return for the same value.
  • Other strings must be equal. Two strings compare as strings, so '2009' is not '2009.0'.
  • Row order counts only when order_matters is true.

docs.title: Strict and lenient accuracy
docs.text:
Every run is scored twice, and the report gives both, strict first.

Score What it is Strict The execution match above, unchanged: the same columns, in the same order, and the same rows Lenient Every gold column is answered by some column of the result, wherever it sits

Strict is the honest headline. Lenient exists because most of what it forgives is shape a person would accept:

  • the same two names as FirstName, LastName or the other way round;
  • one extra key column;
  • a year labelled 2009-01-01 where the gold set writes 2009.

Academic and vendor practice has moved the same way. Spider 2.0 counts a prediction correct when every gold column vector appears in the result (paper). Defog's sql-eval falls back to subset_df, matching each gold column's values against some generated column with names, types and order ignored (post).

A run passes leniently when:

  • every gold column is matched, as a multiset of values, by a distinct column of the result, in any position, with column names ignored and the same numeric tolerance;
  • the rows of the matched columns then line up as the strict score requires, so values swapped between rows still fail;
  • the row count is equal, and row order still counts only when order_matters.

Two guardrails keep it from passing wrong answers:

  • A column cap. The result may carry at most max(2 x gold columns, gold columns + 2) columns: three for a one-column gold answer, four for two, six for three. Without it a SELECT * would pass by carrying the gold columns among many others. Databricks Genie counts any extra column as bad (docs), so a cap is the middle ground.
  • No constant columns. Once a result has more than one row, a column whose values are all the same -- all-null included -- may not answer for a gold column: a hard-coded literal has the right height and tells the gold column nothing. On a single row every column is constant, so the rule is off there.

One value normalisation is added, and only one: date and period labels. When a gold value is a YYYY, YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD string and the predicted value is a date starting with it at a component boundary, the two are equal: '2009' matches '2009-01-01', and '2013-02' matches '2013-02-01'.

  • Only the gold side may be the shorter label.
  • Only strings are read this way: a number is a number, never a year.
  • Nothing else is normalised. Anything broader belongs in an alternative answer, which is reviewed per case and cannot silently widen.

Lenient is a superset of strict by construction: everything strict accepts is accepted. It is not partial credit -- a case passes a score or it does not -- and there is no model in either score, so both stay reproducible. Every record carries status and lenient_status, so a case that passes one score and not the other is visible per case.

docs.title: Alternative answers
docs.text:
A question can have more than one right answer:

  • "Who are the top 5 customers by total spend?" is answered just as well with the name in one column as with FirstName and LastName side by side.
  • "What is the total revenue per year?" is answered with the year written 2009 or 2009-01-01.

alt_sql holds those other answers, one SQL each, and regenerate runs each one exactly as it runs sql. A run passes, strictly or leniently, when its rows match rows or any alternative.

This is how the field handles multiple right answers:

  • Snowflake has humans pick every correct answer out of several models' SQL (post).
  • LinkedIn reports that about 60% of its benchmark questions now have several answers, and that without them it "underreported recall by 10-15%" (post).
  • Spider 2.0 supports multiple gold files per task (paper).

docs.title: When to add one, and when not to
docs.text:
Prefer an alternative to loosening the comparator. An alternative is written down, reviewed once, and only ever affects the case it sits on. A looser rule applies to all forty-seven at once and can quietly start passing wrong answers. The lenient score is deliberately narrow for the same reason.

Add one when all of these hold:

  1. A real run produced it. Alternatives come from SQL a model actually wrote, not from shapes someone imagined it might write.
  2. A person has read the rows and would accept them as an answer to the question as written.
  3. It is the same question, from the same tables: an alternative may not read a table outside tables, and the test enforces that.
  4. It is deterministic -- ties broken on a key, as sql does.

Do not add one when the answer is a different question, however reasonable it looks. Two from the run this was built on, both refused:

  • "Where do our customers from Germany live?" answered with three distinct cities. It drops the customers, so it cannot say who lives where. The alternative kept for chinook_021 is the gold answer with the name in one column, not this.
  • "Who are the top customers by total spend?" answered with one row. "Top customers" is a list with no N; one row answers "who is the top customer", a different question. chinook_007 is not the same case: "which employees support the most customers" carries a superlative, and the one employee who holds the maximum is a fair reading of it, so that one is kept.

To add one:

  1. Write the SQL into alt_sql.
  2. From a checkout of the repo, run engine.evals.regenerate(CHINOOK_SUITE_PATH, allow_packaged=True) to write its alt_rows (CHINOOK_SUITE_PATH from nl2sql.evaluation.suite). The flag is needed because the suite lives in the package.
  3. Read the rows it wrote.
  4. Commit both.

Never type an alternative's rows by hand.

docs.title: Mode plans: gold plans through the code nodes
docs.text:
engine.evals.run(mode="plans") checks the nodes that are plain code -- the logical validator (including RBAC), the SQL generator and the executor -- with no model involved. Every answerable case has a hand-written plan (the typed AST the planner emits) that answers it.

A local FakeLLMServer (nl2sql/evaluation/gold_llm.py) answers every LLM call:

Node The fake answers Datasource resolver The case's datasources for a case with sql, and an empty list for an unanswerable one, so the resolver's refusal is what is scored Decomposer One sub-query whose expected columns are the plan's select aliases Planner The gold plan Refiner "Keep the same plan." Answer synthesizer A fixed sentence

Every answer comes from one table keyed by the structured output's schema name, so a new structured output is one more entry.

The rest is the real pipeline on the indexed demo, so a failing case is a bug in a code node or in the plan, never in a model. The run turns curated answers off, because a verified answer has no plan. It also scores refusals against the generic message: the demo's config names the refused table so the playground can show it, and the run turns that off.

Each plan reads exactly the case's tables (the RBAC outcome is derived from them) and selects the rows' columns in order. PlanModel has no subqueries or window functions, so a few plans express the answer differently from sql:

  • anti-joins for "longest track per genre" (chinook_008) and "never purchased" (chinook_039);
  • conditional sums in HAVING for "jazz but never rock" (chinook_009);
  • COUNT(DISTINCT x) through the aggregate's distinct: true flag (chinook_011 and chinook_034).

The suite file's header lists these.

Mode plans runs on every PR as packages/nl2sql/tests/e2e/test_evals_plans.py, in the key-free integration job. It builds an engine on the generated demo with no API key in the environment, runs engine.evals.run(mode="plans"), and requires every case to pass -- allowed, refused and unanswerable, for every role -- with none skipped. The same job runs nl2sql eval run --mode plans --baseline benchmarks, which gates the run against the newest mode plans record in benchmarks/ (In CI).

When a gold plan fails, the fault is in the engine or in the plan. Fix an engine bug with a regression test. Never change the gold data to make a plan pass.

docs.title: Mode full: the real model, end to end
docs.text:
engine.evals.run(mode="full") runs the whole product -- every LLM node on a real model -- on the cases, and scores it with the same scorers. It costs money, so it never runs in CI and never runs without a dollar cap (max_cost_usd). The key comes from the LLM config (${env:...}).

from nl2sql.evaluation.presets import PRESETS_DIR, load_llm_file, model_config

report = engine.evals.run(max_cost_usd=5)                                # the engine's own llm section
report = engine.evals.run(llm={"gpt-5.4": model_config("gpt-5.4"),       # a comparison
                               "mini": load_llm_file(PRESETS_DIR / "gpt-5.4-mini-helpers.yaml")},
                          max_cost_usd=10)

model_config(MODEL) puts MODEL on all six LLM nodes:

  • A model in VERIFIED_MODELS (nl2sql/llm/providers.py) names its own provider and temperature: gpt-5.4, gpt-5.4-mini, gpt-4.1, gpt-4o, gpt-5.5, gpt-5-mini, claude-opus-5, claude-sonnet-5, claude-haiku-4-5, and others. None is sent where the model rejects one (gpt-5.5, gpt-5-mini, claude-opus-5, claude-sonnet-5).
  • Any other model is written provider/model (openrouter/meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct, ollama/llama3) and runs at temperature 0 (none for anthropic).

From the command line, --llm takes a preset, a file or NAME= either:

nl2sql eval run --mode full --llm gpt-5.4 --llm mini=mini-helpers --max-cost 10

The presets in nl2sql/evaluation/presets/ are llm sections, shipped in the package:

Preset Models gpt-5.4 gpt-5.4 on every node gpt-5.4-mini-helpers gpt-5.4 on the planner and refiner; gpt-5.4-mini elsewhere claude-planner claude-opus-5 on the planner and refiner; gpt-5.4 elsewhere

docs.title: Cost and the cap
docs.text:
Every LLM call is billed from nl2sql/llm/prices.py, a committed table of USD per 1M tokens, dated with the day it was checked (an llm.prices row replaces a model's):

Model Input Cached input Cache write Output Source gpt-5.4 2.50 0.25 2.50 15.00 OpenAI pricing page, 2026-09-21 gpt-5.4-mini 0.75 0.075 0.75 4.50 OpenAI pricing page, 2026-09-21 claude-opus-5 5.00 0.50 6.25 25.00 Anthropic model table (claude-api skill, cached 2026-06-24) claude-sonnet-5 2.00 0.20 2.50 10.00 same claude-haiku-4-5 1.00 0.10 1.25 5.00 same

A call costs (input - cached - cache_write) x input + cached x cached_input + cache_write x cache_write_rate + output x output, from the token counts each wire adapter records in QueryResult.usage:

  • Reasoning tokens are part of output and billed as output.
  • Prompt caching: OpenAI charges nothing extra to write its automatic cache. Anthropic bills a cache write at 1.25x input and a read at 0.1x.
  • Pricing by node: each call is priced by the model its node is configured with, so a dated snapshot name in the response still prices correctly.

How the cap holds:

  • Before any call: every model that any node of any config would use must have a price. A missing one is an UnknownPriceError naming the config, node and model.
  • Before each case: the run adds the most expensive case so far to the running total, and stops if that could pass max_cost_usd. The cap covers the whole run, every config and pass.
  • The first case always runs. So the total can pass the cap only by what one case costs more than the most expensive case before it.
  • A stopped run is still reported. It returns its report with stopped: "max_cost", and each board's completed_cases is short of planned_cases.

The run turns the plan cache off, so a second pass asks the planner again instead of replaying the first. Curated answers are on unless curated says otherwise: a case a verified query answered also runs with them off, and the report's accuracy_generated scores every case on the generated path (Curated answers in mode full).

docs.title: Answer faithfulness
docs.text:
Accuracy scores the rows. The answer synthesizer then writes a sentence about them, and that sentence can state a number the rows do not hold while the rows are right. The faithfulness scorer checks every written answer (its summary and content) against the rows the run returned, deterministically, with no model (nl2sql/evaluation/faithfulness.py).

What the answer writes Supported when A number: 1,297, 1234.5, $523.06, -5 It equals a value in the rows at the precision written (523.1 and 523 match 523.06; 523.60 does not), the row count, or the sum of a numeric column A percentage: 37.2% As above, or it is a share in the rows times 100 (0.3718) A number inside a text cell or the question Always: the year of 2009-01-01, Symphony No. 5, top 5, in 2013 A quoted ("Jazz") or bold (**Rock**) name A text cell, a column name or the question contains it, or it contains a text cell

Some numbers and names are never checked:

  • Not numbers: ordinals (2nd), list markers (1. at the start of a line), numbers glued to a word or identifier (chinook_001, MPEG-4, #7), and the month and day of a date.
  • Names only when quoted or bold. Bold spans with a digit, ending in : (**Note:**), or longer than six words are skipped, so the name check flags little it should not.

1,300 for 1297, a 2013 that neither the rows nor the question hold, and a bold genre the rows do not list are all unsupported.

Each record carries faithfulness: faithful, unsupported_numbers and unsupported_entities (as written), and checked (how many numbers and names were checked). A refusal or error writes no answer, and the scorer does not apply to it. The board's faithfulness gives the rate over the answers written and lists each unfaithful one. Mode plans does not run it: its fake synthesizer writes the same fixed sentence for every case.

docs.title: Reading a run: intervals, flips and pass^k
docs.text:
Forty-seven cases cannot settle much on their own. 27 of 47 is 57.4%, and its 95% Wilson interval is 43.3%-70.5% -- about fourteen points either way. Every board therefore reports that interval next to each accuracy, and the gate below is built on the cases that moved rather than on the headline (Anthropic, A statistical approach to model evals). The interval is taken over the runs a config scored. With more than one pass, the runs of a single case are not independent, so it reads narrower than it really is; pass^k below counts cases and does not.

Compare two runs case by case, not headline to headline. The same cases run both times, so the runs are paired and most of the variance cancels. nl2sql/evaluation/gate.py lists, per config:

  • how many cases went pass -> fail and how many fail -> pass, and which ones;
  • McNemar's exact two-sided p-value on those flips.

Cases both runs got right, or both got wrong, say nothing about a change. Only the discordant pairs do, and under "the two runs are equally good" each flip is a fair coin. Ten lost and none gained is p = 0.002; five each way is p = 1.0.

A case counts as passed only when every pass passed, so over three passes a case that has become flaky reads as a regression.

The regression gate (engine.evals.gate, nl2sql eval run --baseline) compares only comparable runs (the same mode, suite digest, schema and, in mode full, roles and curated answers), and a case passes on execution accuracy (result_match and outcome), the measure 0.6's tier 2 published: a faithfulness miss alone is not a regression. With curated answers on it checks that accuracy as users see it and on the generated path. It fails a run when, for any config both runs name:

Check Default (evals.yaml gate) Why More than max_regressions cases flipped from pass to fail 2 in mode full; always 0 in modes plans and retrieval A handful of named cases is something a person can go and read; with no model, any flip is a bug Mode full: more cases lost than gained, and McNemar's exact two-sided p < alpha 0.05 A small but real drop should not pass because it is under the count Cost per case rose by more than max_cost_increase 0.2 Unchanged

With passes above one the board also reports pass^k: the share of cases that passed in every pass, for both scores, beside mean accuracy. Mean accuracy counts runs, so a case that passes two times of three still lifts it. pass^k counts cases, and a flaky one never counts. It is the number to read when asking whether the engine can be relied on, rather than how often it happens to be right (tau-bench). determinism is stricter than pass^k: it says whether the SQL and rows were identical across passes.

docs.title: Results over time
docs.text:
A recorded run is a JSON file under the repo's benchmarks/ folder:

benchmarks/<kind>/<database>/<YYYY-MM-DD>_<shortsha>_<config>.json
Part What it is mode full, plans or retrieval; 0.6 wrote mode full runs under tier2, read as full database The datasource id (chinook) shortsha The first seven characters of the engine commit config The config name (retrieval for a retrieval run)

-2, -3... are added when the name is taken.

Every record holds:

Field What it is schema, kind The record format (2) and the run's mode recorded_at UTC date and time engine_version The installed nl2sql-engine version (the same for every run until a release) git_commit, git_dirty The engine's commit and whether its tracked files had uncommitted changes. Found by walking up from the installed nl2sql package to its .git, so a run from the demo folder of an editable install still names the repo commit. "unknown" for a wheel install or without git, never null note What changed, e.g. "slim prompts" (null without one) dataset The suite's name and digest (a SHA-256 of its LF bytes, so a Windows checkout hashes the same). A record 0.6 wrote names chinook_gold.yaml database datasource_id, engine (sqlite), schema_fingerprint and the tables and columns counts. The fingerprint hashes the latest indexed schema snapshot's tables, columns, types and keys, so re-indexing an unchanged database keeps it. Built from the datasources the suite's cases name, not every datasource the project registered: the demo registers three and this suite asks about Chinook, so a run there is still chinook with Chinook's fingerprint config The config name, and provider:model per node metrics The headline numbers: execution accuracy (strict and lenient) with their intervals, then accuracy_all_scorers and accuracy_generated, pass_k, answerability, dollars, tokens, latency, determinism and faithfulness; or, for retrieval, the recall summary scoreboard The config's whole board, every case record included

The headline accuracy is execution accuracy (accuracy.execution), the measure 0.6's tier 2 published, so the series reads the same before and after 0.7. The 0.6 records are on the 0.6 gold file, so the first 0.7 run starts a new series beside them.

Records are never edited after writing: a run writes a new file. Two runs are comparable when they share the mode, the suite digest and the schema fingerprint, and for mode full the roles and whether curated answers were on. nl2sql eval publish REPORT ..., run from the repo root, writes the records of the reports nl2sql eval run saved, then reads every record and rewrites docs/benchmarks.md and the README's results block. It reads no clock, so the same records always give byte-identical pages. packages/nl2sql/tests/unit/test_eval_records.py checks in CI, with no key, that the committed pages are exactly what publish makes from the committed records.

docs.title: How mode full is tested
docs.text:
packages/nl2sql/tests/e2e/test_evals_full_fake_llm.py runs mode full with no key and no spending. It points two llm sections at two FakeLLMServers that serve the gold plans with canned usage (cached and reasoning tokens included). One server has a plan deliberately wrong. The fakes learn which case is being asked from each run's run.started event, and the fake synthesizer writes each answer from the case's rows, so the good server's answers are faithful and the bad server's answer on its wrong rows is not.

The test checks:

  • the scoring, the comparison and its differences;
  • the dollars against the price table;
  • the cap stopping mid-run, with a partial report;
  • an unpriced model failing before any call;
  • two passes with the plan cache off;
  • the database identity the report records.

The unit tests cover the rest:

Test What it covers tests/unit/test_eval_run.py The runner: approved cases only, roles and selectors, the derived runtime of each mode, configs compared, curated hits run twice, clarify, the events tests/unit/test_eval_report.py Prices, the boards, the Wilson interval on known counts, McNemar's exact test on a constructed table, pass^k and the gate tests/unit/test_eval_scorers.py Each scorer tests/unit/test_answer_faithfulness.py The faithfulness rules tests/unit/test_eval_records.py The records tests/unit/test_eval_gate.py The gate: same suite and mode, execution accuracy, both accuracies, baselines from records tests/cli/test_eval_command.py nl2sql eval run, regenerate and publish, with their exit codes

docs.title: Retrieval recall
docs.text:
Before the planner sees a schema, the schema retriever picks the tables and columns it is given. A column it never sends is one the planner cannot use. engine.evals.run(mode="retrieval") measures that, per answerable case and role, against tables and columns, with no key, no LLM and no cost.

How it runs (nl2sql/evaluation/scorers/retrieval_recall.py):

  • The search always runs. Chinook's 11 tables are under settings.retrieval.full_snapshot_max_tables (15), which would send the whole schema without a search, so the run sets the limit to 0.
  • Each case is scored against the datasource it names, which for this suite is always chinook, whatever else the project has registered. Routing's ranking is scored separately by the routing scorer; the resolver's answerability check is an LLM call and is skipped.
  • The retriever runs as the pipeline runs it (MMR, k 8 table entries, then k 12 column and relationship entries of those tables), on the index and embedder the project has. The demo's embedder is the local ONNX all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Its query is the question alone, since the decomposer that would add filters, groupings and expected columns is an LLM.

What was sent is read from the retriever's retrieval record, the one a run trace keeps.

The retrieval_recall score's detail has:

  • table_recall (needed tables sent / needed tables) and column_recall (needed Table.Columns sent / needed);
  • the missed_tables and missed_columns;
  • tables_sent and columns_sent.

The board's retrieval has the means, and how many cases had every needed table (perfect_tables) or column (perfect_columns). The report's settings has the k values and the MMR settings, so two reports are only compared like for like.

Read recall with the amount sent: sending all 11 tables would score 100%, so a change that raises recall by sending more is not an improvement by itself. A missed column is one the planner cannot select, filter or join on.

The committed baseline (2026-09-22, engine 0.1.2, 39 questions):

Table recall Column recall Every table Every column Sent on average 98.5% 72.6% 37 of 39 15 of 39 8.3 tables, 24.2 columns

The first 0.7 record (2026-10-15, CI's baseline) scores each answerable case once per role allowed to read it, 96 case runs over 43 cases: 97.9% table recall, 76.5% column recall, 7.98 tables and 22.2 columns sent on average. It is a new series: the suite is not the 0.6 gold file.

Most misses are columns of a table that was sent. Once one column entry of a table is picked, or a relationship entry adds its key columns, only those columns are sent rather than all of them. So Invoice often reaches the planner as BillingCountry or a key without Total or InvoiceDate (chinook_014, "How much did we earn in each year?", gets Invoice with BillingCountry only). The two table misses are chinook_009 (Customer, Invoice) and chinook_034 (Artist).

packages/nl2sql/tests/e2e/test_evals_retrieval.py runs mode retrieval on the generated demo in the key-free integration job. It checks that the run covers every answerable case and reports recall and routing, not what the recall is. The same job gates the recall itself: nl2sql eval run --mode retrieval --baseline benchmarks fails when more than two cases stopped passing (perfect recall, and routing where it applies) against the newest mode retrieval record, or the loss is significant.

docs.title: The real-database test bed
docs.text:
Most tests run on SQLite, DuckDB and mocks. Anything that depends on how a real server behaves (catalogs, quoting, permissions, read-only sessions, timeouts) is tested against real servers instead: PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server, each loaded with a well-known sample database and a large generated schema. One compose file, testbed/docker-compose.yml, defines all of it, and the same file runs on your machine, on GitHub's runners in CI, and on one small GCP VM started on demand.

The design is in Phase 2, section 3.

Server Sample database Generated wide schema PostgreSQL 16 Pagila, in database pagila database wide, schemas sales_01 ... ops_20 and audit MySQL 8.0 Sakila, in database sakila databases wide_s01 ... wide_s20 and wide_audit (MySQL's schemas are databases) SQL Server 2022 AdventureWorksLT, in database AdventureWorksLT2022 database wide, schemas sales_01 ... ops_20 and audit

docs.title: Local use
docs.text:
You need Docker with the compose plugin.

python testbed/passwords.py > testbed/.env               # once: random passwords, ignored by version control
docker compose -f testbed/docker-compose.yml up -d --wait
set -a; . testbed/.env; set +a                           # the tests read the same variables
REALDB=compose pytest -m realdb
docker compose -f testbed/docker-compose.yml down        # add -v to drop the data

In PowerShell, load the variables with Get-Content testbed/.env | ForEach-Object { $name, $value = $_ -split '=', 2; Set-Item "env:$name" $value } and set $env:REALDB = "compose".

The compose file has no default password, so no password is written in the repository: TESTBED_POSTGRES_PASSWORD, TESTBED_MYSQL_PASSWORD and TESTBED_MSSQL_PASSWORD are required, and up stops naming the variable if one is missing. testbed/passwords.py prints three fresh random ones. Docker Compose reads testbed/.env by itself, because it sits beside the compose file. A server keeps the password its data volume was created with, so make a new .env only together with down -v.

The first up downloads the samples, generates the wide schema and loads everything, which takes a few minutes (SQL Server wants about 2 GB of memory). Loading happens once per data volume, so a later up is quick. --wait returns only when every server is loaded.

Install the drivers the tests use with pip install -e "packages/nl2sql[postgres,mysql,mssql,duckdb]". SQL Server also needs Microsoft's ODBC Driver for SQL Server (17 or 18) on the machine; the tests use the newest one installed.

docs.title: The compose file
docs.text:
Service Image What it does samples python:3.12-slim One-shot. Runs testbed/samples.py: downloads each sample from a pinned URL, checks its SHA-256, extracts Sakila from its archive, and writes the wide schema for the three servers with testbed/wide_schema.py, all into the samples volume. Skips what is already there. postgres postgres:16 Starts after samples. On its first start, testbed/postgres/init.sh (the image's own init mechanism) loads Pagila and the wide schema and creates the reader login. mysql mysql:8.0 The same with Sakila, through testbed/mysql/init.sh. The mysql client handles Sakila's DELIMITER blocks. mssql mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest The server. Its healthcheck passes only once mssql-init has finished. It has a 60-second stop_grace_period: after Docker's default 10 seconds a stop ends in SIGKILL, and the next start then recovers every database before any can be opened. mssql-init the same image, for its sqlcmd Runs testbed/mssql/init.sh: waits up to five minutes until the server accepts logins and every sample database it already has is ONLINE in sys.databases (asked from master, since a database still in recovery cannot be opened), then restores AdventureWorksLT from the .bak, loads the wide schema and creates the reader login, skipping each database that already exists. Then it marks itself loaded for its healthcheck and idles instead of exiting.

Every server has a healthcheck that passes only once it is loaded, so up --wait is enough before running tests. --wait fails on an exited container unless another service waits for it to complete, as the servers wait for samples. Nothing waits for mssql-init, and on a later up it skips everything and would exit at once, so it stays running instead; that is what makes the same up -d --wait work on every start.

The file reads four variables:

Variable Default TESTBED_BIND 127.0.0.1 TESTBED_POSTGRES_PASSWORD none: required (testbed/passwords.py) TESTBED_MYSQL_PASSWORD none: required TESTBED_MSSQL_PASSWORD none: required Service Published port Admin user Sample database postgres 15432 postgres pagila mysql 13306 root sakila mssql 11433 sa AdventureWorksLT2022

The ports avoid a clash with a database already installed locally.

Each server also has a login nl2sql_reader, with the server's password, that may read its sample database and nothing else: not the wide schema. Tests use it where a limited login matters.

docs.title: The sample databases and their licences
docs.text:
Nothing is committed to the repository; the samples service downloads each file and refuses one whose SHA-256 differs from the pinned value, so we never redistribute the samples. If one is ever vendored, its licence file goes beside it.

Sample Files Source Licence Pagila pagila-schema.sql, pagila-insert-data.sql github.com/devrimgunduz/pagila, pinned to commit 5ba5a57, from before Pagila moved to PostgreSQL 18 PostgreSQL License (copyright Devrim Gündüz) Sakila sakila-schema.sql, sakila-data.sql, from sakila-db.tar.gz downloads.mysql.com New BSD AdventureWorksLT 2022 AdventureWorksLT2022.bak github.com/microsoft/sql-server-samples, release adventureworks MIT

The server images have their own terms. The SQL Server image runs the free Developer edition, which needs ACCEPT_EULA=Y and is licensed for development and testing, which is all we do with it.

When an upstream file changes, samples stops with the expected and actual hashes. Check the new file, then pin its URL and hash in testbed/samples.py.

docs.title: The generated wide schema
docs.text:
python testbed/wide_schema.py --dialect postgres|mysql|tsql --seed 7 writes one SQL file. The same seed always gives the same schema:

Feature Count What it tests Schemas 20 (sales_01 ... ops_20), plus a small audit Index scope, policy globs Tables 1,200 in the 20 schemas, with 5 to 30 columns each Reflection and retrieval at scale Views 2 per schema Views are indexed Odd column types boolean, uuid, json, binary, xml and array where the server has the type; the nearest plain type where it does not Profiling never aborts Comments on about 30% of tables and columns Descriptions come from the database Foreign keys within each schema Join paths Mixed-case names 10 tables, such as CustomerAccounts Quoting Rows 3 tables with 1,000,000 rows, 50 with 1,000, the rest empty Row estimates, profiling limits

The rows are made on the server (generate_series on PostgreSQL, a cross join of digit tables on MySQL and SQL Server), so the file stays small.

Routing is measured on it too: tests/realdb/test_routing_wide.py indexes Pagila and the whole wide schema side by side on PostgreSQL, and checks that questions about films go to Pagila and questions about payroll runs or ledger entries go to the wide schema, however many tables there are to vote (the routing suite). Indexing the wide schema takes about 17 minutes on CI's runner, so the test runs on PostgreSQL only, and only when REALDB_WIDE_ROUTING is true: the workflow sets it nightly, on demand, and on pull requests that change nl2sql/indexing/ (or the test itself). It skips otherwise.

docs.title: The realdb marker and fixtures
docs.text:
Every test under packages/nl2sql/tests/realdb/ is marked realdb. Its fixtures find the servers from the environment:

Variable Meaning REALDB=compose The compose servers on 127.0.0.1, at the published ports, with the passwords in the three TESTBED_*_PASSWORD variables REALDB_POSTGRES, REALDB_MYSQL, REALDB_MSSQL A URL for one server, such as postgresql://postgres:<password>@127.0.0.1:15432/, with the password percent-encoded. It wins over REALDB=compose. REALDB_REQUIRED=1 A missing server is a failure, not a skip

Without a server, a realdb test skips with the fix in its message. Under REALDB_REQUIRED=1 it fails instead: a green run that skipped the real databases proves nothing.

Fixture or helper What it gives server Each of the three servers in turn (RealServer: its admin URL, its sample database, engine() for a SQLAlchemy engine) datasource(server, database=None, **fields) A Datasource for one database on the server, the sample by default engine_on(database=None, **fields) An NL2SQL engine on one database of server, with a fake LLM and no key

Test code may name dialects and use SQLAlchemy directly; the boundary tests cover packages/*/src, not the tests.

test_conformance.py runs the adapter conformance kit (nl2sql_sdk.testing) on each server. Its seed goes into schemas kit_a and kit_b of the sample database (databases of those names on MySQL), written with the admin login and dropped after each test. Its limited_login is a login nl2sql_kit the test makes, whose password holds @ : / # % and which may read kit_a only.

docs.title: CI: the realdb workflow
docs.text:
.github/workflows/realdb.yml runs the test bed on GitHub's runners. No cloud credentials are involved.

Job Runs What it does changes always Works out whether a pull request touches database-facing code (the paths below). On the nightly and on-demand runs the answer is always yes. realdb on a pull request when changes says so; nightly on main; on demand (workflow_dispatch), which is run before every release generates fresh passwords with testbed/passwords.py into the job's environment, masked in the log; docker compose ... up -d --wait, installs Microsoft's msodbcsql18 for pyodbc and packages/nl2sql[postgres,mysql,mssql,duckdb], then pytest -m realdb with REALDB=compose and REALDB_REQUIRED=1 realdb-gate always, after the other two Passes when realdb passed, or was skipped because nothing database-facing changed; fails otherwise. The decision is testbed/gate.py. This is the check to require.

The paths that make realdb run on a pull request:

packages/sdk/**
packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/adapters/**
packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/indexing/**
packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/storage/**
packages/nl2sql/src/nl2sql/schema/**
packages/nl2sql/tests/realdb/**
testbed/**
.github/workflows/realdb.yml

To run it by hand: Actions, "Real databases", "Run workflow", or gh workflow run realdb.yml --ref main.

The unit job in test.yml runs pytest -m "not integration and not realdb".

The scripts under testbed/ have their own unit tests, which need no database: packages/nl2sql/tests/unit/test_testbed.py (the wide schema, the checksums, skipping what is there, and the gate), packages/nl2sql/tests/unit/test_realdb_fixtures.py (the skip, the failure under REALDB_REQUIRED=1, and the variables) and packages/nl2sql/tests/unit/test_testbed_vm.py (scripts/testbed.py, against a fake gcloud on PATH).

docs.title: The GCP VM
docs.text:
The same compose file also runs on one small VM, nl2sql-testbed in project nl2sql-testbed-261014, zone us-central1-a. It is started for a session and stopped after it. There are no GitHub-to-GCP credentials: the owner, or an agent the owner asks, runs it by hand, at least once before each release.

Setting Value Machine e2-standard-2 (2 vCPU, 8 GB: SQL Server alone wants 2 GB), Debian 12 Docker Installed with the compose plugin by the VM's startup script on its first boot Disk 30 GB standard persistent disk. It keeps the images and the data volumes while the VM is stopped, so a later session skips the load. External IP Ephemeral, for outbound traffic only (image pulls, sample downloads). It is released, and free, while the VM is stopped. Network Its own VPC, nl2sql-testbed, so none of the default network's open rules apply. One firewall rule admits TCP 22, 15432, 13306 and 11433 from IAP's range 35.235.240.0/20 only: no database port is public. Access IAP: gcloud compute ssh and scp with --tunnel-through-iap, and gcloud compute start-iap-tunnel for the three servers Passwords Secret Manager: testbed-postgres-root-password, testbed-mysql-root-password and testbed-mssql-root-password

docs.title: scripts/testbed.py
docs.text:
You need the Google Cloud CLI, logged in (gcloud auth login) as an account with the access listed below. The script is Python so that it runs the same on Windows and Linux; it finds gcloud on PATH.

python scripts/testbed.py run -- pytest -m realdb    # the usual way: up, the command, down
python scripts/testbed.py up                         # or step by step
python scripts/testbed.py status
python scripts/testbed.py down
Command What it does up Reads the three passwords from Secret Manager into memory, starts the VM, copies testbed/ to it (never a local testbed/.env), waits up to five minutes for Docker (the first boot installs it), runs docker compose up -d --wait there with TESTBED_BIND=0.0.0.0, then opens the three IAP tunnels in the background and waits until localhost:15432, 13306 and 11433 answer. The first session loads the samples, which takes several minutes. run -- <cmd> up, then <cmd> with REALDB_POSTGRES, REALDB_MYSQL and REALDB_MSSQL pointing at the tunnels, then down in a finally: also after Ctrl-C, a failing command or a failed up. It exits with the command's code. down Closes the tunnels it opened, runs docker compose stop on the VM so every server shuts down cleanly, then stops the VM. Stopping the VM alone kills SQL Server, and the next session then waits for its databases to recover. If the servers cannot be stopped within three minutes (the VM is unreachable or already stopped), it says so and stops the VM anyway. Safe to run again. status The VM's state, how long it has been running, and whether each tunnel answers. Never a password.

--project, --zone and --instance override the defaults above.

The passwords reach the VM on the stdin of the docker compose command, so they live only in that command's environment there, and reach <cmd> through its own environment. They are never written to a file, put on a command line or printed, and the script never changes its own environment. The tunnels' process ids are kept in nl2sql-testbed/tunnels.json in the system's temporary folder, so a later down can close them.

Every gcloud compute ssh and scp call passes --strict-host-key-checking=no and --tunnel-through-iap. Right after a start, the first connection can fail while the VM boots and its new SSH key propagates (plink says Remote side unexpectedly closed network connection); the copy and the Docker wait retry such a connection failure, and only that, up to five times about a minute in all, then give up, and run still stops the VM.

On Windows, gcloud uses PuTTY's plink and pscp, and by default answers their host-key question by feeding them y on stdin instead of passing the caller's stdin on. The copy and the Docker wait keep that default, which stores the VM's host key in PuTTY's cache; the docker compose step sets CLOUDSDK_SSH_PUTTY_FORCE_CONNECT=false in gcloud's environment only, so the passwords on its stdin reach the VM. OpenSSH ignores the setting.

The script writes that stdin as bytes, one password per line ending in a bare newline: in text mode Windows would end each line with a carriage return, and the servers would be initialised with every password plus \r while the tests use the password alone (MySQL then answers 1045 and SQL Server 18456). The command on the VM also drops a trailing carriage return from each password it reads. A server keeps the password its data volume was created with, so if one was ever initialised with a wrong password, drop the volumes once while the VM is up, then down and up again, which loads the samples afresh:

gcloud compute ssh nl2sql-testbed --project=nl2sql-testbed-261014 --zone=us-central1-a --tunnel-through-iap \
  --command="sudo TESTBED_POSTGRES_PASSWORD=unused TESTBED_MYSQL_PASSWORD=unused TESTBED_MSSQL_PASSWORD=unused docker compose -f testbed/docker-compose.yml down -v"

After up on its own, remember down: a running VM bills by the hour. If the script is killed hard or the VM is started by hand, the nightly stop job below stops it at 03:00 UTC. That stop does not stop the servers first, so SQL Server is killed; the next up then waits while it recovers its databases, which mssql-init allows for.

docs.title: Cost controls
docs.text: Control Why The VM is stopped whenever no session runs A running VM bills by the hour Ephemeral external IP only Released, and free, while stopped No public database port; IAP's range only Nothing else can reach the servers run always stops the VM in a finally A failed test cannot leave it running The nightly stop at 03:00 UTC The backstop for everything above A budget of $10 a month with alerts The last line Item Approximate cost (check the billing report after the first month) Stopped the 30 GB disk: about $1 to $2 a month Running about $0.07 an hour The scheduler job free: one job is inside Cloud Scheduler's free tier

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
The owner's account holds roles/owner on the project, which covers both the set-up below and scripts/testbed.py. Anyone else who runs the script needs:

Role For roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1 starting, stopping and describing the VM, and the SSH key gcloud compute ssh adds to it roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor --tunnel-through-iap and start-iap-tunnel roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor on the three secrets the passwords

docs.title: One-time set-up
docs.text:
Nothing in the repository creates cloud resources. The owner runs these once, in a bash shell (Git Bash on Windows) logged in to gcloud. The three secrets already exist.

PROJECT=nl2sql-testbed-261014
REGION=us-central1
ZONE=us-central1-a
VM=nl2sql-testbed
STOPPER=testbed-stopper@$PROJECT.iam.gserviceaccount.com

# 1. The APIs.
gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com iap.googleapis.com cloudscheduler.googleapis.com \
    billingbudgets.googleapis.com --project=$PROJECT

# 2. A network of its own, so the default network's open SSH and RDP rules do not apply.
gcloud compute networks create nl2sql-testbed --subnet-mode=custom --project=$PROJECT
gcloud compute networks subnets create nl2sql-testbed --network=nl2sql-testbed \
    --region=$REGION --range=10.10.0.0/24 --project=$PROJECT

# 3. The one inbound rule: SSH and the three servers, from IAP's range only.
gcloud compute firewall-rules create nl2sql-testbed-allow-iap --network=nl2sql-testbed \
    --direction=INGRESS --action=ALLOW --rules=tcp:22,tcp:15432,tcp:13306,tcp:11433 \
    --source-ranges=35.235.240.0/20 --target-tags=nl2sql-testbed --project=$PROJECT

# 4. The VM: e2-standard-2, Debian 12, a 30 GB standard disk, an ephemeral external IP,
#    no service account. Its startup script installs Docker and the compose plugin once.
#    printf writes it with LF line endings, which an inline script typed in Git Bash on
#    Windows does not get: with CRLF the VM fails to run it (exit 127) and Docker never arrives.
printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' \
    'command -v docker >/dev/null || curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh' > startup.sh
gcloud compute instances create $VM --project=$PROJECT --zone=$ZONE \
    --machine-type=e2-standard-2 --image-family=debian-12 --image-project=debian-cloud \
    --boot-disk-size=30GB --boot-disk-type=pd-standard \
    --network=nl2sql-testbed --subnet=nl2sql-testbed --tags=nl2sql-testbed \
    --no-service-account --no-scopes \
    --metadata-from-file=startup-script=startup.sh
gcloud compute instances stop $VM --zone=$ZONE --project=$PROJECT    # stopped until a session needs it

# 5. The nightly stop: a service account that may only stop this VM, and a scheduler job
#    that calls the Compute Engine API with its token at 03:00 UTC.
gcloud iam service-accounts create testbed-stopper --display-name="Stops the test-bed VM" --project=$PROJECT
gcloud iam roles create testbedStopper --project=$PROJECT --title="Test-bed stopper" \
    --permissions=compute.instances.stop --stage=GA
gcloud compute instances add-iam-policy-binding $VM --zone=$ZONE --project=$PROJECT \
    --member=serviceAccount:$STOPPER --role=projects/$PROJECT/roles/testbedStopper
gcloud scheduler jobs create http nl2sql-testbed-nightly-stop --project=$PROJECT --location=$REGION \
    --schedule="0 3 * * *" --time-zone=Etc/UTC --http-method=POST \
    --uri=https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/$PROJECT/zones/$ZONE/instances/$VM/stop \
    --oauth-service-account-email=$STOPPER \
    --oauth-token-scope=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform

# 6. The budget: $10 a month, with alerts at 50%, 90% and 100%.
BILLING=$(gcloud billing projects describe $PROJECT --format='value(billingAccountName)')
gcloud billing budgets create --billing-account=${BILLING#billingAccounts/} \
    --display-name="nl2sql test bed" --budget-amount=10USD \
    --filter-projects=projects/$PROJECT \
    --threshold-rule=percent=0.5 --threshold-rule=percent=0.9 --threshold-rule=percent=1.0

To check the set-up, run python scripts/testbed.py run -- pytest -m realdb. To check the nightly job, start the VM with python scripts/testbed.py up, run gcloud scheduler jobs run nl2sql-testbed-nightly-stop --location=$REGION --project=$PROJECT, and python scripts/testbed.py status should then show it stopped; finish with python scripts/testbed.py down to close the tunnels.
